  - **Read plainly.**
    - *Kenya: more like the place, and it still does not hold together.* Seven in ten of the employed are informal (the profile's target is 84%; the gap is the own-account kinds the town cannot hold and farming). The contributory charges collect a third of what they did. Fewer households are unhoused (7 against 27) and less demand goes unmet (5.9% against 14.8%). **Rent is what stops it, and nothing here was going to move it:** the median renting household still pays 85% of its income (it was 75%; the median such household is now one factory wage, 7,121 shillings a fortnight, against a two-bedroom flat at 13,000 a month). That is the profile's own rents and its dwelling mix (three one-bedroom, seven two-bedroom and two three-bedroom flats a block, the first profile's mix at Nakuru's urban rents), its author's to restate; a trader's earnings come to about a wage (about 16,000 shillings a month drawn), so a household with a trader in it is no better placed than one with a job. The town also floods (1,300 to 3,400 acts refused a town for water, before and after alike): the river track's work. And fewer people come: arrivals fell from about 118 to 60 a town, because newcomers come for posted jobs and employers post fewer.
    - *India: holds together, as it did before* (rent 31% of income). A quarter of employees are by the day, half the jobs unregistered, and 23 traders. **Registering a job changes no payment there:** the profile's law takes nothing from pay at these wages and has no contribution, so 205 unregistered jobs differ from registered ones by a note. The provident fund and the state insurance are what registration brings in India, and are the author's to add. Unemployment by the new measure reads nought: the traders are extra work beside the same employers' jobs.
    - *Brazil: a fault, found and fixed.* The first runs had demand unmet at 10.4% (3.1 to 15.5) where main has 1.8%. Followed in one town, fortnight by fortnight: the traders were supplied at first (they and the shops both buy from the town's factories, which undercut the world market's imports), and their customers were counted in the shops' expected sales; but **what the world market is given to take of the factories' output was still reckoned as their output less the shops' purchases alone**, so the traders' purchases were promised abroad. From about day 100 the factories filled a quarter of what shops ordered (9,600 of 60,800 items in one four-week span) and two thirds of what traders ordered, and every seller ran short together. The export figure now leaves the town what its shops and its traders are both expected to buy (generator 0.36.2; one line, and only where a profile states own-account work). Brazil's unmet demand is 2.5% (1.3 to 4.3), Kenya's fell from 9.6% to 5.9% and Mexico's from 3.7% to 1.6%; the tables above are after the fix. Not looked into further: a shop turns to the world market only when every factory has come up short within the week, which with ten factories is slow; that is main's rule and was left. More people draw the payment for those out of work (48 a town against 16): by agreement, fewer are in jobs.
    - *Mexico:* 45% informal against a target of 46.5%, which is the registered share doing nearly all of it.
  - **What went to the citizen redesign** (docs/design/ai-citizens.md, Open, 5): taking up own-account work when out of work, and looking from it; giving it up for a job or when custom fails; choosing it; a household deciding who does what, and unpaid family help; services sold to households; a business that makes what it sells, and a plot; weighing a registered job against an unregistered one and a standing wage against work by the day; turning up each morning to be picked. In a run nobody starts such a business and none closes for want of custom.
  - **Not verified.**
    - The research agent's reading of each source (the ILOSTAT files, the PLFS report's tables 19, 36 and 39, SIDRA tables 4097 and 8529, the ENOE bulletin): its figures were taken as reported, with the URL, and not re-read. KNBS's own tables could not be opened at all; the Kenyan figures are the ILO's.
    - A business following its owner's home, and closing when its owner leaves: seen in the Kenyan runs (6 to 10 moves and 1 to 4 closures a town; in the one town looked at, the businesses' refusals fell from about 7,400 to about 130) and held by no test of its own (the test town had no move in ninety days).
    - Run time: a Kenyan town of 1,000 with 85 businesses of one took 146 to 170 seconds for 180 days against 134 to 145 on main, on a machine other work was loading.
    - `bun run test:all` (the merge's). On the branch before main was merged in: the fast tier, 664 pass; the fast tier and what the change reaches, 812 pass, 0 fail, across 124 files (after: the item below).
  - **Since, with main at f6ac4ee (2026-10-09; the office work, the opening adopted budget, the law-text fixes):** merged, main's offices, budget and law figures as main has them. The first profile's 1,000-person month, seed 1: 5be63866badc311a on the merged tree, which is main's. Fast tier 773 pass; the fast tier and what the change reaches, 899 pass, 0 fail, across 139 files. generator 0.39.0. **Not redone on the merged tree:** the four places' tables above (both sides were measured before the merge, on bea2d7b and on this branch as it stood; the three new tests, which run such towns for 75 to 100 days, pass on it). A business of one issues none of main's forms and takes no directions: it is no office.
  - **Left as it is, and known:** the business of an owner who dies is run by nobody (its prices stay up, an order to it is never answered); a hand by the day reads low on a job board read in order of pay; an unregistered job pays the same wage as a registered one; someone in an unregistered job claims a contributory payment each month and is refused each month; no pitch fee.
  - **Revisit if** a profile's author needs a registered share that differs between firms of one kind (then it is a draw by firm, for towns large enough); an inspector is built (then the share moves, and `compliance` is the employer's answer to it); households buy services (then the kinds not held can be, and the "drawn in jobs" rule goes); businesses of one make a month's run several times slower (they did not: about a tenth); the opening expectation of custom (every seller the same) is shown to leave shops short of hands where traders are few; or the citizen redesign lands (entry and exit are written once, there).

- **A pilot stopped at a usage limit is parked, and the queue goes on** (2026-10-09; `scripts/pilot-queue.ts`, `orchestrator/src/pilot-state.ts`, `scripts/pilot-wave.ts`; closes gap 21 of wave 2's plan, the half of it that is the queue's).
  - **The fault.** A queue waited on the pilot it was at. On the night of 2026-10-09 (`runs/live-check-2-2026-10-09/`) a pilot with Codex seats stopped on day 16 at the Codex subscription's limit and was asked again every 20 minutes for hours; in the other lane a pilot on Claude seats sat at day 0 for an hour for the same limit, because its translator was a Codex model, with two pilots behind it that needed no Codex at all. The owner's word that morning: "I don't have an issue using codex when it's available, but when it runs out, it shouldn't block things."
  - **What a queue does now.** A pilot that stops at a usage limit is parked: left stopped where it was (a run stops cleanly at a limit and resumes from its log, as before), and the queue takes the next entry it can. A limit belongs to a sign-in, not a pilot: the stop's own words say whose it was (each adapter names itself; words that name none count against every sign-in the entry uses), and an entry needs its seats' model's and its translator's. So what is skipped while a limit stands is every entry that needs that sign-in, not only the one that met it: a second Codex pilot is not started just to stop on day 0, and a Claude session limit, which every pilot of a Claude lane needs, makes the queue wait as it did before. The rule for what is next is one line (`nextPilot`): the first entry in the queue's order that is not settled and needs no sign-in still being waited out. Because it is the queue's order, a parked pilot is come back to before anything later in the queue as soon as its wait (`--wait`, 20 minutes) is over; if the limit still stands it is parked again and the queue goes on again. With only parked pilots left the queue waits for the first such time and says so once.
  - **Seen by whoever runs the wave:** the status log (`parked at a usage limit on day N (codex: …)`), an alert (`PARKED`, with the sign-in; and one each time it is tried again), `<queue>.parked.json` beside the queue file, and `pilot-wave.ts status`, which lists a queue's parked pilots first and marks each (`PARKED at a usage limit (codex; next try …)`).
  - **Parking is the default for every sign-in** (the coordinator's instruction after the owner's word; no list of which providers block). `--no-park` is the old behaviour.
  - **Not built, by the owner's decision the same morning:** a fallback translator (a second translator a run switches to when the first is at its limit). The translator a pilot needs is to be a model that is not behind the Codex sign-in, so nothing needs a fallback; and the role is the trained translator's soon.
  - **Tests** (`orchestrator/test/pilot-queue.test.ts`, `pilot-wave.test.ts`): whose limit a stop names; the rule for what is next (a parked pilot first again when its wait is over; the earlier of two waits; nothing left); and the queue itself run against a stand-in for the CLI (`OIKOS_QUEUE_CLI`, which exists for this) whose Codex runs stop at a limit twice: the Codex pilot is parked on day 16, the Claude pilot behind it starts at once and finishes first, the second Codex pilot is not started until the first is through, every pilot ends done and none is run twice; `--no-park` waits as before; the note and the status line of a parked pilot.
  - **Contracts:** none (the queue file's shape is unchanged).
  - **Not verified:** a real limit (the stand-in writes the words the two adapters write; the Claude words are those of the night's log); two queues of one wave both parked on one sign-in (each waits and tries on its own clock, so the sign-in is asked twice as often); a resume of a long parked run that meets the limit again at once (each try replays the log first: minutes for a run of months).
  - **Revisit if** tries against a standing limit cost something (then a parked pilot's wait should grow, or read the reset time the limit's words sometimes give), or a wave wants one clock for a sign-in across its queues.

- **What seats needed and could not find out** (2026-10-09; the model seat 0.13.0; live check, finding 4; `participants/src/llm/render.ts`, `participant.ts`; tests `participants/test/seat-finding-out.test.ts`, `seat-papers.test.ts`). Each case decided within the knowing design (docs/design/knowing.md), and why.
  - **Who holds a post.** Who's who answered "post: Finance officer (finance), for city: Finance officer": the holder was a system of the town's whose title is the post's, so the answer named nobody, and a mayor concluded the post "has no named holder". A town publishes who its officers are, and the look-up already returns it. It now reads: a person, "held by Ada Okafor"; an office that runs itself, "filled: the office answers for itself, with no person named to it (write to the post, by its id: finance)"; nobody, "vacant: nobody holds it". No contract change: the answer is read from what the look-up gives (`held_by` equal to the post's title is an office held by its own system).
  - **A name that finds nothing.** Six names asked, two shown, not a word of the other four. Who's who is open to anyone, so that it has no entry under a name tells the asker nothing that was not there to be looked up: "Nothing is entered under: council clerk, roads office, parks office. (A name is matched whole: ...)". A register asked of its keeper already says "Nothing found." to a question that names its subject, which is all it should say.
  - **People as ids only** ("c0297 (c0297), a person"). The generated town gives its people no names: a person's name is their id. That is the generator's (another's work, and a question for the citizens' redesign); here the id is said once ("c0297, a person"). A seat learns a name where one exists by looking the person up, as before.
  - **A paper by its id; a kind by its plain word.** Done with the look into papers (the entry three above): `paper`, the one id in `named`, or `find` by id; "employment agreement" finds the six, and "employment" is answered with them as kinds like it.
  - **Going to see.** No seat sent anyone anywhere in four pilots. The offer was a clause two thirds of the way through the `look` tool's description, and the `do` tool told a seat that `look` is for looking things up in files. Where a seat has places to send someone to, `look` now begins "Look into one of your reports yourself, or send someone to go and see a place, when you choose.", and `do` ends "To find out how a place stands, send someone to go and see it: that is a look too." (the design's words for it, docs/design/knowing.md section 9). A seat with nowhere to send anyone reads neither. Of the three seats piloted only the mayor has such a report; whether finance and planning should is the generator's.
  - **Left as designed:** who owns what a dead resident held (the land register answers by lot and by title, and by holder only to the bodies a world lists: a seat writes to the registry, as the sol planning seat did).
  - **Contracts:** none. **Text a seat reads that changed:** who's who's lines for a post and for names not found; the first sentence of `look` and the last of `do`, for a seat with places to send someone to (a seat without reads what it read; the writers' instructions are unchanged).
  - **Not verified:** that seats now send someone (no model was called).
  - **Revisit if** a wave still shows no visits (then the tool is the wrong place for it, and going to see wants a tool of its own), or when people have names.

- **No id of the platform's own reaches a seat** (2026-10-09; the model seat 0.13.0; live check, finding 6; `participants/src/llm/render.ts` (`WhoIs`), `participant.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `translator/src/preview.ts`; tests `participants/test/seat-names.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/seat-sight.test.ts`).
  - **The fault.** A participant's id is the platform's handle for whoever acts (`mayor-system`, `bank-payments-system`, `c0297-self`). Letters arrived "From mayor-system", papers were "from finance-system", what waited to be confirmed was `draft.mayor-system.1`, and seats then wrote to `mayor-system`.
  - **Who someone is in the world.** The run answers, for any id, who that is in the world's terms (`whoIs`): an office's system is the post it holds, with the post's title and whose post it is; a person's seat is the person; a post, an organisation and a person are themselves, with what they are called. It is read from the run's own cast as it stands (posts change hands).
  - **Where it is used.** A letter is signed: "From Council clerk (council-clerk), Town of Millbrook (city) (year 1, day 3)", "From Payments (bank-payments), Millbrook Savings Bank (bank)", "From c0297". A paper's writer, where nobody is spoken for, is the post or the person. Then, over everything a seat is shown (each report, what is on file in its instructions, a draft's preview and its reference), any participant's id still standing in someone's words is put as the id the world knows that party by: `draft.mayor-system.1` is shown as `draft.mayor.1`. On the way in, a reference to something waiting to be confirmed is read back as the seat's own draft of that number; a letter to a post or an organisation by its id needed no mapping (the engine has always taken them), and one to a participant's id still goes.
  - **Names in a preview.** Where the seat's own knowledge has no name for someone it names by id, the preview takes what they are called from the same source: "addressed to Town of Millbrook (city), which you act for", "You will write to Council clerk (council-clerk)", "ask Millbrook Savings Bank (bank)". A name is what a letter's signature or the town's own list of offices would give; nothing else about anyone is told.
  - **Why this reveals nothing.** Who wrote a letter or a paper is on it. Putting a party's world id where its platform id stood names the same party, by the id a seat could already write to.
  - **Limits.** The sweep of free text knows a participant's id by the form generated worlds give it (ending `-system` or `-self`); a world written by hand with other ids has its letters' signatures and papers' writers put right (those go by `whoIs`, not by form) but not an id quoted inside someone's words. The log keeps the draft's summary as it was made; what the seat read is in its transcript, with the ids as it saw them.
  - **Contracts:** none. A draft's id in the log, the sign-off and the pilot report is unchanged (`draft.<participant>.<n>`). **Text a seat reads that changed:** the line a letter is headed with; the writer of a paper; the reference of a draft.
  - **Not verified:** a run in which a post changes hands mid-run; any model's use of the new references.
  - **Revisit if** a hand-written world is piloted (then the sweep wants the cast's ids, not their form), or when people have names (then a person's letter is signed with one).

- **Three smaller things from the live check** (2026-10-09; the model seat 0.13.0; finding 11; tests in `participants/test/seat-letters.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/pilot-report.test.ts`).
  - **"From day 1 to day 1"** in a debrief whose notebook ran to day 8: the span was taken from the days the seat acted in the world, so a sitting spent on its notebook did not count. It is the days it sat (fixed with the letters' count, two entries above).
  - **"stopped: aborted (stopped at 1036800), reached its until"** of a run that finished. A run cut at `until`, short of the world's whole length, ends "aborted" in its log by the log's contract, which has two endings; that is left alone. The pilot report now says "finished: it ran to its until" for such a run (and for one that completed), and carries `finished: true`.
  - **The notebook's room.** 4,000 characters were full by day 5 for the seats that write most, and seven changes were refused for room; a seat was told only the count used. It holds 8,000 now: a seat that keeps a line a day for a half-year has about 44 characters a line at 4,000 and 88 at 8,000, and the cost is at most 4,000 more characters in an opening prompt of 10,000 to 40,000. From 6,000 used it is told, with its notebook: "it is nearly full, with N left. To make room before something won't fit, strike out what is settled (change the passage to nothing), or write the notebook afresh, shorter." The tool's description says how to make room too.
  - **Text a seat reads that changed:** the notebook tool's description (8,000; how to make room) and the line under its notebook; the writers' instructions follow.
  - **Not verified:** that 8,000 is enough for a half-year (no model was called; pilot 7's year-long mayors kept within 4,000, sol's seats did not).
  - **Revisit if** a wave's reports still show `notebook_not_changed` for room.

- **A draft that fails its own checks is not put to the seat as its mistake** (2026-10-09; the model seat 0.13.0; live check, finding 7; `translator/src/index.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `participants/src/llm/participant.ts`; tests `translator/test/ask-again.test.ts`, `participants/test/seat-letters.test.ts`). The translator's model is untouched and nothing was retrained.
  - **The fault.** For a budget proposal with a staff line, the trained translator answered `form(... kind=budget, parks="c0007", ...)` at sureness 0.109 against a cut-off of 0.1. The resolver's answer to that call, "not an amount: c0007. Please say it another way.", was passed to the seat as "A note on your request:", two days later, at the head of its next sitting among everything else. The seat had named no such amount, and in that sitting said it had filed the proposal.
  - **Whose words the figure was.** When a draft cannot be read at a figure (an amount, a length of time, a count), the translator's wrapper now asks whether the seat wrote it. If the seat's request has those very words, the seat is asked about its own words: ""about three hundred or so", as you wrote it, could not be read as an amount. Please say it again with that written as a plain figure." If it does not, the call is at fault: the fault goes on record against the call (`invalid`: "the call gave something the request did not: ..."), the translator is asked once more with that as its feedback, and if it fails again the seat is asked for its request again in terms of the form it can see, with nothing of the failed draft: "It could not be set out on the council proposal form from what you said: the form takes these amounts: environment, parks, roads, services, staff. Please say it again, giving each one you mean as a figure and leaving out any you don't." Both are recorded as an asking back.
  - **Marked as about that request, and that nothing was filed.** Every note on a request that came to nothing now begins with the request in the seat's own words and what became of it: "About what you asked for ("File the year 1 budget proposal: ..."): nothing was filed or done." and then what is asked. The heading "A note on your request:" is gone: nothing a seat is told depends on a heading to say what it is about.
  - **At once.** A seat that said it was done for now in the same answer used to leave, and read the note days later. Now the sitting goes on for one more turn (once a sitting): the request's result carries the note, and "done for now" is answered "Not yet: something you asked for in the same answer was not filed or done, so the sitting goes on. See what came back from it, and say it again or leave it; then say when you're done." If it happens again in that sitting the seat goes as it asked, and the note is the first thing under its notebook at its next: "When you were last here, after you had finished: about what you asked for (...): nothing was filed or done. ...".
  - **Text a seat reads that changed:** those sentences. **Contracts:** none.
  - **Not verified:** the trained model's second answer to the feedback (it may give the same call; then the seat is asked by the form, which is the point); a real model's use of the extra turn.
  - **Revisit if** the count of such ask-backs in a wave is high (then the cut-off for sureness, which is the translator's, is the thing to look at), or if seats answer the extra turn by saying done again without reading it.

- **Two faults of the mock seat** (2026-10-09; mock 0.6.0; `participants/src/llm/mock.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`; tests `participants/test/mock.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/seat-sight.test.ts`).
  - **A look asked for while reading what was missed was dropped.** The mock's code brain reads every observation the seat was shown between sittings; a look it asked for while doing so was thrown away, and a brain asks for each thing once and waits, so it was never made (a mock mayor never sent anyone to see a lot, and built no park). Such looks are now made at the sitting, with the brain's look of that moment if it has one; more than one answer takes (eight) are made at the next turn.
  - **The clerk that "counts no votes".** Not reproduced as a miscount: in three runs here (the small town and the 1,000-person one; mock clerk with code councillors, and with mock councillors and mayor) the mock clerk published "Passed: 5 for, 0 against." with all five votes. What a twenty-day run showed was no result at all, and the cause is the mock's rhythm: it said "done for now" with no days, so every mock office sat weekly whatever it was. A proposal filed on day 1 was seen on day 8 and put to the vote then; votes came on day 14; the count came on day 21. The mock now says it is back when its brain would next look in (the time the brain gave, or its module's own rhythm): the same town has the ballot on day 1, the votes on day 3 and the result on day 15, as with a clerk run by code.
  - **What a real model in the clerk's seat meets.** It is shown the proposal ("Council clerk: Proposals (1 new)"), the votes tallied by ballot ("5 votes on rec.527: yes 5"), and the office's own forms for a ballot, a result and an adopted budget (the offices' forms work), so it can put a proposal to the vote, count and declare. What it also meets is the same rhythm: only a letter brings a seat back before the days it gave, and a filed proposal, a vote and a closing ballot are not letters. The `done_for_now` tool now says so: "sooner, at the next sitting, if someone writes to you (a letter: a paper filed with your office, a vote or a notice does not bring you back sooner, so give fewer days when you are waiting on one)". Whether a paper filed with an office should bring its seat back like a letter is not decided here: it would be truer to an office that opens its in-tray each working day, and it would add sittings (and model calls) to every seat whose office is filed with often, the mayor's most of all. For Naz.
  - **The hash of a mock-seat run moves** with the mock's rhythm (its offices act on other days). A run with no mock seat is untouched.
  - **Also:** a figure whose unit is written "basis points" reads as a percentage (a law's "majority": "50%").
  - **Not verified:** the coordinator's first report of "0 for, 0 against" (not seen here; if it recurs, the run's log has the clerk's prompts, which show the votes it was given).
  - **Revisit if** a model clerk in a wave leaves a ballot uncounted for more than a few days after it closes.

- **A seat whose model call fails sits again the next working day, and is told it missed a sitting** (2026-10-09; live check 2, finding 1; `participants/src/llm/participant.ts`, `participants/src/llm/call.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `participants/src/llm/codex.ts`, `claude-code.ts`, `orchestrator/src/pilot-state.ts`, `pilot-report.ts`, `scripts/pilot-queue.ts`; tests `participants/test/llm-participant.test.ts`, `adapters.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/run-machinery.test.ts`, `pilot-report.test.ts`, `pilot-queue.test.ts`).
  - **The fault.** In pilot 3 three seat calls got no answer in 3 x 180 s, and none of those seats observed again for the five or six days left. The cause: a step that failed never told the engine when its unit was due, so the unit fell back to the seat's own rhythm (`cadence_days`, a week) counted from the failed wake: day 25 plus seven is past the run's end. Any failure in the last week of any run emptied the seat for the rest of it; earlier ones emptied it for up to a week.
  - **Now.** The participant treats the failure as a sitting it was not at. Everything it was to be shown is kept (the report, what was waiting, what its last answer's acts showed), the sitting is closed, and the failure carries when it sits next: the next working day's sitting, or a day on for a seat with no office hours, whatever days it had last given. The run finishes the unit's wake with that time. At that sitting the first thing under its notebook is "You missed your sitting on year 1, day 25: you were not at your desk, and nothing was read or done that day. What had come in for it is set out below, with what has come in since." (or, where the call that failed came after an answer: "Your sitting on year 1, day 25 was cut short: you were away from your desk after your last answer there, and nothing more was done that day. How what you had asked for went is set out below, with what has come in since."). Nothing of models or the platform is said.
  - **Why a day is missed, and not asked again within the hour.** The adapter has already tried three times over nine minutes; a person who does not come in is in the next day. Trying again at the next tick would also stop a run for "model out of reach" after one bad quarter of an hour, where three working days running is the better measure.
  - **Noted, counted, alerted.** The log has `sitting_missed` (day, whether midway, when it is back, why) beside the run's `participant_error` (now with `back_at`). The queue alerts each one as it happens ("SITTING MISSED ..."). The pilot report counts them by seat and, if there is any, begins "NOT A FINISHED PILOT: a seat sat for less than its run. ..." (read from old logs too: on pilot 3's log it names all three seats and the day each last sat).
  - **A limit that looks like a time-out.** Why pilot 3's three were retried as time-outs cannot be told from its log: the Codex adapter read what the CLI said for a limit only when the call had not run out of time, and kept none of it when it had. Now what had come by the time limit is read the same way (so a limit reported and then waited under stops the run as a limit, at the first attempt), and a call that ran out of time records the last thing the CLI said. The Claude Code adapter does the same. A provider that limits by saying nothing at all cannot be told from a slow model call by call; three calls in a row unanswered stops the run as before ("the model can't be reached"), and the queue now waits and resumes such a pilot as it does at a limit ("MODEL NOT ANSWERING ...") where it used to count a failure and leave the pilot after two.
  - **Contracts:** none. **Text a seat reads:** the two sentences above.
  - **Not verified:** what the Codex CLI prints while limited and hanging (no model was called); whether those three calls were a limit or a slow model (planning answered between them, which points to slow).
  - **Revisit if** missed sittings cluster on long prompts (then the time limit per call is the thing to raise), or a wave shows runs stopping as unreachable and resuming into the same wall (then wait longer between tries).

- **An office knows its own staff, and its own forms say what they are for** (2026-10-09; live check 2, finding 5; generator 0.38.1; `participants/src/behaviour/roster.ts`, `staffed` on five modules, `papers.ts` (`does`), `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `participants/src/llm/participant.ts`, `translator/src/preview.ts` and `knowledge.ts`, `worlds/generator/generate.ts`; test `orchestrator/test/office-staff.test.ts`; docs/behaviour/office-papers.md, "An office's own staff").
  - **The fault.** The works seat of pilot 4 had no crew, and nothing it was shown said so: the depot read "0 people (room for 20)", which is who was in the room. Its job advertisement form was on file with the words "A paper of the office's own: filled in, it is issued as the form sets it out", beside a staffing *direction* form that only the mayor can give; it took the second for the way to get staff. Two standing work orders, no collection, 301 complaints.
  - **The roster.** A seat in an office that employs is shown "## Works manager: Staff of your office": the posts and by what (a budget line at the office's rate of pay, or its establishment), who is in each and since when, how many are vacant, and, with nobody in post, that the staff's work is done by nobody and that the office takes on its own staff beginning with its job advertisement form. At its first sitting and whenever the list has changed. It is the office's own papers (`mine`): the organisation's employment agreements in the office's role and its adopted budget, read as the office's code reads them. No new channel, nothing asked of the engine, no change in a town without a model seat.
  - **An order of nobody says so.** The standing work order's preview adds "There is nobody in the post whose work this is: your office has no works crew in post, so nothing is done under it until someone is taken on." and the same is said with its result once confirmed.
  - **Forms, a line each.** A form of an office's own now reads "<name>. <what issuing it does> Filled in by the <post>, of the office's own accord (nobody's direction or leave is needed): filled in, it is issued as the form sets it out." Fourteen forms have their sentence (works, environment, registry, planning, inspector, tribunal, police and the job advertisement every employer shares); the rest keep their name alone, with whose it is.
  - **Office by office.** Works, environment, clinic, school, police: roster and forms. Registry, inspector, planning, tribunal member and registrar: no staff; forms with their purpose. Rates, water, energy: no forms of their own and no employees in the world (their routine's staff post is code), so nothing to show and nothing missing.
  - **Contract change:** `contracts/module.schema.json`, `Issued.does` (optional string). A module's `staffed` is a function of its parameters, like `issuesWith`, and is not in the manifest.
  - **The mock** (20 days, the small town, no crew at start): shown "In post: nobody. Vacant: 1."; advertises on `form(form=job_advertisement, ...)` on day 1; offers employment on day 4; shown "In post (1): c0134, since year 1, day 4, under rec.430." on day 5; waste is collected. It also shows the mock taking on three for one post (it advertises twice on day 1), which the roster reports as "2 more in post than there are posts": the mock's, left.
  - **Not verified:** a real model reading it. Names: a person with no name on file is shown by id.
  - **Revisit if** seats take the roster's last sentence as an instruction to hire regardless of budget, or a staffed office appears that `staffed` does not cover (firms' managers have the form but no roster yet).

- **Offices run by code word a sum as money, and a form's length of time in hours and minutes** (2026-10-09; `participants/src/behaviour/firms.ts`, `union.ts`, `institutions.ts`, `bank.ts`, `government.ts`; `participants/src/forms.ts` and `kernel/crates/resolver/src/resolve.rs`).

They write it as the place writes its money. A form's length of time that is not whole days read "3600 seconds"; it reads "1 hour", "1 hour 30 minutes", "45 minutes" in both resolvers, seconds only where nothing rounder fits. Nothing reads a sum back out of these words (the bank's note is recognised by its shape, not its figure).

- **A list is gone through a part at a time, an answer says what was searched, and a paper is set out once** (2026-10-09; live check 2, findings 5 and 11; `participants/src/llm/render.ts`, `participant.ts`; tests `participants/test/seat-looks.test.ts`, `render.test.ts`, `seat-papers.test.ts`).
  - **Paging.** A look into a folder shown as it comes asked its keeper for the newest twenty and said "There may be more: ask for more at once", up to fifty: the works seat's look at its round of 390 addresses gave the same twenty each time. `from_entry` now applies to a list as it does to a long paper: the look asks for as many as one search gives (200), the part from that entry is shown, and every answer that leaves something out says the exact next look ("Entries 21 to 40 of 45. For the next: look again the same way with from_entry: 41."). The same for a list of buildings. Checked for each look a seat can make: papers found, a folder's new papers, a long paper's entries (already paged), places, who's who (named one by one, at most sixteen), places gone to (named).
  - **The limit that remains.** One search gives 200 papers. A list longer than that is reached past its 200th entry only by saying more closely what to find; the answer says so ("there are earlier ones that were not, so this is not everything there"). Paging deeper would need the participant API's search to take a place to start from: a contract change, not made.
  - **What was searched.** Every answer to a look into papers ends with where it looked and how far: "(Looked in "Works manager: Round" (works/round), for: where kind = complaint. Everything kept there was searched: nothing there matches.)", or, where the narrowing is done among the latest papers one search gives, "The latest 200 papers there that could match (year 1, day 202 to year 2, day 36) were read through; there are earlier ones that were not, so this is not everything there." and, with nothing found, "(Not found among those read through, which is not the same as not there: ...)". A folder with nothing new says that what was there before is still there. Who's who says what it enters and that nothing is entered under the name. Places say how much is there to be seen. Nothing is said that the seat's own look did not return: counts and dates are of the papers it was given.
  - **Headings.** Complaints reached the works seat under "Works manager: Budgets (12 new)" (the folder that holds budgets and complaints) and again under "Works-business" (every paper of the town's). A paper that reaches a seat under two headings in one report is now set out once, under the narrower (the one with fewer new papers); and a heading with more than two papers says what came by kind: "(What came: 12 complaints.)". The folder's name is the world's and was left.
  - **Text a seat reads that changed:** the footers of lists, the line of what was searched, the line of what came. **Contracts:** none.
  - **Not verified:** a real model following `from_entry` (the mock does not page).
  - **Revisit if** seats page through whole registers (then a count of what is there, from the keeper, is the thing to give), or a list over 200 is needed whole.

- **A direction from an office to itself, and work asked for with neither how much nor how often** (2026-10-09; live check 2, findings 3 and 14, and the Claude translator check of the same day; translator prompt 0.9.1; `translator/src/index.ts`, `preview.ts`, `knowledge.ts`, `resolver.ts`, `participants/src/calls.ts`, `kernel/crates/resolver/src/resolve.rs` and `calls.rs`, `translator/eval/cases.ts` and `run.ts`, `contracts/calls.md`; test `translator/test/own-office.test.ts`).
  - **The fault.** A works seat asked for a standing work order to collect. Two different models, as translator (gpt-6.1-sol twice, Sonnet 5.5 once), wrote the collection direction form, addressed to the seat's own office, and the preview said "Nothing stands in the way right now." The seat declined each time, rightly.
  - **Why two models wrote it.** The prompt says a direction to an office is that office's form filled in where one is listed, and the list a works seat's request goes with has `works_collection, to=works, fields every`: the same matter and the same field as the standing order it wanted. Nothing told the translator that the office named was the asker's own. The prompt's rule, not the models.
  - **Three changes to what the translator is given** (0.9.1), the smallest that say it: in the list of forms, a form that directs an office the asker holds is marked "(a direction to this person's own office: for whoever directs that office, not for this person)"; the standing-work rule gains one sentence, "A form listed below as a direction to this person's own office is never how that is written, whatever the form's fields: that form is for whoever directs the office, and the office's own order to its staff is work(...)."; and three worked examples (a direction on a form, the same matter from the office itself as `work(...)`, a paper of the office's own on its form), which the prompt had none of. Seen cases: `own-collection-order`, `own-collection-routine`, `own-maintain-routine`, asked as the works office (a case may now name the asker's post); `direction-collection` is the mayor's side.
  - **The preview.** Where the seat has the organisation's rule on directions on file (`proc-directions`, published law data) and the post it writes in is not one the rule names, the preview says: "The office will not follow it: by the rule on directions (proc-directions) it takes written directions only from the Mayor (mayor) and the Council clerk (council-clerk), and this one is given as the Works manager (works)." and, for its own office, "A direction is how others direct an office; what its own staff are to do as routine is set by a standing work order on its own file." The line beneath reads "Nothing stops it being filed, and filed it would change nothing, as said above." It says only what the rule says, to a seat that has the rule.
  - **A standing order with no period.** `work(task=maintain, at=...)` with no `every` is read as a job done once, which needs `units`; the seat was asked "How much of it?" four times and gave a period it had not wanted. The question is now "Is this work to be done once, or as a standing routine of your staff? Done once: say how much of it. As a routine: say how often (every day, every week), and it is a standing work order." (both resolvers). The routine's own rhythm was not made a default: a routine has none on record (the office's code sets it daily of its own accord), and giving one would mean a figure in each module, a line in the office's procedure and both resolvers reading it. Left, with the question made answerable.
  - **"once a week"** was not read as a length of time ("not a duration: once a week"), which cost the same seat a request. Both resolvers read it now (and "once every 2 weeks"); `contracts/calls.md` lists it.
  - **Contracts:** `contracts/calls.md`, one more way to write a duration. The kernel's resolver changes by two lines (a question's words; a prefix read); no state changes.
  - **Not verified:** any model under prompt 0.9.1 (none was called): the three seen cases are untested against a model, and so is every other case under the changed prompt. The trained translator knows neither the mark nor the sentence.
  - **Revisit if** a model still writes the direction form for the office's own order (then leave such forms out of the list for whoever holds the office), or seats want "maintain" with no period often enough to give routines a rhythm of their own.

- **Codex when it is available, never something that blocks: the translator, the readers and wave 2 replanned** (2026-10-09; `docs/waves/wave-2/`, `docs/translator-pipeline.md`, `docs/real-models.md`; runs: `runs/translator-eval-claude-2026-10-09/`, `runs/claude-translator-check-2026-10-09/`, `runs/reader-comparison-2026-10-09/`). **This reverses the standing default** of Codex for the driver seat and the translator (CLAUDE.md, "Models": "Real-model runs go through the Codex CLI… The driver seat is `gpt-6.1-sol`, simple narrow work (the translator) `gpt-6-luna`"; and the handover's "gpt-6.1-sol as the translator in runs").
  - **The owner's words, that morning, in order.** "codex is unreliable… we should really not use it much at all anymore." Then: "I don't have an issue using codex when it's available, but when it runs out, it shouldn't block things." Of the Claude plan: "don't worry about limiting yourself with the Claude sub, just use whatever". Of the translator: "use sonnet 5.5 as the backup translator". Of the largest Claude model: "I'd rather use fable in the seats… I don't think it's an appropriate model for the translator". Of profiles: "for some of these profiles, tbh it doesn't matter if they're unoptimal… unoptimal situations should also create good data". Of what it is all for: "a wide spread of good data so that we can finally get the self trained translator model over the line".
  - **What made it** (`runs/live-check-2-2026-10-09/`): the Codex subscription's limit was met 16 minutes into the night's check. A pilot on Codex seats stood on day 16 for two and a quarter hours; a pilot on Claude seats stood at day 0 for an hour because its translator was a Codex model. Wave 2 as planned had a Codex model as translator or seat in 40 of 43 pilots, and the pipeline's default readers were Sonnet 5.5 with gpt-6.1-sol.
  - **Measured: Claude models as the prompt-driven translator** (`oikos translator-eval --model claude-code/<model> --real`, prompt 0.9.0, the held-out set through the code's own path and never opened; right / no draft / wrong draft):

    | Model | Seen (86) | Held out (66) | Real (180) | Reported cost a call | Model seconds a call |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | claude-code/claude-sonnet-5-5 | 80 / 2 / 4 | 61 / 3 / 2 | 163 / 10 / 7 | 0.008 | 2.6 |
    | claude-code/claude-fable-5-1 | 82 / 2 / 2 | 61 / 2 / 3 | 170 / 5 / 5 | 0.038 | 4.4 |
    | claude-code/claude-haiku-5-5 | 82 / 2 / 2 | 57 / 3 / 6 | 147 / 27 / 6 | 0.026 | 3.4 |
    | codex/gpt-6.1-sol, scored again the same day, real only | | | 169 / 5 / 6 | none | |

    The eval needed no change to drive a `claude-code/` model as translator (the adapter's answer schema carries the translator's one tool as it carries a seat's). The Codex window happened to be open, so gpt-6.1-sol was scored once more on the real requests under 0.9.0 and the keys as re-keyed on 2026-10-08: **169, where 175 was recorded under 0.7.3.** Its held-out and seen scores were not run again (64 of 66 and 63 of 64 stand as recorded under the older prompt). Earlier references: gpt-6-luna 44 of 60 held out and 161 real; the trained model 141 real.
  - **Decided (the owner): Sonnet 5.5 alone is the general translator**, with no chain of fallbacks, and Fable 5.1 is not a translator, though it reads the real requests as well as gpt-6.1-sol. Sonnet is 6 of 180 behind sol like for like and 3 of 66 on the held-out set (unlike prompts). The owner's reading, which the numbers fit: part of sol's lead on the real requests is the prompt having been developed with sol as its reference, the real set in view and the held-out set not. In practice Sonnet's misses are mostly an extra ask-back (five of seven "wrong drafts" are a letter's addressee written as a description, `to="the works manager"`, which the resolver asks back on) and about one wrong draft in 180 reaching a sign-off.
  - **Not done, on purpose:** a line in the translator's prompt about naming a post by its id. The 180 real requests are a test set, and wording the prompt to its failures is how the first held-out set was spoiled. **To try against fresh requests from the wave**, with a line about a standing work order against a direction to an office (below).
  - **In the loop** (four pilots through `scripts/pilot-queue.ts`, all test-marked; the folder's README and `requests.txt` have every request). The brief's one 15-day pilot of three Sonnet seats asked for nothing, so it was taken on to thirty days and three were added (works, registry and environment with and without a crew; a Haiku town hall in the German town). Ten requests: five drafts, four confirmed, one declined, five with no draft; 0.009 a translator call. A payment with a report and a hold on six standing wage instructions written the German way were drafted first time. A works seat needed eight requests for two standing work orders: once the translator copied "once a week" where a duration was wanted, once it drafted **the collection direction form in place of a standing work order** (declined by the seat; gpt-6.1-sol did the same twice the night before, so it is the prompt's ambiguity, not one model's), and four times a maintenance order with no period came back "How much of it?" (the platform's: a standing order with no period cannot be said). **Where the seat and the translator are one model** (three of the four pilots, and up to half the wave) the requests are still good training data, the label being the program the seat confirmed; it is weaker evidence that the translator reads another model's wording.
  - **Measured: readers** (the same 40 requests as 2026-10-08, all Claude candidates read again under prompt 0.9.0, since the stored answers were under 0.7.6; `against-earlier.txt` sets them beside the stored ones). Read whole 40 of 40 each. With the settled labels: Sonnet 33 of 34, Haiku at default effort 34, Fable 34, Haiku at low effort 26. Pairs: Sonnet with Haiku 38 of 40, Haiku with Fable 37, Sonnet with Fable 36 (Sonnet with sol was 36). Cost a request: 0.004, 0.017, 0.026. **Haiku's earlier poor showing was the low effort**, not the model.
  - **Decided: the readers.** The default stays Sonnet 5.5 with gpt-6.1-sol (two families). With the Codex window shut the pair is **Sonnet 5.5 with Haiku 5.5 at default effort**, named in the config when the pipeline is started and recorded in its manifest; no reader is switched mid-run. What is lost by one family: agreement is weaker evidence (a reading both were trained toward becomes a label), and nothing in 40 requests of three calm offices can show how much. The check, which blocks nothing: a sample of a run's examples (100, or one in ten) read again by a Codex model when its window is next open; until then the run's notes say the audit is owed.
  - **Decided: wave 2** (`plan.md`, third version; `make.ts`). No pilot's translation is behind the Codex sign-in (the generator refuses it). Codex models are seats only, twelve pilots in an optional lane that the parking queue keeps from blocking anything. The 35 pilots on Claude seats in the stages complete the wave by themselves. Each pilot says which translator it may have (`sonnet`, `trained-ok`, `trained`), so that our own retrained translator, begun the same day, can take pilots late and cheaply. Fable 5.1 is in training seats; **the held-out seat model is gpt-6-luna**, which makes that part of the test depend on the Codex window (if it never opens: the Fable pilots are marked test in the pipeline's config, at the cost of that voice in training). Haiku stays, in nine short pilots, the first measuring it at lower effort. Registry seats are in pilots long enough to have deaths to register (2 to 10 in 180 days in a code-run town of each profile; one town of seven had one in its first month; no births before about day 275). Kenya and Brazil are in as they are, marked as towns that are not their place. The three model-clerk pilots are held in a file of their own. Expected: about 520 training requests and 55 test requests from the Claude lanes (a third to three times), 130 and 65 more if the optional lane runs; about 365 of plan usage at list prices, 270 of it Haiku's; one to three days.
  - **Said plainly in the plan:** the wave will yield a few hundred requests, not a thousand. The second version expected more than half its requests from gpt-6.1-sol seats on five requests in twelve days; in the second check it made three in twenty-five. What is lost without Codex seats is the other family's voice (about a fifth of the training requests), its letters, and the test's unseen seat model, not volume.
  - **Found on the way, for the owner:** how often a seat sits is `cadence_days: 7`, a constant in the generator, while the seat's instructions say one sitting each working day; Sonnet seats took the week every time. Making it a spec key is a few lines and would cost about four times a Sonnet pilot's calls (still a few dollars a pilot). Not done: it changes what a seat experiences.
  - **Proposed wording for CLAUDE.md's working agreement on models** (the agreements are the owner's; not edited): "**Models:** the mock as long as possible. Real-model runs go through Claude Code on Naz's plan (`claude-code/…`): seats on `claude-sonnet-5-5`, `claude-haiku-5-5` and `claude-fable-5-1`; the general translator is `claude-sonnet-5-5`, until our own trained translator takes its place, pilot by pilot, where its scores allow. Codex (`gpt-6.1-sol`, `gpt-6-luna`; never `gpt-6-astra`) when it is available, and never as something a run waits on: no translator behind the Codex sign-in, Codex seats in a queue of their own that is parked when the window closes, a Codex reader only with a Claude one named to take its place. Paid APIs need his go-ahead. Always name the model."
  - **Contracts:** none. **Code:** none beyond the parking queue (the entry before this one); `make.ts` is the plan's generator.
  - **The dry run:** every entry of the ten queue files on the mock, 20 days, four at a time, on a8fdcba: 50 of 50 would run (the lines are in `plan.md`).
  - **Not verified:** Sonnet as translator over more than ten requests in a loop, or on any refusal; a `claude-code/` translator when the Claude session limit is met mid-pilot (the seats and the translator are then one sign-in: the pilot parks, as tested with a stand-in); gpt-6.1-sol's held-out score under prompt 0.9.0; Fable 5.1 in a seat (cost and pace are guesses); Haiku at low effort in a seat; a retrained translator in any pilot, and `--retrained` beyond the generator writing the name; the two-Claude-reader pair on holds, directions, standing work or an office's own forms (none was among the 40 requests); the audit by a Codex model (described, never run); the deaths by profile beyond one town each; whether a Kenyan or Brazilian pilot's seats cope (the towns generate and run twenty days on the mock); how many pilots the Claude session limit lets run side by side (two queues is inferred from one night); the request estimates after the change coming on main that brings a seat back the next working day when a paper is filed with it.
  - **Revisit if** the first stage's Sonnet-translated pilots show seats declining drafts for one reason three times (then the prompt, against fresh requests); a retrained translator passes on the acts a pilot's offices ask for (then it takes that pilot); the Codex subscription becomes dependable (then a Codex reader by default costs nothing, and its seats may come out of the optional lane, but a translator behind it is still a second sign-in to run out); the optional lane never runs (then the test's unseen seat model is settled as the plan says, or by a fourth Claude model if the owner allows one); Haiku at low effort is not read whole (then its pilots stay at default effort and are cut to what the plan can bear); the audit finds a one-family blind spot (then no run is labelled by two Claude readers alone).
  - **What is recorded for each** (`OutcomeRecord`, `participants/src/module.ts`): `t` (when the citizen came to know it); `domain` and `option` (the area and what it is about, as the decision named them); `of` (the decision it follows, by the citizen's own count of its decisions, now on every decision as `n`); `kind` (served, paid, unpaid, hired, ended ...); `way`; `from` (who told it); `facts` (ordered 9, delivered 6, refund; the amount paid, when, days since the last pay against the period; periods missed and what is owed; others at the gathering; who ended a job or a tenancy and after how many days); `learned` (the payoff the mind computed, the option's attraction before and after, `first` where it had never tried it, `heard` for another's payoff); `need`; `felt` (the emotion, about whom, the cause's strength, the level before and after); `belief` (before and after).
  - **Facts added where the mind evaluates nothing**, so that a choice's whole course is there: a job `hired` (the wage, the days without work before it) and `ended` (who ended it, days held); a home `lease_signed`, `moved_in` or `not_in_yet` (why the move was refused), `rent_increase` (the rent, what it was, whether bearable, whether challenged), `renewed`, `notice_received`, `ended`; a membership `joined` (the dues); a business `founded` or `refused` and its `capital_called`; a petition's `signatures` as its organiser counts them, and `closed`.
  - **Several outcomes over time.** Each is a record of its own when it is learned: a job is hired, paid each pay day, perhaps unpaid, ended. An outcome follows the citizen's latest decision that chose that option. One that follows none (a job or home held from the start; what a friend said; what was expected before trying) has no `of`, and is still recorded: every update of what a citizen has learned is in the log, so `learned` at any decision can be rebuilt.
  - **Decisions the mind does not make by scoring options.** Joining the union, and a vote, were already recorded with the chance or the ranking as scores. **Starting a business** and **a petition** (starting one; signing, and once not signing when first seen) are now recorded as decisions too, from the chance or the threshold as the person came to it, so their outcomes have something to follow. **Trying another shop** for what the trip's shop could not serve was a choice of the mind's that was never recorded; it is now (`follows`: the trip's decision). Outcomes: union, the membership signed, a rise won, a stoppage; business, founded or refused, capital called; petition, the organiser's running count and its closing. **None, ever:** a vote (the result is published; today's citizen reads none); signing a petition, or deciding not to start one; deciding not to join or not to found; leaving town (not recorded as a decision: the citizen is gone). A home or a job applied for and never offered has an empty list: the citizen is told nothing.
  - **Not recorded as decisions, so with no outcomes** (today's rules, not the mind's; their reasons are in the act): claiming support, borrowing, buying or selling a home, a complaint, the tribunal, standing for office, having a child, taking goods at work.
  - **The contract change** (contracts/README.md has it field by field; under the standing permission for readiness changes, to look over). (1) The log's annotations gain the kind `outcome`: `{ annotation: "outcome", subject, data: { outcomes: [...] } }`, one entry for all a citizen learned since its last action; a `decision`'s data gains `n` and `follows`. The engine checks annotations against the schema, so it was rebuilt. (2) The dataset format is 0.3.0: `citizen_decisions.jsonl` rows gain `n`, `follows` and `outcomes` (nested: one row per decision with what came of it; **empty: nothing learned before the run ended, which is "not known", never a payoff of nought**; absent: a log from before this); a new file `citizen_outcomes.jsonl` (the flat list, with `of`, `decision_seq`, `decision_t`); the manifest gains `citizens` (decisions and outcomes in all and by area, and how many decisions have an outcome). An older log still exports, its rows as before (tested).
  - **One entry per wake, not per outcome.** A log entry's chain fields are about 230 bytes, more than most outcomes; all a citizen learned since its last action goes in one entry. Nothing is sampled: sampling would break the chain of what a citizen learned.
  - **A new kind, not fields on `decision`:** an outcome is known days or months after its decision is written, and the log is append-only; and many outcomes follow no decision at all.
  - **On wherever decisions are, off with them.** `--record-decisions none` and a lean log leave both out; nothing new to set. A resumed run reads the setting back from the log's opening note as before (`batch.ts`, `runOne`); a test stops a run at day 10, resumes it as the pilot queue does, and finds the same outcome entries as the run that was never stopped, and none where none were asked for. A pilot started with the queue's standard command records both. `oikos pilot-report` says so in one line: `citizen records: 28137 decisions, 35783 outcomes`, or `citizen records: NONE (...)`.
  - **It does not change the world** (`orchestrator/test/outcomes.test.ts`, and `logs.test.ts` for the small town). The 1,000-person town, seed 1, 30 days: main at f6ac4ee ends at 5be63866badc311a; this branch ends there with outcomes recorded and with `--record-decisions none`. At 60 days all four (main and this branch, recorded and not) end at ce822ecc916b8bc5 with 334,151 commands and 257 refused. What was touched in the citizen is wrappers that read before and after an update the mind was making anyway; two conditions were split to name the chance drawn (a business, a petition), with the draw made under exactly the conditions it was.
  - **Cost, measured** (the 1,000-person town, seed 1, 60 days, mock, plain logs). Log: 311.7 MB with nothing recorded; 336.6 MB on main with decisions; 347.6 MB now (decisions 25.4 MB, 7.3%: 28,137 of them, 605 more than main's 27,532 for the newly recorded kinds, and each numbered; outcomes 10.5 MB, 3.0%: 35,783 in 15,936 entries, about 290 bytes each). Processor time of the whole batch, side by side: 71.0 s recorded, 69.5 s not (main, earlier and on a busier machine: 61.3 s and 60.5 s); the difference is within what the shared machine moves between two runs. The dataset: `citizen_decisions.jsonl` 24.4 MB, `citizen_outcomes.jsonl` 9.6 MB.
  - **What a 180-day pilot will weigh** (three times the 60 days, which holds while the town is steady): about 32 MB of outcomes and 76 MB of decisions in a log of a little over 1 GB before compression (logs compress to about a seventh). Two thirds of the outcome rows are "stayed in" (23,223 of 35,783), the least informative kind; wages are 1,778 rows, 30 a day.
  - **Found in the mind's evaluation, listed and not touched** (this work records; the citizen redesign decides):
    1. *Nothing is learned of a home.* No payoff is ever computed for one, so a home is always chosen by deliberating or by a friend's word, never by experience.
    2. *A job's payoff has two values.* 10,000 for a wage as agreed, 0 for none: the wage's size, the hours and whether the job lasted never enter what is learned. In a calm town every pay day teaches the same.
    3. *Every update fades every other option of the area toward nought,* not toward what was expected of it (experience-weighted attraction with nothing forgone): a gathering never gone to loses about a tenth of its attraction each time the citizen learns anything else in that area. And "stayed in" is learned once for each gathering not gone to that week, so a citizen with five gatherings in reach learns it five times a week.
    4. *What is expected of staying in is itself learned as an experience* (5,000 folded into a prior of 4,000 gives 4,526), not set.
    5. *A rise the union won is worth the same to every member* (8,000 for a 2% rise), whatever they earn.
    6. *A vote's recorded options carried the ballot's number* beside key and score, which the dataset contract does not allow; the record now has key and score (the number is in the act).
  - **Model seats, cheaply: what came of an act, by reference.** No reward is designed for seats. A seat's call already had its commands; each act now says what it made (`created`: the ids of the records and letters written as it was applied), and a later call says what the seat had been shown since that names one of them (`came_back`: `of`, the command's `seq`, and `in`, the record or letter that names it): the council's ballot on its proposal, the permit decided on its application, the builder's signature on its agreement, a reply to its letter. Read from the observations a run already records for model seats.
  - **Found on the way, and fixed in the export: a refused act was written as applied.** An act takes time; its refusal is logged when it ends, with the step of the clock that ended it as its cause, not the act. `oikos dataset` looked for a refusal under the act's own command and never found one: in the dataset test's 40-day town 13 acts were refused and none was written so (0 of 13); in the 1,000-person town's 30 days, 0 of 130. So `applied` in `actions.jsonl`, on a seat's `commands` and on a translation's `executed` has been `true` for every act since acts took time. The export now follows the act's action (`action_started` names both); the test counts the log's refusals against the rows. **Datasets made before 2026-10-09 should be made again from their logs** (the logs are right). **Not fixed, the same fault in another reader:** `orchestrator/src/corpus.ts` (`oikos corpus`, and through it `in-situ.ts`) joins a refusal the same way, so the translator corpus's `executed.applied` is `true` for acts that were refused; in-situ also reads only the lines it filters for, which leave out the entry that starts an action. That is the translator data's code, in other hands today: for whoever has it.
  - **For research, and kept out of the citizen's record on purpose:** what the citizen never learns (who got the home they applied for; whether the shop they left closed; what the wage would have been elsewhere; how the election came out). Whoever measures reads those from the log; putting them in the citizen's record would give a model trained on it sight no citizen has.
  - **Not verified:** a pilot with model seats (the mock only; nothing here depends on a seat); a log longer than 60 days through the export (it holds a run's outcomes in memory, about 10 MB for these 60 days); a citizen whose controller is started again mid-run (its count of decisions starts again; the export joins an outcome to the latest decision of that number, which is the right one, but no test makes it happen).
  - **Revisit if** a trainer wants an outcome joined to the order or the application rather than the latest decision that chose the option (the order's id is in the facts; an application's is not); the citizen redesign changes what the mind evaluates (each new evaluation should be recorded where it is made, through the same four helpers: `learn`, `hearOf`, `felt`, `outcome`); or "stayed in" proves to be noise worth folding into its decision.

## 2026-10-09 · A refused act is written as refused in the translator corpus too

- **What was wrong.** An act takes time: the log says it started (`action_started`, naming the command) and later that it was applied or refused (naming the action, with the step of the clock that ended it as its cause, not the act). `corpus.ts` looked for the refusal under the act's own command, found none, and wrote `executed.applied: true` for every act the kernel refused. The same fault had been fixed in `dataset.ts` earlier today.
- **The fix.** The join is one small module, `orchestrator/src/act-ends.ts` (`actEnds()`: `started`, `ended`, `underWay`), which `dataset.ts` and `corpus.ts` now both use, so no reader looks for the end under the act. In-situ reads the corpus through `corpusReader`; it now also keeps `action_started` and `action_applied` lines (`needsCorpus`), which the corpus needs to join an end to its act. A refusal with no start (refused as submitted) falls back to its own cause, which is the act.
- **Other readers of "was this act applied", checked.** `measure/src/index.ts` (the `acts` view) joins by action through the start event: correct. `story.ts` prints each event by its own action and participant: correct. `run.ts` counts `action_refused` events as they are replied: correct. `pilot-report.ts` and `pipeline.ts` read translator endings, not the kernel's: no `applied` of the kernel's. Participants read `out.status` from the live reply: correct. `dataset.ts`: fixed earlier today, now through the shared module.
- **What existing data carries it.** Only `oikos corpus` output (`translator-corpus.jsonl`) and the dataset's `translations.jsonl` carry `executed`. None of `runs/translator-data-in-situ/` or `runs/translator-pipeline-smoke-*` has an `executed` field (situations, chunks, answers, joined sets and examples were searched), and no training label or filter reads it: in-situ uses corpus rows for the forms the translator was shown, and the pipeline's examples are written from the writers' programs, not from whether a pilot's act took effect. The one place it could have leaked is `translator/eval/pilot-cases.ts`, whose `pilot: "applied"` notes on 58 cases were taken from `oikos corpus` on 2026-10-06; that field is a note (the scored answers were decided by hand, and `pilot` is not used to select or score). Re-read with the fixed reader (pilot8, pilot9, pilot10, pilot-7d, 7e, 8, 8b, 9): 121 acts carried out, none refused, and all 57 cases noted `applied` that could be matched were applied, so the wrong value changed nothing there. Nothing under `runs/` was changed.
- **Not verified.** a log with an act started and refused in different files of one run was not tried.
- **Revisit if** a log kind arrives in which an action id can repeat within a run (the join assumes an id is one act), or a trainer wants to filter on an act having taken effect (then the corpus should be remade from the logs first: `oikos corpus <runs>`).

- **A vote is shown as from the post it was cast in, and a closed ballot as closed** (2026-10-09; live check 2, finding 3, the seat's side; `participants/src/llm/render.ts`; test `participants/test/seat-votes.test.ts`). The institutions' side (a vote carries `in_position`, a closed ballot `data.closed` and its result, a council's result `voted_for` and `voted_against`) is the other branch's.
  - **Votes.** A councillor's vote was shown "from city", the organisation it speaks for, so a clerk could not tell whose it was. A vote cast in a post is shown as from that post, in a list ("vote, year 1, day 2, from councillor-1") and in the tally a report gives of votes as they come ("3 votes on rec.900: no 1 (councillor-2), yes 2 (councillor-1, councillor-3)"). A vote cast in no post (an elector's) is counted and nobody is named.
  - **Ballots.** A ballot whose paper says it is closed is shown "(closed: no more votes are taken; its result is budget-year-1-result; ...)" and no closing day. A result that names who voted which way says so ("voted for: ...; voted against: ..."); one that names nobody (an election's) shows no names, because the renderer shows only what the paper carries.
  - **Not verified:** against a run of the other branch (its fields are read as its code writes them; the two meet on main).
  - **Revisit if** an election's result ever carries names: the secrecy is the paper's to keep, and the renderer would show what it was given.

- **An unread answer is asked for whole** (2026-10-09; live check 2, the table's note; `participants/src/llm/participant.ts`; test `participants/test/llm-answers.test.ts`; docs/real-models.md, "How an answer is asked for and read").
  - **The fault.** The sentence a seat was given after an answer that could not be read ended "Please give your answer again, in the form asked for." In pilot 6 the second answer was only `done_for_now`: the look and the note the first had meant were not given again.
  - **Now:** "Your last answer could not be read: <why>. Nothing in it has been done, so all you meant by it is still to do. Give the whole of it again, in the form asked for: every look, letter, request and note you meant, not only the part that could not be read. This is the same turn over again, not a sign to stop: say you are done for now only if you had meant to."
  - **Not verified:** a real model's second answer under the new words (two cases seen under the old ones, one of which dropped its acts).
  - **Revisit if** second answers still come back as `done_for_now` alone: then the first answer's readable parts could be said back to it.

- **A resumed pilot's record is whole** (2026-10-09; live check 2, finding 14; `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `batch.ts` (`afterResume`), `cli.ts`, `pilot-state.ts`, `pilot-report.ts`, `scripts/pilot-queue.ts`; tests `orchestrator/test/run-housekeeping.test.ts`, `pilot-queue.test.ts`).
  - **Cost and the log.** The cost report and the compressing of a finished log were a batch's last steps, and `oikos resume` is not a batch: a resumed pilot kept the `cost.txt` of its first stop ("No model calls ... 0.00" against 18.54 recorded) and a plain log of 175 MB. A resume now does both for its folder: measures and cost from the run's current log, the log compressed if the run got to its end. The pilot report gives the whole run's recorded cost and calls from the log (which, for a resumed run, holds every part).
  - **Debriefs.** A debrief that met a usage limit, or got no answer, was noted `debrief_skipped` and the run ended as done: pilot 1's planning seat was never debriefed. Now such a run stops at its end, to be resumed ("a debrief could not be asked ..."), the queue does not take it for done, and the resumed run asks the debriefs not yet given (the failed call is asked again, not served as the same failure). Only a run out of its own spending limit skips one. The pilot report says first when a debrief was never given (pilot 1's log: "NOT A FINISHED PILOT: a debrief was not given: planning-system").
  - **Waiting at a limit.** The queue asked every twenty minutes through a limit whose message said "try again at 6:58 AM". It reads the time (a time of day, or "in 2 hours") and waits until then and a minute more, at most twelve hours; with nothing readable, the usual wait. A run stopped with its model not answering is waited for the same way, and left after six waits with no progress.
  - **Contracts:** none.
  - **Not verified:** the Claude plan's own wording of when a limit lifts beyond the forms seen ("resets at 5pm", "will reset at 3pm"); a time given in another zone than the machine's.
  - **Revisit if** a limit's message gives a time the reader takes wrongly (it would wait up to twelve hours): then cap the wait lower, or go back to asking.

- **A paper filed with an office brings its seat back** (2026-10-09; the coordinator's addition after live check 2; `participants/src/llm/participant.ts`, `mock.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `worlds/generator/generate.ts` (`wake_on_papers`); tests `participants/test/seat-papers-back.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/seat-settings.test.ts`; docs/real-models.md, "A seat's settings").
  - **The fault.** Only a letter brought a seat back before the day it gave. Sonnet seats gave a week: a proposal waited a week for the clerk, a ballot took three, a works seat read complaints seven days late.
  - **Now.** A paper that comes into the office's in-tray makes the seat due at the next working day's sitting after the paper came (never at once; a day's papers are one sitting), and it is told why: "You are back before the day you gave: papers were filed with your office (12 complaints, 1 proposal). They are set out below." So that it knows what has come, the seat looks in at each working day's sitting, with no model call.
  - **What an in-tray is.** A folder of the office's own papers that holds some kinds only (by the channel's own match, or the kinds a folder is said to hold). In a folder that holds every paper of the organisation's, a paper addressed to the seat's own post; and, for an office with no in-tray at all (clinic, police, tribunal), whatever comes from outside the organisation. Its own papers and its staff's never count. This is the office's own channels read as they are: nothing new is shown, and nobody else's papers are.
  - **The seat's choice.** `done_for_now` takes `hold`: the kinds of paper that may wait for the sitting it sets. It stands until given again. Default: nothing waits.
  - **The setting.** `wake_on_papers` in the town's description (a queue entry: `"sets": ["wake_on_papers=false"]`); on unless set false; on record with who sat. Off, a seat is as before and its tool says so.
  - **What it costs** (the mock set to come back weekly, 30 days, the first profile's town of 1,000, a calm month): the mayor 5 sittings to 6 (an invoice), finance 5 to 7 (two employment agreements, a death registration, an invoice), the clerk 5 to 5 and works 5 to 5 (no proposal and no complaint was filed). The 200-person town: mayor 5 to 6, finance 5 to 6, clerk and works 5. A town with a council at work or complaints coming will bring those seats back more; that is the point.
  - **The mock** has a setting of its own for the measurement and the test (`mock.back_days`: it says it is back after that many days whatever its brain would).
  - **Not a paper:** a ballot closing, a payment falling due. A clerk waiting on a ballot's close still has to give fewer days: the mock clerk that comes back weekly counted no ballot within sixteen days.
  - **Hash:** a town with no model seat is untouched. A mock-seat run's moves (a seat looks in each working day).
  - **Not verified:** a real model's use of `hold`; how often real towns bring a mayor back (every invoice and complaint to the town is in its in-tray).
  - **Revisit if** a seat is brought back most days by one kind it does nothing with and does not hold it (then the default for that kind is the thing to change), or the daily look-in shows in run time.

- **A seat's effort is a setting of its own** (2026-10-09; live check 2, finding 14; `participants/src/llm/adapter.ts` (`LlmRequest.effort`), `claude-code.ts`, `codex.ts`, `call.ts`, `participant.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `worlds/generator/generate.ts` (`seat_effort`); test `orchestrator/test/seat-settings.test.ts`; docs/real-models.md, "A seat's settings").
  - **What was there.** Effort was part of the run's model name (`claude-code/claude-haiku-5-5@low`): one for every seat and the translator. The Claude Code adapter takes `CLAUDE_EFFORT` out of the environment it runs `claude -p` in (so that a run started inside a session is the run it would be from a terminal), so with no `@` a seat ran at the model's default. Haiku 5.5 at that default spent about three quarters of its output on thinking.
  - **Now.** A town's description may give `seat_effort` (one word for every seat, or by office id), which a queue entry sets with `"sets": ["seat_effort.finance=low"]`. It is the seat's own setting, sent with each of its calls (`effort` on the request), used by the two command-line adapters before any effort named with the model, and recorded with each transcript and in the run's account of who sat. Not given, nothing is passed: the default is unchanged.
  - **Contracts:** none (a controller's parameters and a transcript's data are open).
  - **Not verified, on purpose:** whether a Haiku seat at low effort is still read whole. No model was called. The reader comparison's finding (Haiku at low effort a poor reader) is about the translator's job.
  - **Revisit if** the measurement shows answers unread or acts dropped at the lower effort: then the cost is the price of a Haiku seat.

- **The translator's standing training set, re-keyed to the call language as it stands; and the retrain put off until after the wave** (2026-10-09; `runs/translator-data-in-situ/joined-11`, `runs/translator-model/data-17`; `translator/train/synthetic.ts`, `orchestrator/src/training.ts`, `translator/model/py/train.py`; docs/translator-pipeline.md, "The retrain after the wave"). Begun as an interim retrain before wave 2; stopped by the owner before any model was called: the retrain that matters needs the wave's requests, and writing data now would compete with the wave for the same Claude limit. What needs no model and has to come first was done. **No model call, no pod, no spend.**
  - **Stock-take** (what every model so far was trained on: `joined-10`, 30,651 training rows, 3,255 validation, 228 validation-real; `joined-7`, data-13's, is inside it). Generated and blind-checked by Sonnet: the first set's 24 parts (data 0.4.0, prompt 0.7.3; 12,205 rows), five parts in the seats' voice (0.5.0 to 0.7.0, prompt 0.7.4; 2,569), ten weighted parts (letters, forms, forms of several amounts, pairs, refusals; 0.6.0 to 0.9.0, prompt 0.7.4; 6,927), and 913 built by code. From real situations, each read alike by two readers (Sonnet, Opus) and repeated four times in training: written by Claude in pilots 7a to 9's situations (1,094 distinct, prompt 0.7.4), by gpt-6.1-sol there (1,274, 0.7.4), by Claude in pilot 10's (547, 0.7.5 with 0.7.6's rule for bases), and the seats' own requests that are no test case (111). Nothing in it was labelled under 0.8.0 or 0.9.0. Not in it: part c1 (611 permission claims, data-15 only). The manifest has every source's rows.
