  - **Which labels the rule changes made stale, and what was done** (as the 23 real test cases were re-keyed on 2026-10-08; the script and its lists are `joined-11/build.ts`). *By script:* the generated "held" refusal (a standing payment to be held, named by its accounts and amount; `none(no_such_act)` until data 0.11.0) is `none(look_first)`, 117 examples; the 74 that also cite a record or a standing instruction by id are set aside, since a reader could take that id for the thing held. *By a read of all 223 distinct requests from seats and seats' situations labelled `none(no_such_act)`:* 2 are holds named by id, now `statement(hold=…)` (8 rows); 56 name a standing payment or another paper only by describing it, or act on what a look finds, now `none(look_first)` (224 rows); 67 are set aside (what may be an entry on one's own file, 24; a hold of something that is not plainly a standing record, 12; a payment named by the agreement it is paid under, 11; a look and then an act where the act is not plain, 20); 97 stand (going to see, attending, an office's own routine with no form listed). Five `not_an_act` requests that go on to an act are set aside. In all 175 distinct requests re-keyed (349 rows), 146 set aside (350 rows), kept in `set-aside.jsonl` for two readers. *Found not stale:* directions to offices (no example lists an office's own form, so each is still a letter); withdrawals that speak of pausing; letters asking someone to pause; statements filed with someone; work (no request asks for a routine).
  - **The leak check: the standing set failed it.** The held-out file was not opened; the code's own check (`leaks`, five words running) on `joined-10` names six held-out cases (`h2-22`, `h2-26`, `h2-35`, `h2-36`, `h2-49`, `h2-54`) that share wording with its training side, two of them also with validation-real. 94 rows share it (92 training, 2 validation-real, all from real situations) and are not in `joined-11`, which passes. So every held-out score of a data-13 or data-16 model (44 to 47 of 66; 40 and 44) was measured with those six cases' wording in training: read them as an upper bound. They were let through because nothing checked: generated requests have always been checked against the held-out cases as they are made (data.ts), and requests labelled by two readers never were (the in-situ steps check a real test case's exact words and its beginning, no more). The pipeline's join now runs the check on everything it joins, new and standing, and counts what it drops. None of the 180 real test cases is in training, by exact words or by beginning; none of pilot 10's held-back requests is.
  - **Code.** (1) A part can be made of the new kinds by name (`--only hold,entry,standing_work,direction,paper,…`; holds and entries are tagged as the others were; `generated` counts the function each is drawn among): without it a part of holds meant writing seven statements for each. No program changes; the pipeline's version stays 0.12.0. (2) The trainer's forms augmentation never adds a form that goes to an office the request names: with offices' own forms in the pool, a letter directing the works office shown beside the works office's staffing form would be taught as a letter where the rule says the form. Matched on the office's id whole, so `acc-city` does not stop a council form being added. (3) `--forms-most N` (5 as before unless given): a seat of today's towns knows of 13 to 18 forms, 533 to 760 of the reader's 1,024 tokens before the request is read (measured on two live-check pilots), and every model so far saw at most five beside an example. (4) The pipeline's join drops, and counts, anything that shares five words running with a held-out case (above). (5) A test that the export cuts none of the new shapes (a hold of one and of several, an entry, standing work with `first` and `until`, forms with lists and dates, payments in all 26 ways of writing money): encode and export needed no change, and the trainer's limit of 48 steps is not approached (the longest generated paper is 32).
  - **The retrain's plan** is in docs/translator-pipeline.md: two generated parts by kind (7,642 briefs by dry run), the join, and one pipeline command over every pilot, with the scoring by kind and the live check's pilot 2 as a test set.
  - **Not verified.** Nothing was trained on `joined-11`: that the re-keyed labels help is untested. R3's 56 were keyed by one read, by the rule, not by two readers. Labels of the older in-situ batches under the rule for several bases (0.7.5) were not re-read. Whether the generated refusals for an office's own routine that speak of its rounds or a collector should now be standing work was not settled: the pipeline at 0.12.0 still writes that brief as `no_such_act`, and so they stand. The trainer changes were checked by `translator/model/py/check_forms.py` (run by hand: there is no Python test tier) and by no training run. The six leaking cases were not looked at, so whether the shared wording is a town's stock phrase or a case's own is unknown.
  - **Revisit if** two readers disagree with R3 on more than a few of the 56 (then re-key by readers, not by a read); `--forms-most 18` costs more on the fixed tests than it gains on the wave's test pilots; a seat's requests run past the reader's limit once its forms are counted (then `--max-tokens`, or showing a seat's translator fewer forms); or the held-out scores of the new runs fall by about the six cases (then the old scores were the leak's).

- **The bank's statement: it had paid and said "No payments yet"** (2026-10-09; bank.payment_system 0.14.0; docs/behaviour/bank-payment-system.md, "A statement"; the second live check's finding 2, `runs/live-check-2-2026-10-09/README.md`).
  - **The fault.** A letter to the bank was answered "your accounts with us: acc-city, balance ... No payments yet." after the bank had paid the town's wages. In two pilots that sentence became the month: the seats decided the wage instructions were "the wrong figure", then "unauthorised", and one mayor withdrew six of them.
  - **The cause, traced.** The answer read its "latest payments" from the observation in which it was written (`channels.transactions(obs)`). A participant is shown a payment once, at its first look after the payment (D42: perception is changes), and the bank writes its answers at the start of a day's wake, before it pays. Every payment of the day before had reached it at a later look of that day and was gone by the next morning. So the list was empty at almost every answer, whatever had been paid. The bank kept no ledger: its own register (`keeps`: "accounts") was only ever what one look showed.
  - **What a bank does.** It keeps a ledger and writes statements from it: for each transaction a reference, the amount, the date, the other party and the words sent with the payment, with the balance; periodically and on request (docs/research/references.md, "What the second live check found": to confirm).
  - **Built.** The bank enters every payment it is shown into a ledger of each account (a count, the sums in and out, the latest 40 entry by entry), and answers a letter with a statement of each of the writer's accounts: the period (from the last statement to that writer, or from the ledger's beginning), the balance brought forward, each entry by date with the account paid or paying, what it was for and its references, the totals, the balance carried forward; then the standing instructions as before. Dates and sums as the town writes them. Each writer has their own period, so a mayor who writes after the finance officer is not told "nothing since yesterday". A payment in does not name the payer's instruction (the payer's paper; the payee could not otherwise know its reference); it names what it settles and what it was for, which the payer sent with it.
  - **Not built, on purpose:** a statement sent unasked each month to every customer. It is what a real bank does, and here it is a thousand letters a month that no code customer reads; a seat asks, or keeps a look for every sitting. Listed in the behaviour doc.
  - **Cost.** The bank holds up to 80 entries an account between trims (the payments it was shown anyway, kept rather than dropped). Not measured at 10,000 people; by count, at most 80 small objects for each account.
  - **Contracts:** none. **Tests:** `participants/test/bank-statement.test.ts` (four; the first fails on main with "No payments yet"); `orchestrator/test/llm.test.ts` reads the new words.
  - **Not verified:** a real model reading a statement (no model was called); memory at 10,000 people; the sources (to confirm).
  - **Revisit if** seats ask the bank for the payee's name (then the bank looks its own customer up, which is its own register, and a payee at another bank stays an account number); a seat needs entries older than the latest 40 (then the ledger is kept whole for accounts whose holder has named signatories, that is, organisations); or monthly statements are wanted for seats (then for customers who ask for them once, as a standing request).
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days: 5be63866badc311a, twice (main's: the same; 166,784 commands, 130 refused). No code customer writes to the bank, so a code town does not move; any town with a seat that writes to it does.

- **The standing payments a town opens with say who set them up; the papers behind what a town is paid and charged** (2026-10-09; generator 0.39.0, bank.payment_system 0.15.0; docs/behaviour/bank-payment-system.md, "The instructions a town opens with"; live check 2, finding 2).
  - **The fault.** A town's opening wage instructions read "Please pay c0004's wages every 14 days.", made by the world's beginning. `signatories-city` said only the finance officer may instruct payments, and nothing on file said the finance officer had. Seats in three pilots asked who issued them and under what authority; the code finance office answered with its account report.
  - **What a real town has.** Its bank holds a mandate (a resolution naming who signs); a payroll payment is set up by the payroll office on the contract of employment (docs/research/references.md: to confirm). As with the opening budget, genesis writes the papers a real town would have, made before the year began.
  - **Built.** Every opening standing instruction (wages for every employer, union dues, mortgage repayments, rent, a household member's share of the rent) says in its words who gave it, that it was given before the year began, and the agreement it pays under, which it already cited. The town's say it was given by its finance officer as the signatory `signatories-city` names, and give the sum as the town writes money with how it comes from the agreed wage ("$2,393.34 (the agreed $3,000 less $606.66 withheld under law-income-tax)": pilot 2's seats spent days on a difference of 0,84 between a wage and its instruction) and the first pay day. `signatories-city` now reads as the council's mandate to the bank, resting on the charter, and says that holding, changing and withdrawing a standing instruction are the finance officer's too (the next entry makes the bank hold to it). The town's signature on each opening employment agreement is made in the works manager's post. The bank's list of a customer's standing instructions says of each who gave it, when, and what it cites.
  - **The same check on every other opening commitment a town office is shown** (the first profile's 1,000-person town: every record at the start that the town is party to or that is addressed to it):

    | What | Paper behind it before | Now |
    |---|---|---|
    | Six employment agreements (the crew) | Signed for the town by nobody in particular; no first pay day | Signed in the works manager's post; the wage instruction gives the first pay day (the agreement's own first pay day: the entry on payroll notices) |
    | Six wage instructions | In the finance officer's post, unsaid in words | As above |
    | The grant the budget "expects" | None: the first paper was the first payment's notice, on day 31 | `grant-city`: the funder's determination (so much for each resident by the published estimate, every 91 days from day 31, into acc-city). One each for the clinic, the school and the police |
    | The landfill's invoices (the services line) | None: the charge a tonne was in no paper | `landfill-charges`, where the place has a charge |
    | The town's 984 titles | The land registry's register entries | Unchanged: a title is the register's entry, and the registry answers for it |
    | The budget, its ballot and result | On file since the opening budget | The entry on the ballot |
    | Leases, supply agreements, loans | The town has none at the start | Nothing to add. What it commissions in the run rests on its own construction agreements and the builder's published prices |
    | The laws, the charter, the procedures, the forms | Each rests on the charter or is the town's own | Unchanged |
  - **Not done:** a paper showing the council's resolution itself (the mandate says it was by resolution; no minute is on file: the council's opening minutes are the budget's alone). The rates the budget expects rest on the rating law and the valuer's roll, which no single paper sums: left.
  - **Contracts:** none changed. Two new statement kinds are world content (`grant_determination`, `charges_notice`); nobody's channel was changed (both are addressed to the body concerned and reach it among its own papers).
  - **Tests.** `orchestrator/test/places.test.ts`, "every standing payment a town opens with says who gave it ..." (all nine profiles; fails on main at its first line); `participants/test/bank-holds.test.ts` (the list's words).
  - **Not verified:** a real model reading them; the sources.
  - **Revisit if** seats ask for the council's resolution behind the mandate (then an opening minute of the council, as the budget's papers are); or a seat takes "before the year began" for a date it can look up.
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days: 2fccad004297b061, twice (before: 5be63866badc311a). The same 166,784 commands and 130 refusals: words and five papers changed, nothing anyone does.

- **The bank acts on a withdrawal only from whoever may instruct on the account** (2026-10-09; bank.payment_system 0.16.0; docs/behaviour/bank-payment-system.md, "Who may withdraw"; live check 2, finding 14).
  - **The fault.** A mayor seat that is not the town's signatory withdrew six wage instructions and the bank stopped paying the crew. The cause is wider than the mayor: the bank stopped an order on any withdrawal record it was shown, and never looked at who made it. A withdrawal is a record anyone can make of any paper (the kernel judges nothing), so anyone whose withdrawal reached the bank could end anyone's standing order. The hold, added the day before, did check; withdrawal, lifting a hold and replacement did not.
  - **Whether a mayor may, by the town's own published rules: no.** `signatories-city` names the finance officer alone; the payments procedure gives the mayor written approval of large payments and nothing else in a payment; the rule on directions has the mayor direct offices on their forms, and says a direction changes nobody's employment. The mayor's way to stop a wage is the finance officer; the council's way to change who signs is a new mandate.
  - **Built.** One check (`mayInstruct`) for a payment, a hold, a withdrawal of a standing instruction, a withdrawal of a hold, and an instruction that names the one it replaces: written for the holder of the paying account, by one of its own seats, in a signatory's post where the holder has named any. Anything else is answered once and what it named stands: to the holder's own non-signatory, "Withdrawal W is not acted on, and X stands: mayor is not an authorised signatory for acc-city."; to anyone else, the hold's sentence ("... does not apply to X: we have no standing instruction of yours by that reference."), the same whether X exists or not. The hold's answer to the holder's own non-signatory changed to match (it had the neutral sentence, which told a mayor the town had no such instruction).
  - **What it reveals.** To a stranger, nothing. To the account holder's own officer, that their post is not on their own organisation's mandate: the organisation's paper, and what the bank already said of a payment instruction from that post.
  - **A hold and its withdrawal arriving together** are read in order (the hold taken, then lifted); a withdrawal of a paper the bank has not been shown yet is kept and looked at again.
  - **Found, not fixed:** the mandate itself. The latest `signatories` statement made for the holder stands, whichever of its seats made it; a mayor seat that filed one naming itself would be taken at its word. A bank wants the governing body's resolution. No pilot's seat has done it (the call language has no act that writes one); for Naz: whether the bank should take a new mandate only from the clerk's post on a council result.
  - **Contracts:** none. **Tests:** `participants/test/bank-holds.test.ts`, three new (the first fails on main: the clerk's withdrawal stops the firm's order); the twin test in `bank.test.ts` now has withdrawals by the writer, by someone else and by nobody placeable.
  - **Not verified:** a model seat reading the refusal and going to the finance officer; a year with holds and withdrawals by seats.
  - **Revisit if** a seat needs to stop a payment urgently and the finance seat is absent (then the mandate should name a second signatory: the council's act, by the mandate's own words).
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days: 2fccad004297b061, twice (unchanged from the entry before: in a code town every withdrawal is the payer's own signatory's).

- **A ballot with a result is closed, the clerk refuses a late vote, and a council's result names who voted** (2026-10-09; generator 0.40.0, city.council_clerk 0.10.0, city.councillor 0.5.2, city.electoral_office 0.6.0; docs/behaviour/government.md, `city.council_clerk`; live check 2, finding 3).
  - **The fault.** Two councillor seats voted on `budget-year-1-ballot` on the first day: it was on file with a closing time of the first moment, beside its result. The record then held seven yes against a result of five, and the clerk seat spent thirty days trying to reconcile it.
  - **Causes, three.** (1) Nothing refuses a vote: a vote is a record anyone can write on any statement at any time (physics; the kernel judges nothing). The code clerk simply did not count a late one, and said nothing to whoever cast it. (2) The opening ballot said "held before the year began" and carried `closes_at` nought, which a reader takes for today. (3) A result gave a count and no names, so a reader with the votes in front of it could not tell which five the count was of.
  - **What a real council does.** The question is put, members vote while it is open, the chair declares the result and the minutes record it; where votes are recorded, who voted which way is in the minutes and public. A vote offered after the declaration is not taken. The election of persons is by secret ballot (docs/research/references.md: to confirm).
  - **Built.**
    - *The opening ballot says it is closed:* "Council ballot, held and closed before the year began (result budget-year-1-result: passed, 5 for, 0 against): ...", with `data.closed` and `data.result` beside the closing time a record has to have (a record's time cannot be before nought, as with the other opening papers).
    - *Who refuses, and how:* the clerk, who keeps the ballot. A vote on a ballot of its council that is closed (its closing time passed, its result declared, or it says so), or by anyone not in a councillor's post, is not counted, and the clerk writes to whoever cast it, once, saying which and giving the result if there is one. Nothing is blocked: a clerk held by a model, or a clerk that follows no procedure, may do otherwise.
    - *Whose a vote is:* a result names who voted for, who against and who did not vote, in its words and its content (`voted_for`, `voted_against`), and the clerk's report gives the same for recent results. The opening result names its five. The clerk's form for a result has the two lists, so a clerk seat can write the same paper. A vote paper already carries the post it was cast in.
    - *The secret ballot stays secret:* an election's votes are seen by the electoral body alone and its result names nobody's. Checked the same things there: a vote after the poll closed was already not counted (0.3.1) and is now answered ("not counted: the poll closed on ..."), saying nothing of anyone's vote; the result already names its count (formal votes, electors, turnout, the rounds).
    - A code councillor leaves a ballot that says it is closed alone (it already left one past its closing time).
  - **For the seat-facing work (another's files):** what a seat is shown of a vote ("from city") and of a ballot ("closing year 1, day 1") is drawn by the seat's renderer. The papers now carry what it needs: a ballot's `closed` and `result`, a result's lists, a vote's post.
  - **Contracts:** none changed. The ballot's and result's content gained keys (world content); the clerk's result form gained two optional fields.
  - **Tests.** `participants/test/council.test.ts`: the result's names; a vote on the opening ballot, after a closing time and after a result, each answered and uncounted (fails on main: nothing is said, and the result has no names); `orchestrator/test/places.test.ts`: every profile's opening ballot is closed and its result names the councillors.
  - **Not verified:** a clerk seat using the lists; a model councillor reading the refusal; the sources.
  - **Revisit if** the renderer shows a closed ballot as closed and seats still vote on it (then the opening ballot should not be on the councillors' list of ballots at all: a channel's question, and a contract one); or a profile's place counts council votes in secret (none of the nine was found to; it would be the profile's to say).
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days: 378df88de62ecc96, twice (before: 2fccad004297b061). The same 166,784 commands and 130 refusals: two papers' words and content changed, and no code councillor votes late.

- **A new starter is on the payroll because the hiring office says so: payroll notices, and what else one office did silently for another** (2026-10-09; generator 0.41.0, city.works 0.5.0, city.environment 0.5.0, city.finance_officer 0.10.0; docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Payroll notices"; live check 2, finding 9).
  - **The fault.** The code environment office hires a scientist on day 1. Where finance was a seat, in two pilots of three the scientist was never paid, resigned and filed a claim. The agreement named no first pay day and nothing asked finance to pay.
  - **What happened where finance was code.** It set the payment up by itself: the code finance office looks through every paper of the town's, and on any employment agreement in force with no wage payment it made one, first due a pay period from whenever it looked. Nothing was sent to it. A seat in that office has no such habit and was told nothing.
  - **What a real town does.** The hiring manager sends payroll a new-starter notice (who, the post, the pay, the period, the start, the bank details, the contract), and payroll sets the payment up; a leaver the same way (docs/research/references.md: to confirm).
  - **Built.** The offer of employment states its first pay day ("First pay 14 days after both have signed."). An office that hires and does not pay (the town's works and environment offices) files a payroll notice for each new starter once both have signed, and for each leaver once the employment has an end or the member of staff has died: the organisation's own paper, marked with the payroll office, resting on the agreement, on a form of the office's stationery (`payroll_starter`, `payroll_leaver`), so a seat in the hiring office sends the same paper. The code finance office sets the wage up on the notice, from the first pay day it gives. With no notice after three days it sets it up from the agreement on file and says so: a real payroll clerk with a signed contract in front of them does not leave someone unpaid, and without this a works seat that hires and sends no notice would have its hires unpaid by a code payroll that until today paid them. A seat in the finance office sees the notice among its payroll papers, with what it needs to act.
  - **In the first profile's 1,000-person month** (code offices): the scientist signs on day 2, the notice is filed that day ("first pay day year 1, day 16"), finance sets the payment up from it the same day; the scientist gives notice on day 9, and the leaver's notice says the employment ends on day 23; the next scientist signs on day 24 and is noticed and set up that day.
  - **Every other place a code office did something for another office, or because of another's paper, with nothing asking it** (surveyed across `participants/src/behaviour/`; "asked" means a paper addressed to the acting office's organisation that plainly calls for the act):

    | # | What one does | Who acts on it, unasked | Now |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | 1 | Works or environment takes someone on | Finance set the wage up | **Fixed**: the starter's notice |
    | 2 | A member of staff gives notice or is let go | Finance ended the payment when the employment ended | **Fixed**: the leaver's notice (a code payroll ends the payment as before) |
    | 3 | The registry registers the death of a member of staff | Finance alone ended the employment on record and stopped the wage; the hiring office did nothing, so with a seat in finance the dead stayed on the staff and the post was never advertised | **Fixed**: the hiring office ends the employment on record and sends the leaver's notice; the payroll gives no second notice |
    | 4 | An invoice over the procedure's figure reaches the town | Finance waited in silence for the mayor's approval; the code mayor approves only invoices for work it commissioned, so any other (the landfill's) would wait for ever, and a mayor seat was never told | **Fixed** (the same shape, turned round): finance asks the mayor in writing, once |
    | 5 | The clerk publishes an adopted budget | Works and environment recruit, or make redundant, to their line; finance resets its limit | Not changed. The budget is a public paper each office is shown and reads for itself; a seat in those offices is shown it too. A real clerk would send each office its approved establishment: listed |
    | 6 | The electoral commission declares a result (public) | The clerk seats the winner | Not changed. A clerk seat is shown the result and is not asked; a returning officer sends the declaration to the council's proper officer: listed, a letter from the commission to the clerk would do it |
    | 7 | The registry's entry names children left with no adult | Child protection takes them into care | Not changed. It reads the entry among the town's papers; a real registrar or the police make a referral: listed |
    | 8 | The builder gives the town notice of building work | Works adds the address to its round and inspects a new asset; the mayor plans roads by it; environment marks the ground built | Not changed. The notice is addressed to the town; each office reads it. The inspector's visit is asked for by the notice itself |
    | 9 | The valuer values a property | The rates officer levies on it | Not changed. The valuation is the valuer's return to the rating authority; the office keeps the roll |
    | 10 | The land registry notes land changing hands | The valuer and the water corporation change their rolls | Not changed (outside bodies; the notice reaches each) |
  - **Papers nobody acts on, found by the same survey and listed, not fixed:** a tribunal's hearing notice or order against the town (no town office reads one); the inspector's fine (a claim that names no account, which no office collects); the council's directions, which the town's rule says the clerk files and the code clerk never does; pay for the part of a pay period before a leaver's last day (the payment ends and the days since the last pay day go unpaid).
  - **Contracts:** none changed. A new statement kind (`payroll_notice`) and two forms are world content; three modules gained a parameter each (`payroll_office`, `payroll_wait_days`).
  - **Tests.** `participants/test/payroll-notice.test.ts` (the starter's notice and its words; the payroll acting on it, waiting without it, then acting on the agreement; the leaver and the death; the request for an approval: each fails on main); `orchestrator/test/office-papers.test.ts` (the notice on its form is the notice the module sends).
  - **Not verified:** a finance seat acting on a notice (no model was called; the demonstration shows what it is shown); a year of it; the sources.
  - **Revisit if** a finance seat is shown the notice and still does not pay (then what it is shown, not the paper); works seats hire and never send a notice (then the form is not found, or the fallback hides it: count the fallbacks in a pilot's log by its reason, "no payroll notice has come"); or leavers' unpaid days show up as claims.
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days: f63961fb76e05942, twice (before: 378df88de62ecc96). 166,910 commands, 166 refused (were 166,784 and 130): the run takes another course from day 2, when the scientist's pay is set for another day. The 36 more refusals are firms' own (factories and shops), not looked into further: recorded, not chased.

- **A code-run office acknowledges a letter** (2026-10-09; docs/behaviour/letters.md; `answers` on 33 modules, `answering` and `Letters` in `participants/src/behaviour/common.ts`; live check 2, finding 11).
  - **The fault.** A code office answered a seat's letter with its standing report whatever was asked, or, if it had none, with nothing. A works seat wrote twice to a code-run mayor for a staffing direction and saw no reply; a mayor asked finance who authorised a payment and got the account report. Seats could not tell silence from a fault.
  - **What a real office does:** acknowledges, and does it, declines, or says who to ask and how (references: to confirm).
  - **Built, without a model in any office.** Each office's module carries fixed words (`answers`): its name, what it acts on and how, and for a thing it has a form or a set way for, a sentence to add when the letter has one of a few words about it. An office with no report of its own now acknowledges each letter once, when it has done its own work for the wake (`answering`, applied where modules are registered: the module itself is untouched). An office with a standing report sends it and then says that it is the standing report, that the office does not act on a letter's words, and the same fixed words. The table of which office says what is in the behaviour doc.
  - **The works seat's letter, now:** "From the mayor's office: your letter is received. This office does not act on a letter's words. What it acts on: a petition once its organiser's published count reaches the town's threshold; an invoice for work this office commissioned, which it approves in writing; and each year's budget, which it puts to the council. It gives no direction by letter. If your letter asks for a direction: this office has given none on the matter, and an office needs none to act within its own powers and its budget line."
  - **What a reply reveals:** nothing the writer could not know. The words are the same for everyone; which sentence about a form is added turns on the letter's own words. A standing report was already sent to whoever wrote: unchanged here, and what a report may hold is each office's own question.
  - **Offices do not answer each other's notes.** A letter in the fixed words offices write (a report, "From the ... office: your ...", the bank's notes) is not a question. Until now an office with a report answered the bank's note of a hold with its report; it no longer does.
  - **Not covered:** shops, factories and landlords (a letter to a firm's manager is still unanswered), and people. The tax clerk is in no generated town.
  - **Honest limits.** The office still does not read the letter or do what it asks. The keyword match is crude: it adds a sentence and never withholds the rest. A works seat that needs the mayor to do something a code mayor never does is told so, in effect; it is not helped further.
  - **Contracts:** none (a module's manifest gained an optional field).
  - **Tests.** `participants/test/letters.test.ts` (the acknowledgement and its once; the report's tail and the form's sentence; every office has words and none of them is a platform word; what counts as an office's note): each fails on main.
  - **Not verified:** a model reading an acknowledgement and using the form; whether seats take the acknowledgement for an answer and stop writing (the pilots will say: count letters to code offices before and after).
  - **Revisit if** seats keep writing to an office after its acknowledgement (then the words, or the office needs to be a seat); a seat is misled by a form's sentence the keyword added wrongly; or code offices should issue the directions they are asked for (a decision about the code mayor, not about letters).
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days: 8a2ca8c818146838, twice (the merged tree's, unchanged: in a code town nobody writes a letter in words to an office, and the one new office note, finance's request for an approval, is not answered).

- **A grant several times the town's whole budget: what is wrong, and whose it is** (2026-10-09; `worlds/profiles/` notes for jp-akita, br-mg, ke-nakuru, mx-jal; `orchestrator/test/places.test.ts`; live check 2, finding 14).
  - **The fault as seen.** The Japanese town's budget "expects about ¥480,379,900 in grants" against ¥64,915,711 of spending; both councillor seats spent the month asking about the surplus. It is not only words: the grants office really pays that sum into the town's account, a quarter at a time.
  - **Which it is.** Not a mistake of transcription, and not mainly a per-resident grant meeting lines that do not scale (the two flat lines, parks and the environment office, are ¥13.1 million of the ¥64.9 million; with every line reckoned for each resident the budget is about ¥64,900 a resident against a grant of ¥479,900). **The spending lines leave out what such a town spends the grant on.** The figure is Ikawa's whole local allocation tax for each resident (47% of that town's revenue), which there pays for welfare, schools, health, administration and debt. The town in the simulation runs waste collection, the upkeep of its parks, hall and roads, a park and some roads a year, and a wildlife survey; its clinic, school and police are bodies of their own with grants of their own. A real municipality's general grant has met a town with five functions.
  - **The nine towns** (`worlds/town-1000.yaml`, the opening budget; grants expected over all spending, and rates and grants together over spending):

    | Profile | Grants / spending | Rates and grants / spending | What the grant figure is |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | au-vic | 0.08 | 1.16 | general-purpose grants only (its note still says "the town has no roads yet": stale) |
    | br-mg | 8.53 | 8.55 | Aguanil's whole general-purpose transfers (the same fault as Japan's) |
    | de-ni | 0.47 | 0.69 | key allocations; its own note says the trade tax and the income-tax share are not modelled |
    | gb-eng | 0.12 | 1.17 | a placeholder |
    | in-tn | 0.75 | 1.26 | a placeholder |
    | jp-akita | 7.40 | 8.25 | Ikawa's whole local allocation tax |
    | ke-nakuru | 2.22 | 2.40 | a placeholder, sized to a county's equitable share |
    | mx-jal | 1.92 | 1.94 | a placeholder, sized to all federal and state transfers |
    | us-oh | 0.04 | 0.73 | a placeholder |
  - **Done: flagged, not tuned.** No figure and no formula changed, so no town's hash moves. The four profiles whose grant is more than one and a half times the whole budget carry a flag in their own note on the figure, saying what it is, what the town does not run, and what is wanted: the grant for the functions the town has, which the same source's spending by purpose would give (Ikawa's settlement has it; not opened here). A test holds that a profile whose grant is that large says so (it fails on main for all four), so a tenth profile does not arrive with the same surplus unremarked.
  - **Why not fix the derivation.** There are two honest ways and both need what no profile gives: the share of the real town's spending that goes on the functions the simulated town runs (then the grant is scaled by it), or the real town's spending by purpose (then the budget has lines for what the grant pays for, and offices to spend them). The first is a figure for each profile's author to source; the second is new institutions. Cutting the grant to fit the budget would be tuning.
  - **What a seat will still see** in the Japanese and Brazilian towns until their authors act: a surplus of about seven times the budget. Recommended: hold the two profiles' council pilots, or run them knowing the councillors will ask about it.
  - **Not verified:** the ratios at other sizes or seeds (the flat lines weigh more in a small town: the test's 300-person towns give other ratios, the same four over the line); what a run takes in against what it spends over a year; the sources' spending by purpose.
  - **Revisit if** a profile's author gives the share (then the generator scales the town's grant by it, a profile figure with its source), or the town gains the functions the grant pays for.
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days: 8a2ca8c818146838, twice (unchanged: notes and a test). The ratios were measured again on the tree after main's informal-work changes were merged: the same.
  - **Test.** `orchestrator/test/places.test.ts`, "a town's opening budget against the grant it expects" (a town of a thousand for each profile).

- **The opening budget proposal's sums are written as the town writes money** (2026-10-09; generator 0.43.0; live check 2, finding 12).
  - **The fault.** The proposal a town opens with held each line in its content as a bare count of the smallest unit ("environment: 4321834; parks: 15000000"), beside words that gave the same sums properly. A seat is shown both.
  - **Done.** At generation the content's sums are written as the proposal's words write them ("£43,218.34"). The paper was made before the run and no office's code reads it: the clerk does not ballot a proposal a ballot stands for, and the budget itself (`budget-year-1`) holds the lines as numbers, which is what offices read.
  - **A difference to know of.** A proposal a seat files on the council proposal form in the run still holds its amounts as the form reads them (a count of the smallest unit), because the clerk's code reads them to write the budget. What a seat is shown of those is the seat renderer's to word.
  - **Contracts:** none. **Test:** `orchestrator/test/places.test.ts` (every profile; fails on main).
  - **Revisit if** anything comes to read the opening proposal's content as numbers (then it reads the budget's).
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days: 5098693b1c379072, twice (before: 8a2ca8c818146838; the same 166,910 commands and 166 refusals: one paper's content).

- **What the demonstration found: a payroll notice on the town's own file is not put in front of a finance seat, so it goes as a letter too; and a mock finance seat that sees an offer before it is signed never pays it** (2026-10-09; firms.ts `Staffing`, `PAYROLL_NOTE`; `scripts/institutions-demo.ts`; after merging main at e50b3a0, generator 0.44.0).
  - **The demonstration** (`bun scripts/institutions-demo.ts --out DIR --set a|b --seed N`; three towns from seeds 1 to 3, 1,000 people, 60 days, no model called; set a: the mock in the mayor's, finance and planning seats; set b: in works, registry and environment). In every town: the finance seat's letters to the bank on days 9 and 23 were answered with statements (six wage payments and the builder's invoice in the first; "since our last statement to you" in the second); the mayor's vote on the opening ballot was answered by the clerk the same day ("held and closed before the year began"); a proposal put on day 3 had its result on day 18 naming each councillor's vote; the mayor's withdrawal of a wage instruction was refused ("mayor is not an authorised signatory for acc-city") and the wage went on being paid; the works seat's two letters to the code mayor were each acknowledged the same day; every new starter in set b (eight), and three of four in set a, had a notice and a wage instruction from the notice's first pay day, and was paid on it where it fell within the sixty days (the fourth is the second finding below).
  - **Found 1: the seat was never shown the notice.** A seat is shown what is new to it; a paper its own organisation files is on its file and is not put in front of it. So the finance seat's sittings after a notice showed no payroll paper at all. The form-written notice is the record; what reaches the office is a letter. The code hiring office now sends one to the payroll office's post with each notice, in the notice's words, with what the payment should be; the forms' own words (`does`) tell a seat in a hiring office to write to the payroll office too. An office's note of this kind is not answered with a report (`officeNote`).
  - **Found 2, not fixed (another's files): a mock finance seat that is shown an employment offer before the worker has signed it never sets the wage up.** Set a, the first town: the second scientist's offer reached the finance seat on day 24, the signature on day 30 and the notice on day 31, and no wage instruction was ever made; the scientist resigned unpaid on day 52. The code finance office reads whether an agreement is in force from the reading that came with it, and the mock seat's brain appears not to be given the later reading (the same office run by code, set b, paid every starter). It is in how a mock seat feeds its brain (`participants/src/llm/mock.ts`), was so before this work (the wage was set up from the same reading), and does not touch a real model, which reads the papers itself. It does make a mock finance seat an unreliable stand-in for payroll.
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days, on the tree merged with main at e50b3a0: 6f2531651315bf10, twice (166,908 commands, 166 refused).
  - **Not verified:** that a real model's finance seat, shown the letter, sets the payment up.
  - **Revisit if** the seat's renderer comes to show an organisation's own new papers addressed to an office (then the letter is a duplicate and should go).

- **The outcome signal for citizen models: how a choice turned out, as the citizen came to know it** (2026-10-09; Naz, before the pilot wave: "make sure we capture the reward signal data for the AI citizens"; `participants/src/behaviour/citizen.ts` (recording only), `participants/src/module.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `dataset.ts`, `pilot-report.ts`; contracts: the log's `outcome` annotation, dataset format 0.3.0; `orchestrator/test/outcomes.test.ts`; citizen behaviour unchanged, no version bump).
  - **What was missing.** A run recorded each decision a citizen's mind made and what it had before it ("What a pilot records for citizen models", 2026-10-08), and nothing of how the choice then went for the citizen: whether the shop served them, whether the employer paid, who came to the gathering. That is the payoff the mind itself learns from, and the nearest thing a run has to a reward signal.
  - **The rule it is built on.** The signal is the citizen's own: the evaluation its mind makes of what happened, at the moment it makes it, from what the citizen itself came to know. The platform adds nothing: no reward, no score of good or bad (the dataset schema refuses a field it does not know, and a test refuses any key that reads like a judgement). An outcome is recorded when the citizen comes to know it and says how (`way`: `mine`, `here`, `published`, `ask`, the four ways of docs/design/knowing.md), and holds nothing the citizen did not have before it: every figure in a record is one the citizen's own code had just read from its own observation or its own state.
  - **What the mind already evaluated, and where** (every place `citizen.ts` judges how something went and updates what it has learned; each is now a record):

    | Area | What the citizen comes to know | The mind's evaluation | How known |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | shop | a delivery note for its order: delivered n of m, the refund | payoff = the share served (0 to 10,000), into the shop's attraction; `satisfied_here` for the next trip | mine |
    | job | a wage, as agreed, in its own account | payoff 10,000 into the employer's attraction | mine |
    | job | no wage a pay period and five days after the last | payoff 0; anger with the employer 8,000; it resigns and claims the debt | mine |
    | job | an enterprise agreement at its workplace, read at the notices at work | its wage as it now knows it; pays at the new rate that came before it read of the rise are counted as paid | published |
    | membership | the same agreement, as a union member | payoff 6,000 plus ten times the rise in basis points; gratitude to the union 5,000; surer of what the union teaches | published |
    | membership | a stoppage called at its workplace | payoff 3,000 (pay lost) | mine |
    | practice | back from a gathering: who else was there, or turned away | payoff = 2,500 times log(1 + others) plus what its teaching means to them (0 if turned away); surer of what the host teaches by how many came | here |
    | practice | choosing to stay in | payoff = its social need's level, into "stay" | mine |
    | practice | before a first choice | what it expects of staying in (5,000) and, for a gathering a membership of its own names, of that (7,000 plus meaning) | mine |
    | shop, job, practice | what someone it knows answers when asked how things are | another's payoff (how well their shop serves; whether their employer pays; that they go somewhere), weighed below its own | mine (a letter to it) |
    | belief | told that someone holds what a host teaches | surer of it, if it holds it already | mine |
    | home | a rent increase; a landlord's notice | anger with the landlord (no attraction: **the mind learns nothing of a home**) | mine |
    | home, job | a lease or a job that came of a lead | gratitude to whoever gave it, and a closer tie | mine |
    | goal | the need behind a goal recovered, or a method's three months ran out | the need's level against what was wanted | mine |
    | (state) | money short; waste uncollected; the week's approval of the town's government | fear for money, anger with the town, approval: **not recorded as outcomes** (they follow no choice; the strongest feeling is in the next decision's `state`, approval in the vote's scores) | |

  - **What is recorded for each** (`OutcomeRecord`, `participants/src/module.ts`): `t` (when the citizen came to know it); `domain` and `option` (the area and what it is about, as the decision named them); `of` (the decision it follows, by the citizen's own count of its decisions, now on every decision as `n`); `kind` (served, paid, unpaid, hired, ended ...); `way`; `from` (who told it); `facts` (ordered 9, delivered 6, refund; the amount paid, when, days since the last pay against the period; periods missed and what is owed; others at the gathering; who ended a job or a tenancy and after how many days); `learned` (the payoff the mind computed, the option's attraction before and after, `first` where it had never tried it, `heard` for another's payoff); `need`; `felt` (the emotion, about whom, the cause's strength, the level before and after); `belief` (before and after).
  - **Facts added where the mind evaluates nothing**, so that a choice's whole course is there: a job `hired` (the wage, the days without work before it) and `ended` (who ended it, days held); a home `lease_signed`, `moved_in` or `not_in_yet` (why the move was refused), `rent_increase` (the rent, what it was, whether bearable, whether challenged), `renewed`, `notice_received`, `ended`; a membership `joined` (the dues); a business `founded` or `refused` and its `capital_called`; a petition's `signatures` as its organiser counts them, and `closed`.
  - **Several outcomes over time.** Each is a record of its own when it is learned: a job is hired, paid each pay day, perhaps unpaid, ended. An outcome follows the citizen's latest decision that chose that option. One that follows none (a job or home held from the start; what a friend said; what was expected before trying) has no `of`, and is still recorded: every update of what a citizen has learned is in the log, so `learned` at any decision can be rebuilt.
  - **Decisions the mind does not make by scoring options.** Joining the union, and a vote, were already recorded with the chance or the ranking as scores. **Starting a business** and **a petition** (starting one; signing, and once not signing when first seen) are now recorded as decisions too, from the chance or the threshold as the person came to it, so their outcomes have something to follow. **Trying another shop** for what the trip's shop could not serve was a choice of the mind's that was never recorded; it is now (`follows`: the trip's decision). Outcomes: union, the membership signed, a rise won, a stoppage; business, founded or refused, capital called; petition, the organiser's running count and its closing. **None, ever:** a vote (the result is published; today's citizen reads none); signing a petition, or deciding not to start one; deciding not to join or not to found; leaving town (not recorded as a decision: the citizen is gone). A home or a job applied for and never offered has an empty list: the citizen is told nothing.
  - **Not recorded as decisions, so with no outcomes** (today's rules, not the mind's; their reasons are in the act): claiming support, borrowing, buying or selling a home, a complaint, the tribunal, standing for office, having a child, taking goods at work.
  - **The contract change** (contracts/README.md has it field by field; under the standing permission for readiness changes, to look over). (1) The log's annotations gain the kind `outcome`: `{ annotation: "outcome", subject, data: { outcomes: [...] } }`, one entry for all a citizen learned since its last action; a `decision`'s data gains `n` and `follows`. The engine checks annotations against the schema, so it was rebuilt. (2) The dataset format is 0.3.0: `citizen_decisions.jsonl` rows gain `n`, `follows` and `outcomes` (nested: one row per decision with what came of it; **empty: nothing learned before the run ended, which is "not known", never a payoff of nought**; absent: a log from before this); a new file `citizen_outcomes.jsonl` (the flat list, with `of`, `decision_seq`, `decision_t`); the manifest gains `citizens` (decisions and outcomes in all and by area, and how many decisions have an outcome). An older log still exports, its rows as before (tested).
  - **One entry per wake, not per outcome.** A log entry's chain fields are about 230 bytes, more than most outcomes; all a citizen learned since its last action goes in one entry. Nothing is sampled: sampling would break the chain of what a citizen learned.
  - **A new kind, not fields on `decision`:** an outcome is known days or months after its decision is written, and the log is append-only; and many outcomes follow no decision at all.
  - **On wherever decisions are, off with them.** `--record-decisions none` and a lean log leave both out; nothing new to set. A resumed run reads the setting back from the log's opening note as before (`batch.ts`, `runOne`); a test stops a run at day 10, resumes it as the pilot queue does, and finds the same outcome entries as the run that was never stopped, and none where none were asked for. A pilot started with the queue's standard command records both. `oikos pilot-report` says so in one line: `citizen records: 28137 decisions, 35783 outcomes`, or `citizen records: NONE (...)`.
  - **It does not change the world** (`orchestrator/test/outcomes.test.ts`, and `logs.test.ts` for the small town). The 1,000-person town, seed 1, 30 days: main at f6ac4ee ends at 5be63866badc311a; this branch ends there with outcomes recorded and with `--record-decisions none`. At 60 days all four (main and this branch, recorded and not) end at ce822ecc916b8bc5 with 334,151 commands and 257 refused. What was touched in the citizen is wrappers that read before and after an update the mind was making anyway; two conditions were split to name the chance drawn (a business, a petition), with the draw made under exactly the conditions it was.
  - **Cost, measured** (the 1,000-person town, seed 1, 60 days, mock, plain logs). Log: 311.7 MB with nothing recorded; 336.6 MB on main with decisions; 347.6 MB now (decisions 25.4 MB, 7.3%: 28,137 of them, 605 more than main's 27,532 for the newly recorded kinds, and each numbered; outcomes 10.5 MB, 3.0%: 35,783 in 15,936 entries, about 290 bytes each). Processor time of the whole batch, side by side: 71.0 s recorded, 69.5 s not (main, earlier and on a busier machine: 61.3 s and 60.5 s); the difference is within what the shared machine moves between two runs. The dataset: `citizen_decisions.jsonl` 24.4 MB, `citizen_outcomes.jsonl` 9.6 MB.
  - **What a 180-day pilot will weigh** (three times the 60 days, which holds while the town is steady): about 32 MB of outcomes and 76 MB of decisions in a log of a little over 1 GB before compression (logs compress to about a seventh). Two thirds of the outcome rows are "stayed in" (23,223 of 35,783), the least informative kind; wages are 1,778 rows, 30 a day.
  - **Found in the mind's evaluation, listed and not touched** (this work records; the citizen redesign decides):
    1. *Nothing is learned of a home.* No payoff is ever computed for one, so a home is always chosen by deliberating or by a friend's word, never by experience.
    2. *A job's payoff has two values.* 10,000 for a wage as agreed, 0 for none: the wage's size, the hours and whether the job lasted never enter what is learned. In a calm town every pay day teaches the same.
    3. *Every update fades every other option of the area toward nought,* not toward what was expected of it (experience-weighted attraction with nothing forgone): a gathering never gone to loses about a tenth of its attraction each time the citizen learns anything else in that area. And "stayed in" is learned once for each gathering not gone to that week, so a citizen with five gatherings in reach learns it five times a week.
    4. *What is expected of staying in is itself learned as an experience* (5,000 folded into a prior of 4,000 gives 4,526), not set.
    5. *A rise the union won is worth the same to every member* (8,000 for a 2% rise), whatever they earn.
    6. *A vote's recorded options carried the ballot's number* beside key and score, which the dataset contract does not allow; the record now has key and score (the number is in the act).
  - **Merged with main at 130fa3a (2026-10-09, later), which gave the citizen work by the day and work for oneself.** Their outcomes: a day's pay is a `paid` like any wage (`period_days` 1; the mind learns 10,000 of the employer); work by the day that brought no pay for most of a week is `no_work` (a fact: the mind computes nothing, nothing is owed, the job then `ended` by the worker); what a person's own business pays them is `own_work` / `drawn` (the amount and when: a fact, following no decision, since working for oneself is how the person starts and the mind makes nothing of it; the business's takings are the business's, and the person knows what it paid them). The hash check again on that main: the 1,000-person town, seed 1, 30 days, ends at 8a5441ddc8a1408a on main, and on the merge recorded and not. A town from a profile with informal work (30 days): 142 drawings recorded, no `no_work` yet.
  - **Model seats, cheaply: what came of an act, by reference.** No reward is designed for seats. A seat's call already had its commands; each act now says what it made (`created`: the ids of the records and letters written as it was applied), and a later call says what the seat had been shown since that names one of them (`came_back`: `of`, the command's `seq`, and `in`, the record or letter that names it): the council's ballot on its proposal, the permit decided on its application, the builder's signature on its agreement, a reply to its letter. Read from the observations a run already records for model seats.
  - **Found on the way, and fixed in the export: a refused act was written as applied.** An act takes time; its refusal is logged when it ends, with the step of the clock that ended it as its cause, not the act. `oikos dataset` looked for a refusal under the act's own command and never found one: in the dataset test's 40-day town 13 acts were refused and none was written so (0 of 13); in the 1,000-person town's 30 days, 0 of 130. So `applied` in `actions.jsonl`, on a seat's `commands` and on a translation's `executed` has been `true` for every act since acts took time. The export now follows the act's action (`action_started` names both); the test counts the log's refusals against the rows. **Datasets made before 2026-10-09 should be made again from their logs** (the logs are right). **Not fixed, the same fault in another reader:** `orchestrator/src/corpus.ts` (`oikos corpus`, and through it `in-situ.ts`) joins a refusal the same way, so the translator corpus's `executed.applied` is `true` for acts that were refused; in-situ also reads only the lines it filters for, which leave out the entry that starts an action. That is the translator data's code, in other hands today: for whoever has it.
  - **For research, and kept out of the citizen's record on purpose:** what the citizen never learns (who got the home they applied for; whether the shop they left closed; what the wage would have been elsewhere; how the election came out). Whoever measures reads those from the log; putting them in the citizen's record would give a model trained on it sight no citizen has.
  - **Not verified:** a pilot with model seats (the mock only; nothing here depends on a seat); a log longer than 60 days through the export (it holds a run's outcomes in memory, about 10 MB for these 60 days); a citizen whose controller is started again mid-run (its count of decisions starts again; the export joins an outcome to the latest decision of that number, which is the right one, but no test makes it happen).
  - **Revisit if** a trainer wants an outcome joined to the order or the application rather than the latest decision that chose the option (the order's id is in the facts; an application's is not); the citizen redesign changes what the mind evaluates (each new evaluation should be recorded where it is made, through the same four helpers: `learn`, `hearOf`, `felt`, `outcome`); or "stayed in" proves to be noise worth folding into its decision.

- **Wave 2's final pass: ready to start on origin/main 923d139** (2026-10-09; `docs/waves/wave-2/`). Everything the wave waited for is on main, so: the three pilots with a model council clerk leave their held file and run in their lanes, w2-01 in the shake-down as the test (the "0 for, 0 against" was the mock sitting weekly; a ballot closing is no paper and brings no seat back, so a real clerk must arrange to be at the count: stopped if no result is declared within three weeks of a ballot opening); the three works pilots with a crew to take on wait for nothing; the Haiku low-effort measurement uses `seat_effort=low` and names its model plainly; `wake_on_papers` stays on everywhere, and every estimate predates it; a report saying `citizen records: NONE` stops its pilot; five towns are marked as flooding until the river's change lands. Nine queue files, 50 pilots, 38 of which need no Codex. Mock dry run of every entry, 20 days, on d6d6a24: 50 of 50. The plan has the commands that start the shake-down and the stopping rules as a checklist. **Not verified:** the translator under prompt 0.9.1 (no model was called in this pass); a ballot under a clerk seat, real or mock; how much more seats sit with papers bringing them back. **Revisit if** w2-01's clerk declares nothing (then w2-03 and w2-07 come out of the body), or the shake-down's usage is far over the estimates (then the rates in `make.ts` before 2b).

- **An office held by a seat gets its work done: why a hired crew did nothing, and what a seat is now shown** (2026-10-09; the wave's shake-down review, fault 1; docs/behaviour/firms.md, "An offer made on an advertisement"; standing-work.md, "The staff's report"; office-papers.md, "An office's own staff"; `scripts/office-work-replay.ts`).
  - **What happened** (`runs/w2-10-works`, read from the log). The works seat (Sonnet) advertised six posts on its form on day 1 (rec.1081), set `work(at=town-hall, every="once a week", task=collect)` and `work(at=town-hall, every="every day", task=maintain)` the same day (rec.1082, rec.1083: both in the shape the staff routine reads), offered employment to five applicants on days 4 and 5, and filed their payroll notices on day 8. All five signed. In 180 days there was not one arrival at the depot, not one act of the crew's, and 471 complaints.
  - **Why.** The staff routine was sound and so were the orders: the crew does the work with whoever of the staff is at the depot. Nobody ever was. The seat asked to "offer employment as works crew to c0113 on my posting rec.1081, at this pay", and the translator wrote `agreement(basis=rec.1081, template=employment, we_do=money(...), with=c0113)`: the pay and the advertisement cited, and nothing of where the work is. The code that runs an employer writes the place of work into every offer (the worker "will be in" the workplace); a person goes to work where their agreement says, and these five agreements said nowhere. They were employed, were put on the payroll, and stayed at home. Nothing was missing from the staff post, the orders or the roster's count; the mock demonstration of the same morning had worked because the mock's offers are the code's.
  - **Why the seat could not tell.** Its roster said "In post (6)" (five of the crew and, wrongly, the environment office's scientist, whose offer in the same words named no post and so was counted with the crew: the seat stopped recruiting one short). Its look at the depot said "0 people" at every sitting, which it took for the hour of the day. No paper said that an order was not being carried out. Its debrief: "I treated 'crew 6/6, budget full' as a wall and then stopped".
  - **The fix, in three parts.** (1) *An offer made on an advertisement is on the advertisement's terms*: an employment agreement that says nothing of where the work is, and cites a job advertisement or an application that answers one, is for work where the advertisement says, and in the post it advertised. Read so by the worker (who saw the advertisement when applying) and by the employer (whose advertisement it is), each from papers they have; no agreement is rewritten and the kernel knows nothing of it. What an agreement itself says stands. (2) *The preview of such an offer says where the work will be*, or that it names no place and cites no advertisement, "whoever signs it is paid and has nowhere to come to work". (3) *The staff report to their office*: what they did under each standing order, or that one is not being carried out and why (nobody of those in post at the depot; no routine of that name; on hold; not begun), on the organisation's own file, the day it changes and about weekly otherwise; and the seat's roster says for each person in post when they last worked, or that they have not come in and why, and under it each order as the staff last reported it. With nobody in post the roster says each order is "carried out by nobody".
  - **Why read the advertisement, not write the place into the agreement.** The fuller agreement would be the better record, and it belongs where the request is read (the resolver could add the advertisement's terms to an offer that cites one). That file is being changed by other work today; this fix had to hold whatever a seat's offer says, including an offer that cites the application only. Both can stand together: an agreement that states its place is read as it states.
  - **Real-world basis.** Written particulars of employment include the place of work, and a silent contract takes its terms from what was advertised; a depot returns to its manager what was done against the schedule and what was not (docs/research/references.md, both to confirm).
  - **The replay** (`bun scripts/office-work-replay.ts works --out DIR`): the pilot's own town (seed 110, the same profile, the crew still to be taken on), a mock seat making the pilot's requests in the pilot's words on the pilot's days, the translator's calls as logged. The same five people apply and sign. On main, 30 days: 0 arrivals at the depot, 0 collections, 289 complaints (the pilot: 288 in its first 30 days). On this branch, 180 days: the five come to the depot from day 4 (30 arrivals a week), 6,047 collections (430 in the first week, the backlog; 215 a week after, 234 as the round grows), 339 upkeep jobs, 4 complaints in all (week 8). The pilot, by week: 0 collections; complaints 0, 0, 146, 110, 76, 24, 17, 6, 7, 5, 3, 1, 3, 0, 14, 12, 12, 11, 8, 3, 3, 3, 1, 2, 2, 2 (471). The roster reads "In post (5) ... Vacant: 1" (it read 6 of 6), each with "last at work year 1, day 172 (maintain)", and the orders "carried out: 234 calls at addresses, 750 loads" and "carried out: 5 upkeep jobs, 236 units of upkeep; 321 worn assets were left when the crew's hours ran out". 26 reports from the crew in the half year.
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days, no model seat: 6f2531651315bf10, twice (main at 0c30df9, run from the wave's pinned copy: the same; 166,908 commands, 166 refused). No code-run office changed: its offers state the place of work and name the post, and it has no staff post to report.
  - **Also found, not changed.** A seat's look at its premises is of the moment of its sitting, which is before its staff arrive (the factory seat of `w2-09` read "0 people" and "1 of 40 present" for a month while about 38 came in each working day, a quarter of an hour after it looked): the roster's "last at work" now says who came. The works seat is shown the applications to every advertisement of its organisation and not which advertisement is its own (it looked both up). An order's `at` is recorded and not checked: the staff work from their own premises.
  - **No contract changed.** One new kind of paper, `staff_report`, a statement like any other; a seat with routines has one more channel of its own papers ("Reports from the staff on the work under the standing work orders"). The generator is 0.45.0, `city.works` 0.6.0, `citizen.default` 0.43.2.

- **A date for when a standing payment starts; a count with grouped digits; a value the call could not be read at is tried again** (2026-10-09; wave 2a's review, fault 5; translator prompt 0.9.2; `participants/src/calls.ts` (`parseWhen`, `parseCount`), `participants/src/contracts.ts` (`firstDue`), `translator/src/resolver.ts` and `index.ts`, `kernel/crates/resolver/src/calls.rs` and `resolve.rs`, the bank, the employer and the tenant that read a standing instruction, `contracts/calls.md`, `contracts/outcomes.schema.json`, `contracts/test/when.json`; tests `translator/test/when.test.ts`, `ask-again.test.ts`, the kernel resolver's `when_and_counts_as_the_shared_table_says`).
  - **The faults.** Seats write dates. "From year 1, day 1" and "first pay year 1, day 22" became `first="year 1 day 1"`, which both resolvers read as a length of time and refused; because the words were in the seat's request, the exchange ended there with no second attempt and the seat was told to write "a plain figure", which a date cannot be (six ask-backs in two pilots; every seat got through only by deleting the date). `quantity="60,000"` was refused because a count took bare digits only, where an amount takes the place's grouping.
  - **What is right, by the world and the contract.** A standing order's first payment date is a date ("first payment on 15 March"); a length of time is the other honest way to say it ("in a fortnight"). The contract had only the second. So `first` (payments and standing work) and `until` (standing work) now take either, each read one way: a date as the world's papers write one ("year 1, day 22", comma or none, "day 22" of the year it now is, "year 2", "tomorrow") or a length of time ("14 days", "today": none), with the words people put round them read past ("from", "on", "starting", "in", "after", "until", "... from now"). Bare digits are neither.
  - **A date is kept as a date.** A date turned into a length of time when the draft is made would be a second off by the time the paper is lodged (the act is recorded a second after the draft; a bank that goes through its instructions a day apart could pay a day late) and days off if a draft were confirmed later. So a request, or a standing work order, carries `first_at` (the moment the day begins) where a date was given, and `first` (seconds after it is lodged) where a length of time was, and everyone who acts on one reads it by one function, `firstDue`: `first_at`, never before the day the paper was lodged (so nothing is made up for days before it); else `first` after it; else the keeper's default (a payment: one period; a work order: at once). The request's own words say a date where one was given ("…every 14 days, the first on year 1, day 45"). A date before today is a question back with today's date, and so is `first` on a payment asked for once (the bank makes it when asked; until now the date was silently dropped). An end date is the end of that day.
  - **A count** takes the digits an amount would: `parseCount` with the world's currency reads the grouped digits through the amount reader with no decimals and no sign or word of money ("60,000"; "60.000" where a point groups; "1,50,000" where the place groups in twos; "60k"), and refuses what an amount's digits could not be. Nought only on a form's count, as before.
  - **Whose fault a value is.** The rule built for forms (a value the request never wrote is the call's fault: tried again, and never put to the seat) now holds for every value that can't be read, the seat's own words included, because it is the call that put those words where a figure goes ("£8,643.66 per 73 days" in a wage field was the translator joining two things, and was reported "as you wrote it"). One more attempt, told which value could not be read and how such a value is written; if that does no better, or gives the request up, the seat is asked once, about its own words: `"next Tuesday", in what you asked, could not be read as a date or a length of time. Please say it again with a date, written like "year 1, day 12", or a length of time from now, like "14 days".` (for a length of time: "…written as a number of days, weeks or months, like "14 days""; for a number or an amount: "…written in figures").
  - **The translator's prompt, 0.9.2**, exactly: one line added to the rules ("first= is when a payment or a job done again and again is to start, only where the request says when: the request's own words for the date ("year 1, day 22") or for how long from now ("14 days", "today"), copied whole and by themselves, never joined with how often."); in the standing-work rule, "first= only if it says how long until it starts, and until= only if it says for how long it is to go on" became "first= only if it says when it starts (a date, or how long from now), and until= only if it says when it ends (a date) or for how long it is to go on"; one worked example (a standing payment with a first date); and the contract's syntax, which the prompt quotes, gained its line on when. Seen cases: `pay-standing-first-date`, `pay-standing-first-date-plain`, `pay-standing-first-length`, `standing-work-from-date`, `move-goods-grouped`. Nothing was worded to the held-out cases, which were not read.
  - **Contracts** (under the standing approval; to look over): `outcomes.schema.json`, `RequestData.first_at`; `calls.md`, when and counts; `contracts/test/when.json`, which both resolvers are held to. `calls.schema.json` and the blocks are unchanged. No state changes: no code participant writes a date (the state hash of the 1,000-person town is main's).
  - **Not verified:** any model under prompt 0.9.2 (none was called); the trained translator knows none of it, and will go on writing lengths of time, which are still read.
  - **Revisit if** seats write dates another way (a weekday, "the 15th": there is no calendar to read them by), a keeper other than the bank acts on standing requests and counts differently (it should use `firstDue`), or the retry makes a translator drop what the seat meant (the preview is then the seat's check: a dropped `every` reads as a payment made once).

- **The preview says when a standing payment's first payment falls, as the bank will count it** (2026-10-09; wave 2a's review, fault 2; `translator/src/preview.ts`, `participants/src/llm/render.ts`; test `translator/test/first-falls.test.ts`).
  - **The fault, which corrupted training labels.** A finance seat wanted a wage to start on year 1, day 22. On day 8 its draft said `first="14 days"`, which was right, and the preview read "with these details: first: year 1, day 15": a length of time, counted by the bank from the day it has the instruction, shown as a date counted from the world's start. The seat declined four right drafts for it, then on day 15 confirmed `first="21 days"` because the preview read "first: year 1, day 22", and the wage started on day 36. With no `first` at all the preview said nothing, and the seat declined for fear of a payment going out that day. A seat's sign-off is the label the translator learns from.
  - **What a seat reads now**, in a sentence of its own after the request's words, counted by the function the bank counts by (`firstDue`): for a date, "The first payment falls due on year 1, day 45, and then every 14 days from that date."; for a length of time, "The first payment falls due 21 days after this is lodged: on year 1, day 52 if it is lodged today (year 1, day 31), and then every 14 days."; for neither, the bank's own rule, "No first date is given: the first payment falls due 14 days after this is lodged, one whole period: on year 1, day 45 if it is lodged today (year 1, day 31), and then every 14 days."; for today, "…falls due as soon as this is lodged…". "Falls due", not "is paid": the bank pays what is due when it next goes through its instructions.
  - **Every other time a preview shows, checked against what the keeper does** (the drafts of the six finished pilots were read for it):
    - a standing work order's start and end were not shown at all beyond the order's own words ("the first in 3 days, for 56 days"): now "It is in force as soon as it is on file." / "It comes into force 3 days after it is put on file: on year 1, day 34 if that is today (year 1, day 31)." / "It is in force from year 1, day 40.", and "It stands until year 1, day 87, 09:00." or "It stands to the end of year 1, day 90." (only when it comes into force is said: that is all its staff read of it);
    - a payroll notice's first pay day read "first pay: 6652800" (seconds), in the preview and in the seat's own copy, 33 times in one pilot: dates by the names office papers give them (`first_pay`, `last_day`, `last_from`, `period_end`, and a new rent's `from`) are read as dates, and a `fine` as money;
    - `every`, an agreement's `term` and `notice`: lengths of time, shown as such, and right; a ballot's close (`closes_at`, made from "open for" when the paper is drafted) and a form's date fields: moments, shown as dates, and right; `until` on a work order: a moment, right;
    - not changed: a request's own words round a period under half a day to "every 0 days" (no seat or code asks for one; the preview's sentence says the period rightly).
  - **A seat's own copy of the paper** said nothing of when a standing instruction first falls due, and showed a work order's `first` as a date from the world's start. It now reads "…every 14 days, the first due year 1, day 36, 09:00", and a work order's details carry "first due". In any paper's details, `first` beside what the paper is for reads "21 days after it is lodged".
  - **No contract change.** What a seat is told is its own request, today's date and the rule the bank publishes by acting on it; nothing it could not otherwise know.
  - **Not verified:** a model seat reading the new sentences (none was called).
  - **Revisit if** a draft can be confirmed on a later day than it was made (the "if it is lodged today" would then want the day it is confirmed), or the bank comes to pay on a calendar of its own.

- **The tax law says how a pay's withholding is reckoned, step by step: the thirty hundredths** (2026-10-09; wave 2a's review, fault 4; generator 0.44.1; `participants/src/behaviour/tax.ts` (`withholdingInWords`), `worlds/generator/generate.ts`, `docs/behaviour/public-finance.md`; tests `participants/test/tax.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/places.test.ts`).
  - **The fault.** In the Ohio town a works crew's wage is 2,360.00 for 14 days. The bank's opening wage instruction pays 1,942.46 (417.54 withheld). The finance seat worked the withholding out from the tax law and came to 1,942.76 (417.24), judged the instructions wrong, and withdrew all eight; eight workers went unpaid for the month.
  - **The thirty hundredths, exactly.** Both sums use the law's schedule correctly. They differ in how a pay becomes a year's pay. Every payroll here reckons by days: 2,360.00 x 365 / 14 = 61,528.57 a year (26.07 pays), on which the income tax is 995.00 + 312.37 + 4,871.71 = 6,179.08, Social Security 3,814.77 and Medicare 892.16: 10,886.01 in all, of which 14/365 is 417.54. The seat reckoned as a person with a calendar does, 26 pays: 61,360.00 a year, income tax 6,154.23, a twenty-sixth of it 236.70, and 6.2% and 1.45% of the pay itself (146.32 and 34.22): 417.24. The two contributions come to the same either way (a flat rate on a pay is the same by any route); the income tax does not: by days it is 6,179.08 x 14 / 365 = 237.00 a pay, by 26 pays 236.70. Two things make up the 0.30: the year by days is 168.57 longer in pay, all of it in the 14.75% band (24.85 more tax a year: 0.95 a pay), and that year's tax is spread over 26.07 pays, not 26 (0.65 a pay less). Nothing was rounded separately and no ceiling or rebate is involved: it is the year's length in pays.
  - **Not a disagreement in the code.** The opening instructions, every employer's payroll, a worker's check of their own pay and a payment reckoned on net pay all call one function (`withheld`; ten call sites, checked). The disagreement was between that function and the law's words, which said only "Employers withhold each from every pay, reckoned as a year's pay": a rule a reader completes from habit, and the habit (a whole number of pays) is not the function's.
  - **The fix: the law says the rule, with each rounding.** "What is withheld from a pay is reckoned in three steps, and in no other way.
