One: the pay is taken as a year's pay, by multiplying it by 365 and dividing by the number of days the pay is for, rounded down to the smallest unit of money. (A year is 365 days: a pay for 14 days is 14/365 of a year's pay, and a year is not taken as a whole number of pays.) Two: each charge is reckoned on that year's pay as set out above, each band's part rounded down. Three: the year's charges are added together, and that sum, multiplied by the number of days the pay is for and divided by 365, rounded down, is what is withheld from the pay. Of what is withheld, each charge's part is its own year's amount multiplied and divided the same way, rounded down, and what that leaves over goes with the first charge that takes anything. Pay for a day's work is taken as pay for 1.4 days: a week over its 5 working days." The words are made beside the function (`withholdingInWords`), and a test works the three steps by plain arithmetic and gets the function's figure.
  - **Every profile has the same gap** wherever its rates step (the opening instruction against a year of 26 pays, on the profile's lowest, middle and highest wage for 14 days; the instruction's figure is the first):

    | profile | withheld by days (the instruction) | by 26 pays | apart |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | au-vic | 323.00 / 606.66 | 322.03 / 605.69 | 0.97 |
    | br-mg | 109.34 / 109.78 / 120.30 | 109.23 / 109.64 / 120.16 | 0.11 to 0.14 |
    | de-ni | 598.95 / 863.65 / 1,057.98 | 598.35 / 862.81 / 1,057.14 | 0.60 to 0.84 |
    | gb-eng | 222.08 / 284.52 / 329.15 | 221.71 / 284.15 / 328.78 | 0.37 |
    | in-tn | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 | none (no tax at these wages) |
    | jp-akita | 27,080 / 29,576 / 33,594 | 27,071 / 29,554 / 33,572 | 9 to 22 |
    | ke-nakuru | 729.86 / 879.09 / 879.10 | 729.86 / 879.09 / 879.10 | none (the charges that bite are flat) |
    | mx-jal | 410.61 / 525.84 / 673.05 | 410.15 / 524.58 / 671.43 | 0.46 to 1.62 |
    | us-oh | 182.25 / 335.83 / 417.54 | 181.95 / 335.52 / 417.24 | 0.30 |

    In all nine the opening instruction equals the law's three steps worked by hand, for every wage instruction of a 300-person town (the new test): there was never a second figure in the world, only a second route in a reader's head. Contribution ceilings and rebates were looked at for a separate rounding and have none: a ceiling and a rebate are applied to the year's pay inside step two.
  - **Why the rule was not changed to whole pays.** It would match a reader's habit (a payroll's tables are made for 26, 52 or 12 pays a year). But the world's year is 365 days and a pay is paid every 14 of them, 26.07 times a year: on 26 pays a year a worker's yearly tax would be reckoned on less than they are paid, and a pay period that does not divide the year (30 days, 73 days) has no whole number to use. It would also change every wage in every town. The words now carry the rule instead; no figure changed.
  - **The state hash changes, for this reason and no other:** the law's text is a record of the world, and it is longer. The 1,000-person town (seed 1, 30 days): main `6f2531651315bf10`, this change `c893810bf9113fcb`, twice. Its 166,908 commands and 166 refusals are main's: the same acts.
  - **Not verified:** a model seat reading the new words and coming to the instruction's figure (none was called). It is the claim the change rests on.
  - **Revisit if** a seat still reckons by whole pays with the words in front of it (then the next step is to show the working on the instruction itself: the year's pay and each charge, which the opening instruction could carry), or the pay period becomes a calendar's (monthly pay on a calendar would make whole pays the true rule).

- **The council's standing orders, and what a councillor has on the desk** (2026-10-09; wave 2a's review, fault 6; generator 0.45.0, city.councillor 0.6.0; `worlds/generator/generate.ts`, `participants/src/behaviour/government.ts`, `docs/behaviour/government.md`; test `orchestrator/test/council-seats.test.ts`).
  - **The fault.** Seven Sonnet seats (clerk, five councillors, mayor) made no request in 45 days. A councillor's standing instructions were 1,026 characters and its only papers one closed ballot: no charter, no form, no proposals, no petitions, no budget. Two said afterwards they had not known what they could do. The clerk told one it had found no rule on file that says who may make a proposal.
  - **What the town's law data said.** The charter does say who: "The council makes the town's laws by majority vote, on proposals from the mayor or any councillor." The clerk was not shown the charter. And nothing anywhere said how: on what form, filed with whom, how it comes to a vote, how the vote is taken, counted and declared, what becomes of a petition. That was the gap, and it is filled as law data: `proc-council`, the council's standing orders, a published procedure under the charter in seven orders (docs/behaviour/government.md has them). They are written from what the clerk's office does (every proposal on the form to a ballot open 14 days; the latest vote of each councillor in post; more yes than no and more than half of all; the result naming who voted), so they bind nothing new. One point is the orders' own: who may put a proposal follows the charter (the mayor or a councillor), where the code clerk ballots whatever is filed on the form; no code participant but the mayor files one, and a model clerk now has the rule to hold to.
  - **What a councillor seat now has** (a model's; the code's post is unchanged, which reads ballots and nothing else): on file, the charter, the standing orders, the town's laws and the forms (the council proposal form, each law's amendment form); coming to it, the proposals put to the council and its ballots as papers of its own body, and the petitions lodged, their counts, budgets adopted and results declared; its files and who's who on request. The clerk's seat gains the charter and the standing orders on file, and the council's table. Each is published, or the seat's own body's papers: nothing is a whole view of anything, and `orchestrator/test/no-god-view.test.ts` passes with nothing owed.
  - **Brought back in time to vote.** A councillor's ballots came through a published channel, which is no in-tray: nothing brought the seat back before the week it had named. Proposals and ballots now also reach it as its own body's papers, so one filed brings it to its desk at the next working day's sitting.
  - **The mock council** (the test, and run by hand): councillors who say they are back in a week; councillor 4 given a motion (a law, bearing on tenants). Day 8, its next sitting, the proposal on the form, drafted and confirmed; day 9 the clerk's ballot, open 14 days, and four councillors back at their desks for the proposal; day 10 all five back for the ballot and voting (2 yes, 3 no, by their leanings); day 23 the clerk's result: "Rejected: 2 for, 3 against. Voting for: councillor-4, councillor-5; against: councillor-1, councillor-2, councillor-3." No request was asked back.
  - **A councillor's motion as a parameter** (`motion`, none by default): how a mock council is given business. It is content of a town's description; nothing generated sets one.
  - **The state hash changes again**, because `proc-council` is one more published record in every town (the 1,000-person town, seed 1, 30 days: `c893810bf9113fcb` to `3ce67a2b28f9a07c`, twice; the same 166,908 commands and 166 refusals).
  - **Not done, on purpose:** nothing prompts a seat to act; the mayor's seat is unchanged (it had the forms and the charter and judged a petition of 1.3% of the town not worth acting on, which is its to judge); the wave's council pilots still have no business unless a scenario gives them some (the review's point about w2-26 stands).
  - **Not verified:** a model councillor reading this and moving or voting (none was called); a model clerk counting at the close (a ballot closing is still no paper: the clerk must be at its desk, which the mock's daily rhythm is).
  - **Revisit if** councillors given all this still do nothing where there is business (then the question is the seats' framing, not their papers), the prompt's size matters (a councillor's standing papers are now the town's laws and forms, as the mayor's are), or the orders and the code clerk part ways on who may propose in a run (then the clerk's code should hold to the orders too).

- **Smaller things a seat read or wrote, from wave 2a's review** (2026-10-09; faults 7 to 9 and the notes on the low-effort seats; `participants/src/llm/participant.ts`, `translator/src/preview.ts`, `worlds/generator/generate.ts`; test `participants/test/seat-letters.test.ts`).
  - **A name with its id in brackets is that id.** A seat is shown people and organisations as "Town of Millbrook (city)", and a seat at low effort wrote a letter to exactly that; it was refused as no id. Whom a letter goes to, what it is about and the paper a look names are now read out of that form too ("Name (id)", with the square brackets a report uses or without). A name alone ("Millbrook Savings Bank") is still no id: nothing knows a name's id for a seat that has not looked it up, and guessing one would send a letter astray. The refusal now says where the id is: `"Millbrook Savings Bank" isn't an id: a letter goes to people and organisations by the ids your reports give them, the word in brackets after a name, as in "Name (id)" (to find one, look them up in who's who)`.
  - **Words to find, given as something to find.** A look takes the words to look for as `words` and what papers are about as `about`; a seat gave them as `find: [{ field: "words", ... }]` and was told `"words" isn't something papers can be found by`. Given so (field `words` or `text`, or `about`), they are now taken as the look's own. Any other field papers cannot be found by is refused as before, in that sentence.
  - **Complaints came to the works manager under the heading "Budgets"** (the folder holds both): it is headed "Budgets, and complaints about the town's services". (One line of the works office's channels, in the generator: the other agent of this wave is in that office's staff; the line is the heading only.)
  - **"a employment agreement"**, "a invoice": the preview's article follows the word.
  - **Left, with why.** The wage offer's words, "a rise of 100 hundredths of a percent" (true, read rightly by the seat from the details beside it, "1%"; mending it means a paper's words knowing a rate from a count, in both resolvers and the shops' and factories' forms, which are the other agent's this wave). A form-made paper's words ending ".." where what was filled in ends in a full stop (the words are a record's; changing them changes every such record). The water office's `bill` order that produced no bill (utilities: the other agent's). The mayor's search counts that differed between looks, and complaints copied to the environment office: not traced.
  - **The state hash** moves with the folder's heading (a channel's title is part of the world): the 1,000-person town, seed 1, 30 days, `3ce67a2b28f9a07c` to `5ba83fb8c13d1657`, twice, the same commands.
  - **Revisit if** seats write names with no id often (then who's who could be looked up for them at the letter, as an office's post room would: it is an ask of a keeper, not a view), or the wage papers' words mislead someone.

- **An office that buys from outside can place the order; shops and factories cannot be seats yet** (2026-10-09; the shake-down review, fault 3; docs/behaviour/utilities.md, "Buying from the grid"; office-papers.md, "Who buys from outside"; standing-work.md, "Shops and factories").
  - **What happened** (`runs/w2-44-utilities`). The energy office's staff bought once, on day 1, as code does: an `order` paper to the outside's market (rec.1098: 91,080 energy) and a payment with it. The town was generated under the dear-grid scenario, and from about day 10 stock was below a fortnight's use and a month's supply cost more than the account held (45,144.00 against 34,927.20), so the staff, who buy a whole month or nothing, bought nothing and said nothing. The seat saw stock falling and tried, from day 15: a move of goods (refused: it held none to move), a payment alone (sent back by the market the same day: "no order of yours is waiting", words the seat is not shown), a payment to the market's post (no account), a letter in an order's words, an agreement with the outside (never signed), and twice the staff's own order rec.1098 named as a form ("You haven't seen a form by that name"). The market answered nine letters with "What it acts on: an order for what it lists, paid for at its published prices", which does not say what an order is. Stock was empty from day 24.
  - **The cause** is the one the review named: the office had no stationery, so the paper the seller acts on could not be written by a seat.
  - **The fix.** The energy office issues `order` (the form shops and factories had), and so does the builder. The form says what it does: it places the order at the seller's listed price and pays nothing by itself; the whole sum is paid into the account the price list names at the same sitting; the seller delivers once paid in full, sends back money that comes with no order, and declines an order unpaid after a week. The world market's answer to a letter says the same. The energy staff's weekly report says what is held and, when stock is low and nothing was bought, why, with the figures.
  - **Left as it is, for Naz.** The staff's rule of a month or nothing (a mechanism of the code-run office too: under a dear grid a code-run retailer is out of energy for the week before its first bills are paid; nothing downstream reads an empty substation today). A seat is not shown the words that come with a payment (a refund's reason).
  - **The replay** (`bun scripts/office-work-replay.ts energy --out DIR`, and `energy-as-drafted`): the pilot's town and scenario, the three seats' standing orders as they made them, and the energy seat's request of day 15 in its words ("Order 60000 energy from outside at 0.36 each ... paying with the order ... delivered to the substation"). As the pilot's translator drafted it (a payment alone): 21,600.00 out and back on day 15, nothing delivered, and the staff's report of day 16 reads "31526 energy held, below a fortnight's use (58520); a month's from the grid (125400 at ... each) comes to 45,144.00 and the account holds 34,927.20, so nothing was ordered: a smaller order is the office's to place on its order form". As an order on the form with the payment: 60,000 delivered on day 15, the stock never empty, and the staff buy a month's themselves on day 32 once the bills are paid.
  - **Who buys from outside** is tabled in office-papers.md: the energy office (a seat can, now), shops, factories and the builder (each has the form; none can be a seat yet), the works (nothing bought; the landfill is paid by the finance office on its invoice), water (nothing).
  - **Shops and factories cannot be seats yet.** `runs/w2-09-trade`: the factory seat's 40 staff came in every working day (about 38 arrivals a day) and made nothing, because making is an act of the manager's each day naming who is there; the shop seat published no prices (no form writes a price list), so nobody could order from it, and its staff served nobody. Neither was told how its office's work gets done. Converting them means splitting each module's one plan into what the staff do, what they report of demand and stock, and what the manager decides, plus a price list form: a redesign of two modules, not done here and not half-done. Recommended: drop the second trade pilot (w2 shop-2 and factory-2) until then.
  - **Contracts:** none changed (`utility.energy` 0.2.0 and `firm.builder` each issue one more form; the module manifests were regenerated).
  - **Revisit if** a seat still drafts a payment without the order (the translator's prompt lists a seat's forms; no real model has used this one), or energy running out is given consequences (then the month-or-nothing rule matters in every town).

- **A billing order is followed from when it is made; every staff post reports** (2026-10-09; the shake-down review, fault 7; docs/behaviour/standing-work.md, "The staff's report"; utilities.md).
  - **The trace** (`runs/w2-44-utilities`). The water seat set `work(at=lot-19-28, every="every 30 days", task=bill)` on day 1 (rec.1097; it had asked first with "from year 1 day 1", refused as a length of time). The order was in force and the billing staff were following it; but they took only *how often* from it, and kept the office's own first date, a quarter in (day 92). In 43 days nothing was due. Not the fault of the works crew: nobody was missing. The energy bills went out on day 31 (380 of them) because that office's own first date happened to be the order's.
  - **The fix.** Under a standing order the round is the order's: the water and energy staff send the first bills one period after the order came into force, the meter round before them, and a new order starts its own count. The rates notices are left to the rating law's instalments, as the routine's words say.
  - **And nothing told the seat** ("Silent success and silent failure look identical"). The staff's report, built for the works crew in the first of these three entries, is now made by every staff post: the water staff (the days' draw, "the meters are read from year 1, day 41 and the next bills go out on year 1, day 62"), the energy staff, the rates clerks ("the next notices go out on year 1, day 122, as the rating law's instalments fall", or that no property has been valued yet), the doctors and the teachers (who of them worked, patients seen, lessons, classrooms left without a teacher; "none of the N in post was at the clinic when it opened"). The clinic's and the school's rosters show it as the works manager's does.
  - **The replay** (`bun scripts/office-work-replay.ts energy --out DIR`, the pilot's three seats and their orders as made): 215 water bills on day 31 (the pilot: none in 43 days), 380 energy bills the same day, as before.
  - **Hash.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, seed 1, 30 days, no model seat: 6f2531651315bf10, twice, main's: a code-run office keeps its own dates and has no staff post.
  - **Leaves out.** The reports of the utilities and the rates office come about weekly whether or not anything changed (a daily draw is always something done): seven or so short papers a half year for each. A seat's sight of a bill not paid is its account, as before. An order's `at` is still not checked (the water seat's named the lot, not the works).
  - **Revisit if** seats find the weekly reports noise (make them on change only, with a monthly one), or a billing order should be able to name its first date (`first` does that already: the round is counted from when the order comes into force).

- **Wave 2 after the shake-down: stages 2b and 2c rebuilt as a new pinned wave, `wave-2b`, on origin/main 4b496b7** (2026-10-09; `docs/waves/wave-2/`; `runs/pilot-queues/wave-2a.review.md`). The shake-down's eight Claude-lane pilots gave 129 requests for about 76 recorded, twice the requests expected and narrow (payments, five forms, standing work, employment agreements, withdrawals), with a council in a calm town deciding nothing. So: no shop or factory seat (w2-30 dropped; serving and making are not standing work); every council or election pilot under `dear-rents` or `lean-council`, so that its business comes from the town and nothing is said to a seat (and a full council under both, w2-55); the trained translator's council pilot reworked on Sonnet seats for about a dollar (w2-56) where w2-26 cost 27 for one request; the utilities again on another profile (w2-57); every remaining Haiku pilot at `seat_effort=low` (0.090 an answer against 0.205 for the same offices at default effort, w2-54 against w2-04); one pilot of 400 days for a budget year's end and the first births (w2-58, about 22); a stopping rule for a seat that withdraws or holds wages over a figure of its own; rates corrected from the finished pilots. Forty-two pilots to come, 33 needing no Codex: about 1,060 requests and 260 of plan usage expected from those (a third to three times). Mock dry run of every entry, 20 days, on 1b7785c: 42 of 42. **Not verified:** a council's business reaching real seats; a hired crew working under a model manager; the translator under prompt 0.9.2; Haiku at low effort outside a town hall. **Revisit if** w2-55's council has no proposal by day 30 (then the council pilots after it wait), or a retrained translator of ours passes (then `make.ts --retrained` for the `trained-ok` pilots of a stage not yet started).

- **A wide part of the translator's training data, and what is banked for a later translator** (2026-10-09; Naz: "the translator data is too narrow", "a wide spread of good data so that we can finally get the self trained translator model over the line"; data pipeline 0.13.2; `translator/train/data.ts`, `synthetic.ts`, `v2.ts`, `choices.ts`, `orchestrator/src/broad.ts`, `training.ts`, `in-situ.ts`, `pipeline.ts`, `cli.ts`; tests `translator/test/train-broad.test.ts`, `v2.test.ts`, `choices.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/broad.test.ts`; docs/translator-pipeline.md, "A wide part"; `runs/translator-data-broad-2026-10-09/README.md` has every count). **No model trained, no pod, the prompt untouched.**
  - **The later translator ("translator v2": language in, language out) is a note, not current work:** docs/design/translator-v2.md, with the owner's hard requirement that it be unbiased by design.
  - **Why generated.** The pilots' requests are few, of a few kinds, in one careful register, all from office seats. Pilots give realism and the test; breadth has to be made.
  - **What "wide" is, in the plan of a part** (`--broad`, `--world-forms`, `--styles`): three registers beside the styles (`rambling`, `flat`, `slips`), dealt two turns in five with the terse line, the seats' voices one turn in five; who is asking said in every brief (twelve kinds: an office-holder in an office-holder's style, otherwise someone who would honestly ask for such an act); every paper the worlds' own offices issue with every field of it filled; `look_first` for any act on a record the speaker cannot name (the request must not hold the id) and `no_such_act` for attending; large counts with the place's digit grouping and starts given as days. A plan made without the options is what it was.
  - **Written and checked through the adapters, one resumable command** (`oikos translator-data-batch`): a batch of briefs at a call, the mechanical checks, each request read blind by a model that did not write it, compared by meaning, the leak check on what is kept; every call in a ledger. Until now generated parts were written by subagents started by hand.
  - **A writer that really is simple** (`plain`): Haiku 5.5 at low effort, given the plain situation, no way of saying it and no style (`own`). A capable model asked for a flat register is a capable model's idea of one: the simple writer is shorter (65 characters at the median against 78 to 121), loses 18% to the mechanical checks against about 1%, and is read alike 93% against 96%.
  - **Groups, and a parity test** (`oikos translator-data-collect`): every example carries writer, register, asker, currency, way of writing it, source; a tenth is cut by gold program within each function and never trains. The floor of 20 a cell (group by function) is not met everywhere: the manifest lists each cell under it. Asker by function has zeros by design.
  - **What came of it:** 15,644 examples through the blind check (95% of 16,436 read), 14,178 to train and 1,466 the parity test; forms 99%; every function, refusal label, office paper, register and asker present. Banked, in their own files: 2,653 turns read as a seat's other tools (among them 403 real whole answers and 310 built whole turns), 2,491 citizens' choices with their decisions' `seq`, 240 plain replies to real previews.
  - **The bulk writer was changed part way, on the owner's word** (Fable 5.1 to Opus 5.5; then Haiku's default-effort share to Sonnet 5.5). What was written was kept as its writer's (`keepWritten`; each request says who wrote it). As a writer Opus is read alike as often as Fable (95%) at a quarter of the reckoned cost and a fifth of the time; Haiku at default effort is the dearest per brief.
  - **A prompt ambiguity found, and the ruling.** A direction to an office with no form listed for it ("Direct the water office to take in no new applications") was read alike 69 times of 165: the reader mostly answered `none(no_such_act)`. The prompt says both that directing someone is a message to them and that changing what an office does of its own accord is no act; with no form listed both fit. Ruling (coordinator, 2026-10-09, on the rule the owner accepted on 2026-10-06, "have or get X to do Y is a message to X"): a request that addresses an office and tells it to do something is a message to that office; `no_such_act` is for what addresses nobody. The gold labels stand. The prompt gets a sentence saying so in its next version (not made here). The 96 read otherwise are set aside with their gold programs (`all/set-aside-direction-unlisted.jsonl`) to be read again under that prompt; the brief no longer offers "X is to …", which addresses nobody and was read as an order for work.
  - **Two things fixed on the way.** The pipeline's reader task says a thing that starts now has `first="0 days"`, and one reader applied it to every standing routine said to hold "from now on" (standing work 69% in the pilot part): a sentence added to the task for generated parts, 97% after. An asker's line let "for our members" into requests, read as `for=`: the line now forbids saying in whose name unless the call does.
  - **Not done, and why.** Requests written in real pilot situations: the retrain's own pipeline run does that for the wave's pilots with two readers, and doing it here would have labelled the same seat-days twice. `codex/gpt-6-luna` as a second simple writer: its window was shut. Counts of cells were not topped up to the floor for the ways of writing money.
  - **Not verified.** Nothing was trained on it, so that breadth helps is untested. The readers are of one family (Claude models): the audit of docs/translator-pipeline.md ("The readers") is owed before it trains anything. I read about 150 requests in all, not a sample of every cell. The built whole turns agree 310 of 731, for reasons that are the later translator's design questions (where an act's words begin; a letter said as an act; a part that cannot be read is left out), not settled here. Fable 5.1 through `claude -p` hit the shared session limit once, so its tier is not wholly separate.
  - **Revisit if** the retrain's parity test shows a group well below the rest (then that group's cells are the next part to write); the clarified prompt is on main (then re-read the 96 and add what agrees); a count or a day written a new way reaches the contract (the generator draws what the contract reads); or the audit by another family disagrees with more than about one label in ten in some function.

- **A wage drafted at the figure it was to be worked out from: what failed, and three things changed** (2026-10-09; wave 2b's review, fault 1; `translator/src/index.ts`, `preview.ts`, `knowledge.ts`, both resolvers; `contracts/test/payments.json`; tests `translator/test/payments.test.ts`, `payments_as_the_shared_table_says`).
  - **What happened, from the log** (`runs/w2-45-lean`, `draft.finance-system.1`, day 3). The finance seat asked: "Set up a wage payment from acc-city to acc-c0027 every 14 days, first on year 1, day 18, citing employment agreement rec.1225: gross pay 1.944,46 € less what law-income-tax says to withhold (...)". The translator answered `none(needs_calculation)`, which is right: the amount is not in the request. The platform then asked it again ("That didn't work: Please state the amount itself ... write it as a call if any call can say it ... Answer none(...) only if no call can"), and its second answer was `money(amount="1.944,46 €", basis=["rec.1225","law-income-tax"], ...)`. The preview read "pay 1.944,46 € ... every 14 days, for wage ... citing rec.1225 and law-income-tax" and the seat confirmed, noting "citing law-income-tax so withholding applies". 863,65 € a fortnight overpaid until day 17.
  - **So the rule covered it and the model obeyed it; the retry undid it.** Read across the wave's 424 requests (23 pilots): a first answer of `needs_calculation` was asked again four times and ended as the gross figure three times (one confirmed, one declined, one failing on its date) and as a payment with no amount once; `look_first` three times, ending as a wrong draft twice (an agreement withdrawn in place of the payment under it; a second standing wage beside the one to be changed; the seat declined both) and a failure once. Never a right draft. **Those two refusals are no longer asked again**: each sends the seat for something only it can bring (a figure; an id), and the seat reads the refusal's sentence at once. The other labels are still tried once more (`too_much` became a right draft four times of six).
  - **The preview sets a payment against the agreement it cites.** Where a payment cites an agreement the seat has seen, under which the payer pays one sum, the preview ends: "This is the whole of the pay agreed in rec.1225 (1.944,46 € every 14 days), with nothing withheld from it." or "This is 863,65 € less than the pay agreed in rec.1225 (1.944,46 € every 14 days)." (more; another rhythm: both figures, no difference; paid once: "one period's pay"). Both papers are the seat's own; nothing is said of an agreement it has not been shown. A seat's knowledge now keeps, of each agreement it sees, who pays what to whom and how often.
  - **`per_request` was a hole.** It names the request a keeper's payment carries out (a bank's transfer under a customer's instruction). Both resolvers read it only where the payer keeps the account, and there took a name for an id ("the bank" would have become the bank); on a payment that is a request to the keeper it was never read, so `per_request="report"`, `"worker-by-worker report"`, `"the bank"` and a table of pays went through (w2-45 .8, .9, .16, .18; the payments themselves were right). Now it is a record's id, bare, or the call is refused; and on a payment its maker does not move it is refused whatever it holds. Both are the call's fault: the translator is asked again and the seat reads nothing of it.
  - **The prompt's part** (the rule said plainly for a figure named and another described; what `per_request` is) is in the entry on prompt 0.9.3 below.
  - **Not verified.** No model has been run on any of this. That the finance seat in w2-45 had rec.1225 in what it had been shown at day 3 is inferred from its note ("confirmed on file"), not replayed. The comparison says nothing where an agreement states pay some other way than one sum by the payer.
  - **Revisit if** seats decline right drafts because of the comparison (a net wage reads "863,65 € less than the pay agreed", which is true and may alarm: then say less, or only when the two are equal); a refusal of the two kinds turns out to be wrong often on first answers (then the retry's wording, not its absence, is the thing to change); or a seat that keeps money itself needs to name what it carries out by other than a record.

- **A paper made on an office's form says why each recipient is on it** (2026-10-09; wave 2b's review, fault 2; `translator/src/preview.ts` `madeOn` and `goesTo`, `participants/src/behaviour/papers.ts`, `worlds/generator/generate.ts` `stationeryForm`; contract: `FormWrites.sends`; test `orchestrator/test/office-form-preview.test.ts`; docs/behaviour/office-papers.md, step 5).
  - **What happened** (`runs/w2-41-works`, registry seat, seven drafts from day 3 to day 38). Each death registration was right, and its preview read "addressed to c0363, Millbrook Savings Bank (bank), Energy retailer (energy-co), The outside world (outside), Electoral commission (electoral-commission)". The seat had asked for the reporter, the bank and the energy company; it took the other two for the draft's mistake ("the draft adds the outside world and the electoral commission as recipients ... I will re-register with only those recipients") and declined every one. Four deaths stayed unregistered, one for 72 days. The two are the form's own (`feeds`: a registrar sends every entry to the electoral roll's keeper and to whoever pays support, docs/behaviour/deaths.md), and nothing on the form or in the preview said so.
  - **What a seat now reads.** "You will publish a death registration: "Death registered: c0362.", with these details: ..., citing rec.1496. It goes to: c0363 (reported by on the form: "Who reported the death: they are sent the entry."); Millbrook Savings Bank (bank) and Energy retailer (energy-co) (tell on the form: "Those the notification asks to be told, who are sent the entry too."); The outside world (outside) and Electoral commission (electoral-commission) (not for you to choose: the form, form-registry-death-registration, sends every paper made on it to them: "They are sent every entry in the register of deaths as of right, to keep their own records by: whoever keeps a roll of electors takes the dead off it, and whoever pays someone a pension or support stops paying it."). It is seen only by you and those it goes to." The form on its file says the same sentence.
  - **How.** A paper of this kind does not cite its form, so the preview finds the form by writing the paper back to its fields (`forms.fieldsFor`, as the mock does). A recipient a field names is said with the field and the form's description of it; one the form itself names is said with the form's reason (`sends`), and where a form gave none, "named on the form itself". Fourteen forms had such recipients and none said why: each does now (the registry's two entries, the transmission application, the nomination, the valuation request, the docket, the habitat register, the garnishee order, the landlord's return and notification, the funding draw, the charge, the police notification, the crime report), and a test refuses a form that does not.
  - **With it, a fault of fault 6:** a paper's details read as the form says each is, so the landlord's return shows "rent received: £3,813.75" where it showed the sum in its smallest unit ("381375", four previews in w2-02).
  - **A contract change** (standing approval): `FormWrites.sends`, optional. Nothing reads it but the form's words and the preview; a paper is the same paper. Forms are published only where a model holds the office, so no code-only town changes.
  - **Not verified.** No model has read the new preview. The reasons are mine, from docs/behaviour/deaths.md and each module's own account of who acts on its paper; no source was opened for the forms. The preview is long: about 700 characters for a death registration.
  - **Revisit if** a seat still declines for a recipient it was told of (then the reason is not believed, and the question is whether a seat should be able to leave a statutory recipient off: it cannot today); or seats stop reading previews of this length.

- **The translator's prompt, 0.9.2 to 0.9.3: an amount described and not stated, and a direction with no form** (2026-10-09; wave 2b's review, fault 1, and the ruling in "A wide part of the translator's training data" above; `translator/src/index.ts`; seen cases in `translator/eval/cases.ts`; test `translator/test/payments.test.ts`). **Exactly what changed, and nothing else:**
  1. In `needs_calculation`, after its first sentence, one sentence and a bracket: "So is an amount given only as a figure with something to be taken off it or added to it that the request doesn't state as a figure ("their wage of 2,000 less tax", "the invoice plus interest"): the figure named is what the amount is worked out from, and is never written as the amount. (Where the request states the result itself, "1,640, being 2,000 less 360", the result is the amount.)" Two worked examples after "Pay Acme half of what we hold": the wage less what the tax law says to withhold (`none(needs_calculation)`), and the same wage with its result stated (`money(..., amount="1,640", ...)`).
  2. In `no_such_act`, after the bracket on an office's own accord, one sentence: "That is for a request that tells nobody to do it ("we stop taking applications on Fridays"): one that addresses an office, a post or a person and tells them to do, stop or change something is a message to them where no form is listed for that direction, never no_such_act." One worked example after "Go to str.9 ...": "(Where no form is listed for it.) Direct the depot to take in no new applications from now on. -> message(to="the depot", text="take in no new applications from now on")".
  3. The gloss of `money` in the list of functions gains "; per_request only where the person keeps the account the money leaves and is carrying out a request to pay: that request's id". (The argument was listed with nothing said of it, and a translator filled it with "report", "the bank" and a table: four of one pilot's 14 payments. Both resolvers now refuse that; this saves the second call.)
  - **Why 1, when the model had it right.** The rule did cover the pilot's request and the translator's first answer obeyed it; what wrote the gross figure was the platform's second asking, now gone (the entry above). The sentence is for the reader that meets such a request cold: "the amount isn't stated" is arguable of a request with a figure in it, and the sentence says which figure is not the amount. The bracket keeps the commonest right request (the result stated, with how it was got) from being refused.
  - **Why 2.** Blind readers under 0.9.2 answered `no_such_act` for 47 of 72 generated directions to an office with no form listed: the prompt said both that directing someone is a message and that changing what an office does of its own accord is no act. The ruling (2026-10-09, on the rule accepted 2026-10-06, "have or get X to do Y is a message to X"): told to an office, it is a message to that office; `no_such_act` is for what tells nobody.
  - **Seen cases, both ways** (five added): `direct-office-no-form` and `have-office-stop-no-form` (messages), `own-routine-nobody-told` (`no_such_act`); `wage-less-tax-not-stated` (`needs_calculation`) and `wage-net-stated` (the stated result). None is worded from a real test case: the 180 real requests and the held-out cases were not opened.
  - **What it leaves.** The 96 generated requests set aside (`runs/translator-data-broad-2026-10-09/all/set-aside-direction-unlisted.jsonl`) can now be read again under this prompt; not done here. Wave 2's documents say 0.9.2 because its pinned stages ran on it; the next stage's pin will carry 0.9.3.
  - **Not verified.** No model has read 0.9.3: not the seen cases, not the real requests, not the set-aside 96. A score on either test set under 0.9.2 is not comparable until it is run again.
  - **Revisit if** readers under 0.9.3 still split on directions with no form (then the sentence belongs in the rule on telling someone, not in the refusal); a translator starts refusing wages whose result is stated; or `not_yours` and a direction are confused ("make the office stop" against "tell the office to stop"), which this does not touch.

- **A standing work order follows the rhythm its office's procedure states** (2026-10-09; wave 2b's review, fault 4; both resolvers' `work`, `participants/src/calls.ts` `parseDuration`, `StandingWork` in `participants/src/behaviour/common.ts`, each module's `routines`, the generator's procedure paper, `translator/src/preview.ts` `rhythmOf`; `contracts/test/standing-work.json`; test `orchestrator/test/office-rhythm.test.ts`; docs/behaviour/standing-work.md, step 5).
  - **What happened** (`runs/w2-36-offices`, rates seat, day 0, four requests). It asked for its levy "every instalment the rating law sets (2 a year ...)": the translator wrote `every="2 a year"` and the seat read that it "could not be read as a length of time. Please say it again with that written as a number of days, weeks or months". It gave 182 days, read the preview "every 182 days" and declined ("the 182-day interval is not the rating law's schedule"). It asked "at each instalment the rating law sets" with no interval and was asked "once, or as a standing routine?". It gave "every day" and declined that too. No order in 30 days, so nothing was levied. The seat was right each time: the code-run rates clerks send notices from the office's first levy day and then by the law's instalments, whatever `every` says, and the order had no way to say so. The school's "each school day" was refused the same way.
  - **What a seat can now say.** Nothing of how often (`work(at=rates, task=levy)`): the order is "Standing work order: levy at rates, as law-rates sets.", and the preview reads "It gives no rhythm of its own: when levy is done is set by law-rates, as your office's procedure (proc-rates-routines) says: "At each instalment the rating law sets, the rates clerks send every owner on the rate book a notice ... the first once the valuer has valued the town's properties and not before the office's first levy day, then one for each instalment the law sets, evenly through the year (two instalments a year are 182 days apart, four are 91). ..."". Or the paper by name ("as law-rates sets"). Or days of its own, and then the preview says "By your office's procedure (proc-rates-routines) when levy is done is set by law-rates, whatever an order says of how often: the staff keep to that." A routine with a rhythm of its own takes it the same way ("It gives no rhythm of its own: every 1 day is the office's own rhythm for enrol, by its procedure"). "Each working day" and "each school day" are read as a day.
  - **What it is told when how often cannot be read.** From its own procedure: ""2 a year" could not be read as how often. By your office's procedure (proc-rates-routines) the staff do levy when law-rates sets: say "as law-rates sets", or leave how often out and the order follows it." Of a task no procedure speaks of: "How often can be a length of time ("every 7 days", "weekly", "each working day"); or, where a law or a paper on your file sets when the work is done, that paper named by its id ...". Never "a number of days, weeks or months" for a schedule.
  - **The default the shake-down's review asked for.** It was not given then because no rhythm was on record. Each module now declares one for every routine (`every`, or `follows` for a paper), the generator writes it into the procedure, and a test refuses a routine with neither. The figures are the code offices' own (the round every 7 days, upkeep, treatment, teaching, enrolment, the draw and the supply daily, water bills every 91 days and energy bills every 30).
  - **Contract changes** (standing approval): a routine's `every` and `follows` in `module.schema.json`; a work order's data may hold `schedule` in place of `every`, and `by_procedure`; work with neither how much nor how often is a standing order where the procedure states the rhythm, and a question as before where it does not. The prompt is untouched: the translator copies the request's words for how often or leaves them out, and both now resolve.
  - **Which dates.** The preview quotes the procedure, which says how the clerks keep the law's time in words; it gives no dates, because the first notices wait for the valuer. The clerks' report gives the date ("the next notices go out on year 1, day 31, as the rating law's instalments fall").
  - **Not verified.** No model has asked for an order this way. A request that says "maintain the hall" with no amount, meant once, is now drafted as a standing order where the procedure states a rhythm: the preview says so plainly, and a seat that confirms it without reading has a routine it did not want.
  - **Revisit if** that happens (then work with neither is asked about again, and only a request that says "standing" adopts the rhythm, which needs a word from the translator); a second paper comes to set a routine's time (the reading is general, the only one today is the rating law); or staff should follow an order's own days for a routine a paper sets.

- **A council's machinery in the hands of seats: the whole count, a member's own vote, and a passed amendment put in force** (2026-10-09; wave 2b's review, fault 3; `participants/src/behaviour/tally.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `city.council_clerk` 0.11.0, the generator; test `orchestrator/test/council-machinery.test.ts`; docs/behaviour/government.md, last section).
  - **What happened** (`runs/w2-07-election`, the first council vote a model carried through). The clerk declared "4 for" on two ballots where five had voted: councillor-2's votes came on day 10, were shown to the clerk that day in a list of what was new, and were not in the day-11, day-17 or day-22 lists; at the count it had its notebook and the day's two new votes, and a search of the votes "citing rec.2626" found nothing (a vote names its ballot and cites nothing). The mayor acted on the 4-0 figure; it was corrected a day later on a councillor's letter. Councillors could not see their votes on file and re-cast them (12 vote drafts for 6 votes). And the passed amendment never took effect: the clerk asked four times to publish it; a law in words was published and the tenancy law's figure stayed as it was, because writing the law from its schedule is code (`draftLaw`) that only the code clerk ran.
  - **The count.** Whoever keeps a council's ballots reads, at every sitting where it has changed, "The count on each ballot of the council not yet declared, from every vote on file": "- rec.310 (on rec.241), closed year 1, day 10, 09:00: 5 posts have voted: yes 5 (councillor-1, councillor-2, councillor-3, councillor-4, councillor-5). It is closed and no result is declared yet.", with what was not counted where there is any ("8 votes on file in all: 1 earlier vote replaced by the same post's later one; 1 cast at or after it closed, not counted; ..."). It is read from the seat's own papers (the votes on its body's ballots: `mine`), as the roster is; no channel was added for it.
  - **A member's own vote.** A councillor reads "your vote on file is "yes" (rec.2824, cast year 1, day 10). It is the one that counts unless you cast another before the ballot closes." Its desk now has the council's votes (public record, and the council's own).
  - **Putting a passed amendment in force.** Who really does it: the clerk's office drafts and engrosses, the clerk certifies. So the clerk's office has drafters as its staff, like every office with routine work: the routine `enact`, daily by the office's procedure. A seat makes the standing order once (`work(at=council-clerk, task=enact)` is enough since the entry above), declares results on its form, and the drafters write each passed and declared amendment into the law by its schedule, publish it in place of the law in force and withdraw that one. The result form now says "Declaring a result does not by itself change a law", and the office's procedure says what does. The code clerk is unchanged (the enactment is one function both use; the 1,000-person month ends where it did).
  - **The mock council** (the test, 19 days, six seats following a script, no model): motion rec.241 by councillor-1 on day 1 ("amend tenancy: notice 90 days"); ballot rec.310 by the clerk on day 2, open 8 days; votes on days 3, 4, 4, 4 and 5; on day 12 the clerk is shown all five, declares "Result of rec.310: 5 for, 0 against." naming the five posts, and the drafters publish rec.811 in place of law-tenancy within the hour: notice 60 days to 90.
  - **Not changed.** A search of the votes by `citing`. Who has not voted. Elections: a clerk seat still seats nobody (the electoral office declares). Nominations and candidates' platforms on a councillor's desk (the review's item 4).
  - **Not verified.** No model has read the count or made the standing order. A clerk seat that never makes the order has no amendment put in force, and only the procedure and the result form tell it so; its drafters report nothing until an order exists (the works pilots showed seats do read that procedure, and one Haiku seat waited 14 days).
  - **Revisit if** a clerk seat declares and never orders (then the drafters should write to the clerk when a declared amendment waits with no order in force, which is a letter, not an act); or a council wants its drafters to enact what the clerk has not declared.

- **Wave 2 after stage 2b: stage 2c rebuilt as a new pinned wave, `wave-2c`, on origin/main d769817** (2026-10-09; `docs/waves/wave-2/`; `runs/pilot-queues/wave-2b.review.md`). The owner stopped all use of the largest Claude model ("it drains usage too much"): no pilot still to run seats it (the generator refuses one), its two finished pilots stay training data, and the test's held-out things are now two profiles, two offices and, only if the Codex window opens, gpt-6-luna seats; there is no unseen seat model otherwise. No pilot of councillors alone (two made no request). The 400-day pilot with a council stays, last in its lane, with the named risk that a clerk seat which never sets its drafters' standing order gets no amendment in force. One test pilot more (the tribunal, a landlord and planning in the Mexican town). Rates and spending limits from stage 2b's finished pilots (about half the earlier estimates; a lender's seat counted apart at about 0.22 a call). Eleven pilots, eight needing no Codex, nine test-only: about 170 requests (55 of them test) and 73 of plan usage expected. Mock dry run of every entry, 20 days, on 502e330: 11 of 11. **Not verified:** the translator under prompt 0.9.3; the clerk fixes under a real seat; whether 55 test requests is enough to score a translator on. **Revisit if** the test pilots yield too few requests (then lengthen them: they cost two or three each), or the Codex window stays shut (then say plainly that the test has no unseen seat model).

- **A refusal says its cause** (2026-10-09; wave 2b's review, fault 5; both resolvers, `translator/src/index.ts`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`; `contracts/test/holds.json`; test `orchestrator/test/refusal-causes.test.ts`).
  - **What the five were.** "That couldn't be put into effect, and nothing was done. Saying it another way may not help." was said five times in the wave's 424 requests (the review counted four; w2-33 had a fifth). Every one was a draft the log refused because the resolver had made an act the contract does not take, and none was the seat's wording being unclear: `statement(withdraw=draft.finance.7)` (w2-42: a draft's name where a record's id goes); `message(re=rec.msg.4132)` (w2-41: an id the seat made up); `statement(kind=law, on=schedule-tenancy)` twice (w2-07: a law's schedule written as the place to put a paper up, which must be a cell); and an offer of employment with words and no commitment on either side (w2-33: the block needs one). "May not help" was wrong advice for all five: saying it another way was exactly what helped.
  - **Each is now a question back with its cause**, in both resolvers: "draft.finance.7 is the name a draft went by before it was confirmed, not a paper on record. Once confirmed it is on record under an id of its own (rec. and a number): look it up in your papers and name that."; ""rec.msg.4132" (for re) is not the id of anything on record: an id is written exactly as your papers show it, like rec.412. Look it up and name it so."; "A paper is put up at a place on the ground: a lot, or a cell of one. schedule-tenancy is neither, as far as you know. To publish it and put it up nowhere, leave the place out; to put one paper in another's place, withdraw the other and publish this."; "An agreement says what each side is to do or pay, and this one says nothing either side commits to. Say what you will do or pay, and what they will: money, goods, a building, occupancy or an account." Each tells the seat only what it wrote and what an id or a place is.
  - **Found with it: a paper could never be put up on a lot.** calls.md said `on` takes a lot; the block's `place` is a cell. A lot of one cell is now that cell; of several, the seat is asked which. Three tests held acts the contract never took (a notice on a lot's id; two agreements with nothing on either side) and were brought to what is recordable.
  - **What still cannot be recorded is the platform's fault, and is treated as one.** It is on record (`translation_failure` with `platform_fault` and the engine's own words, for the log), the request is drawn up once more, and if that fails too the seat reads: "About what you asked for (...): nothing was filed or done. The draft could not be drawn up, and the fault is not in what you asked: it has been noted. Please ask for it again; if it fails again, ask for it in smaller steps." A check of the acts that itself fails is the same (it used to end the request at once). The test's case is words longer than a paper may hold, which nothing asks about yet.
  - **Not verified.** No model has read these. Drawing a request up again costs a second translator call and, in the reports, a second draft number for one request.
  - **Revisit if** `platform_fault` appears in a pilot's log (each one is a resolver gap to close with its cause, as these were); or seats take "ask for it in smaller steps" as a reason to split what should be one act.

- **Four smaller faults of what a seat reads** (2026-10-09; wave 2b's review, fault 6; `translator/src/preview.ts`, `knowledge.ts`, both resolvers' commitments, `jobTerms`, `orchestrator/src/run.ts`, `corpus.ts`, `dataset.ts`; tests `orchestrator/test/smaller-previews.test.ts`, `office-form-preview.test.ts`; `contracts/test/standing-work.json`).
  - **A return's sum in its smallest unit** ("rent received: 381375", w2-02, four previews): fixed with the forms' reasons (the entry on recipients above): "rent received: £3,813.75".
  - **A withdrawal that named an id and nothing else** ("You will withdraw job-c0004.", w2-45: the employment agreement in place of the wage under it; an earlier check found six people's wages stopped behind "You will withdraw job-c0008-wages."). The preview now says what the paper is, from the seat's own papers: "You will withdraw rec.44. It is your standing request to Millbrook Bank (bank): "Please pay XYZ 2393.34 from acc-city to acc-c0003 every 14 days, for Wages.". Once it is withdrawn nothing more is to be done under it: what it pays or has done stops."; "You will withdraw job-c0004. It is the employment agreement itself, between you and c0004: not a payment or an order made under it. Anything standing under it is a paper of its own, and goes on until that paper is withdrawn."; a hold ("Withdrawing it lifts the hold"), a work order ("your staff no longer do that work under it"), a direction, a paper already withdrawn, and "No paper by that id is among your own papers as you have been shown them: check that it is the one you mean." A seat's knowledge keeps a line on each paper of its own (its kind, its first 300 characters, whom it is addressed to); nothing of anyone else's.
  - **Every offer of employment's first attempt refused** (w2-42, 8 of 8: `they_do=work(at=town-hall/workplace.1, task="works crew")`, answered "A commitment can be money, goods, a building, occupancy or an account, not work."). The translator was right to write it: the request says the person works as crew at a place, and the blocks contract's commitments have a `work` outcome. The resolvers lacked it. It now resolves ("c0003 will do works_crew at town-hall/workplace.1"), and the worker's place of work is read from it where the agreement names no place to come to, so such an offer also has a place of work (the fault that left a crew of five at home in the shake-down).
  - **A draft left open at a seat's last sitting** (w2-02, landlord-1's rates payment). A run that ends writes, for each draft still on a seat's desk, a note `draft_unanswered`, and the corpus and the dataset read that draft's sign-off as "unanswered". It is not asked about at the debrief: nothing could be done with the answer once the run is over. A run stopped to be resumed keeps its drafts open.
  - **Not verified.** No model has read the new withdrawal previews. Nothing else in the town reads a `work` commitment's `units` or `every`: they are words on the agreement.
  - **Revisit if** a seat withdraws an agreement after reading that it is "the agreement itself" and is surprised by what follows (what withdrawing an agreement does in the town is not said, because nothing defines it); or training data should leave unanswered drafts out altogether.

- **A form's name and office are pointed at where they are shown, not learned by heart** (2026-10-09, the retrain after the wave; `translator/model/encode.ts`; test `translator/test/model-encode.test.ts`). **What was wrong.** The trained translator writes every step as a choice from a closed set or a span of what it was shown. The export made a choice of every value the request implies and does not say. That is right for a yes or no and for `visible=own`; since 2026-10-09 the data also has an office's own form asked for by what it is for ("register the death of ..."), where neither the form's name nor the office it goes to is in the request. Each of those became a choice: exported from the standing set joined with the wide part, the closed set had 266 choices, 149 of them form names and office ids (95 and 54; `const:death_registration`, `const:pos.100`, `const:garth-parks`), from 660 and 846 training rows. A model so trained could write only the forms and offices it had memorised, and a real world's own office (never one of those ids) not at all.
  - **Now** such a value is a span of the forms shown: the form's name at the head of its line, the office after `to=` in the line of the form being filled (a pointer of the kind a form's field already was). Where no form shown has it, it is still a choice. The same export has 117 choices and `cannotSay` names none. Decoding is unchanged (a pointer was always into the whole input), so every model on disk answers as it did, and the exact-rebuild tests hold.
  - **Why not leave it and add the worlds' form names to the set.** The platform is general: a profile or a pilot's office may issue a form no training row had, and its offices' ids are its own. A name that is shown can be copied; a name that must be remembered is a place in the code by another route.
  - **Not verified here:** that a model learns to point into a line of 13 to 18 forms as well as it chose among 95 names; the retrain's scores by form say (docs/translator-pipeline.md).
  - **Revisit if** forms asked for by what they are for score under forms named in the request (then the reader needs the form's own words for what it is for, which the line does not carry), or a world lists two forms an unnamed request could mean.

- **Nothing trains that shares a source program with the parity test** (2026-10-09, the retrain after the wave; `orchestrator/src/broad.ts` `collect`; test `orchestrator/test/broad.test.ts`). The wide set's parity slice is cut by gold program within each function, so a refusal made from a payment's program (another function's example) could train while that payment was a parity case. Of the first wide set's 14,178 training rows, 324 share a source program with a parity case, 91 are rows a parity case was built from and 27 were built from a parity case or its program: 442 in all (and 28 more on the validation side). The retrain's join leaves them out (`runs/translator-retrain-2026-10-10/scripts/base.ts`, counted in its manifest), and `collect` now sets such rows aside as `shared-with-parity.jsonl`, on neither side, so a set collected from now on has none. The cut itself is unchanged (the parity file on disk is the same file), so parity scores stay comparable.
  - **What it means for earlier numbers:** none were published on the parity test before this; the old model's parity score is unaffected (it trained on none of the wide set).
  - **Revisit if** the parity test is cut again (then cut by source program across functions in the first place, and the set-aside file is empty).

- **The pipeline's guard on readers can be set by a run, and writers' files are named for the seats they wrote for** (2026-10-10, the retrain after the wave; `orchestrator/src/pipeline.ts`; docs/translator-pipeline.md, "The config"). Two faults met on the pipeline's first whole run over a wave. (1) The run stopped at its third reader batch: 14 of 30 answers were `none(not_an_act)`, over the guard's 40% of one program. Read by hand, all 14 were right: a writer put in a seat asks to be shown a record or a register about one time in three, and that is no act. The limits were constants; a config may now give `uniformity` (this run: `topShare` 0.65). The default is unchanged, and the guard still stops a run: whoever raises it reads the rejected batch first. (2) A writer's call was filed under the writer's name alone, so where two families of seat model share a writer (seats on the largest Claude model and on Codex models, both written for by one model) each family's calls took the other's files, and every resume asked them again (about 22 calls a restart, five restarts). The file now carries the family where a writer is shared, and an answer stored under the older name with the same fingerprint is adopted. No request was lost: a run's answers are gathered in memory as it goes.
  - **Revisit if** the share of look-requests among written requests stays near a third (then the writers' instructions, not the guard, are what to change: such requests teach one refusal label over and over), or a guard raised by config lets a rule-made batch through.

- **The translator retrained after the wave: much better, and not over the line** (2026-10-10; docs/translator-pipeline.md, "The retrain's results", has every table; `runs/translator-retrain-2026-10-10/`). **What was done:** the wide set audited by another family (gpt-6.1-sol agrees with 287 of 297; nothing set aside); 85 directions and 81 set-aside requests rescued by two readers under prompt 0.9.3; the pipeline run over 39 training pilots and 21 test-only ones (two folders, chained); joined-12 and data-18 (49,496 rows); three seeds of the small reader with `--forms-most 18`; scored beside the old model the same day; the v2 first decision measured (689 of 698).
  - **Result:** 146 to 149 of 180 real requests (old 130), wrong drafts 12 to 16; 46 to 48 of 66 held out; parity test 93% (old 68%); test-only pilots' own requests 71 to 81% (old 8 to 13%). The pass mark is 90% right and 1% wrong: not met overall, by kind (forms, money, statements, agreements) or by group (real requests differ 15 to 40 points across seat models and profiles).
  - **Choices made, and why.** (1) Readers: Sonnet 5.5 with Haiku 5.5, though the Codex window was open at the start: a window carries about twenty minutes of use and the pipeline's readings take hours and wait on a limited reader; sol audited instead (297 and 120 requests). (2) Weighting: pilot examples four times, generated once, as before: pilot examples are then 35% of rows; a different weight was not tried, since three seeds of one setup were asked for. (3) Late pilots as a second pipeline folder whose standing set is the first's joined set, so that no writer call was made twice. (4) `--token-budget 4096` on every seed, so the seeds differ in the seed alone. (5) The 13 `too_much` examples sol reads otherwise were left in: found after the first seed, and the seeds were to be one data set.
  - **What it says about the data.** Two blind readers of one family dropped 1,040 of 3,555 real and in-situation requests as disagreements, most in money, messages, agreements and work: the kinds the model is weakest at are the kinds least of the real data survives in. A third reader (another family) to settle them is the cheapest next gain. The wave's writers, put in a seat, ask to be shown things one time in three (`none(not_an_act)`: 625 of the 1,951 training examples from pilots): the writers' round-two instruction does not hold them to acts.
  - **Not verified:** the models in a pilot (nothing ran with them in front of a seat); a different weighting or more epochs; why the second pod's queue stopped.
  - **Revisit if** a third reader's settled labels and a round of bank and finance requests do not move real requests past 85% (then the small reader, not the data, is the limit, and the next reader up is the experiment), or parity gaps on real requests stay over 15 points once cells are 50 or more.

- **Generated parts can be made of a bank's and a finance office's payments, and weighted toward an asker and toward some worlds' money** (2026-10-10, round 2 of the trained translator; data pipeline 0.14.0; `translator/train/synthetic.ts` `payments`, `translator/train/data.ts` `askerFor`, `orchestrator/src/training.ts`, the CLI; tests `translator/test/train-broad.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/training.test.ts`). **Why.** The retrained model had two examples of `per_request` in 49,496 rows, 369 rows asked by someone at a bank, and was weak on a finance office's payments and on four ways of writing money. The generator left `per_request` out by design (`whyNot`: a code keeper's payment under an instruction is bookkeeping nobody words), and that was right for logs; since the bank is a seat, it is an act asked for in words. **What.** Four options of `translator-data`, each off unless given, so a plan made without them is what it was. `--bank-payments N` adds N payments a keeper makes out of an account it keeps, carrying out a request on record (`per_request=<its id>`; kind `per_request` in `--only`; the asker is always the bank). `whyNot` is unchanged: a log's own such payments still stay out. `--finance-payments N` adds N of four kinds in turn (kind `finance_payment`): a net wage where the request also states the gross and what was withheld (the writer is given the two figures; the call's amount is the one stated as paid), what was withheld remitted to an outside account, a payment resting on several records (`basis` a list) that mostly settles something, a standing payment with `first`. `--askers banker=0.3` gives an asker that share of a wide part's requests (those not in an office-holder's style, and not of a program that says who asks), whatever the act: the part's `--only` is what keeps it honest. `--money CODE=3,...` draws those currencies that many times as often. **Not done:** the holder who asked is named only inside the payment's purpose ("c0585's order of 9 goods"), never beside it ("as c0675 requested in rec.4560"), since an id outside the call is a stray id to the mechanical checks; a writer at low effort is not shown the note that gives the gross and what was withheld, so its wage requests are plain payments. **Revisit if** real bank seats' requests turn out to say the request they carry out in ways these do not (then add those ways to the note), or the weighted askers ask for acts they would not (then give the option a list of functions).

- **The translator's prompt is 0.9.4, and copied free text is no longer compared: nine rulings on what blind readers disagreed over** (2026-10-10, round 2 of the trained translator; `translator/src/index.ts`, `translator/train/meaning.ts` `sameButForFreeText`, the label step in `translator/train/readers.ts`, `unionBasis` and `agree` in `orchestrator/src/`, `translator/eval/set-run.ts`; 17 seen cases `r94-*`; tests `translator/test/free-text.test.ts`, `payments.test.ts`). **These are the coordinating agent's decisions, taken on the round's evidence under the owner's standing permission to change what readiness needs; they are not the owner's rulings and wait on his review** (D alone follows his ruling of 2026-10-09 that telling an office to act is a message to it). **Why.** Two Claude readers disagreed on 802 of the training pilots' requests and those were dropped, so the hard kinds trained on their easier half. Read by cluster, and a third time by `codex/gpt-6.1-sol` (`runs/translator-round-2-2026-10-10/step1/`): 319 differ in copied free text alone, about 290 turn on a rule the prompt left open, about 80 are one reader's slip; the third reader agreed with one of the two on 401 and with neither on 400, so a third reading alone settles half. Of the pipeline's 172 refusal examples other than `not_an_act`, sol read 35 otherwise (`too_much` 11 of 13).
  - **A. Copied free text is not compared** where two readers, or a model and a label, are compared: a letter's text and `re=`, a statement's text, an agreement's text and terms, a payment's `for=` (there or not), a form's text fields, a closing full stop, an empty list against a field left out. The scorer of the 180 real requests always worked so; the label step and the set scorer now do. The label that trains is still one reader's own program with every word found in the request (the first reader's, else the second's; neither, and it is dropped as reworded). The set scorer reports `text_exact` beside `passed`, so exactness stays in sight. The prompt says what `for=` is (the thing paid for, not the reckoning; what is settled by record gives none), where a letter's text ends, and what `re=` is. *Revisit if* free-text exactness of a trained model falls under about 80% of what passes, or a letter's wrong extent is seen to change what a recipient does in a pilot.
  - **B. An act together with its report is one program**: the act's lines, then `statement(kind=report, …)`; never the act alone, never `too_much`. No seen case keys such a request; one real case accepts this reading among three (checked by ids and shapes, `scripts/keys-b.ts`). *Revisit if* seats' reports turn out to be an office's form in most worlds (then the second line is that form).
  - **C. An act made to hang on something still to be found out or not yet so is `look_first`** ("only if", "once … is registered", "provided … confirms"); a reason or a time is no condition. The third reader and one Claude reader read it so 32 times of 43. *Revisit if* the call language gains a conditional or deferred act.
  - **D. Telling someone else to act on things described is a message to them**, not `look_first` (both Claude readers had trained `look_first` here).
  - **E. Sending someone unnamed to see is `no_such_act`** (nobody is addressed). *Revisit with* docs/design/knowing.md, if going to look becomes an act a seat can order.
  - **F. An amount that is so much for each of a number still to be counted is `needs_calculation`**, whatever else must be looked up.
  - **G. `unknown_form` only where a form is named.** An office's own decision or notice with no form listed is a statement (`kind=` the request's word, `basis=` what it decides); what is done only through an office's form that is not listed and not named (an entry in a public register, taking on staff with nobody named) is `no_such_act`. *Revisit if* the worlds give every office a decision form (then B.6 of docs/design/call-language-gaps.md covers it and the statement reading goes).
  - **H. No `first=` on a single payment made now.** A single payment on a later day has no way of being written and none was invented: docs/design/call-language-gaps.md B.9; such requests are set aside from training and from scoring.
  - **I. Offering an agreement is one line; "sign it for us" adds none.** The prompt has a paragraph on agreements (template, what each side does, terms, basis); seats' agreements are labelled by readers under 0.9.4, not from older readings (three readers had given three programs on 38 of 44).
  - **What it costs.** The prompt is a quarter longer (23,100 to 29,000 characters), on every translation a prompt-driven translator makes. Scores by the set scorer are not comparable with those before this change: old and new models are scored again under it. The pipeline-made test sets carry labels of the older reading; they are read again under 0.9.4 by sol, kept as they are, and scores are reported on the old labels and on the part where label and reading agree.
  - **Not verified:** that Sonnet 5.5 under 0.9.4 keeps its score on the 180 real requests and the held-out cases (no prompt-driven model was scored after the change; owed before 0.9.4 is used in front of a seat).

- **Round 2 of the trained translator: a better-labelled set and one seed; it does not pass, and data of the same kinds is no longer what it lacks** (2026-10-10; docs/translator-pipeline.md, "Round 2's results"; `runs/translator-round-2-2026-10-10/`). **What was done.** The 802 disagreements read again under 0.9.4 by Sonnet 5.5 and a second reader (sol for 390, Opus 5.5 for 412 when the Codex window shut): 541 settle. The last round's examples a ruling could touch checked under 0.9.4 (40 relabelled, 26 dropped). w2-58 through the pipeline; 200 situations of finance, bank, landlord and manager seats written under a round-three writer text (`runs/…/writer-round3.txt`: payments, bank business, agreements, statements, forms of several amounts); 3,014 generated examples of the weak kinds (the generator's new options, the entry above). `joined-13` / `data-19`: 57,591 rows. **Result.** `pod-small-r2-s1` beside last round's seed 1, same code, same day: real 153 against 147 of 180 (wrong 12 against 13), held out 48 against 46 of 66, parity 1,379 against 1,367; banker as asker 47 against 43 of 52; agreements 35 against 30 of 49 with the same 14 wrong; forms 186 against 183 of 250. **What it says.** Settling labels and filling kinds bought about three points on real requests. Forms of several amounts and agreements did not move with 1,096 and 426 more examples, so the limit there is the small reader or the decoding, not the data. **Choices made.** Haiku at default effort was not used as a reader (the dearest last round); Opus 5.5 was the fallback second reader (about 0.013 a request, half of Haiku's figure), which makes most of this round's new labels one family's. Plan usage 115 against 216. **Not verified:** a second seed (one was asked for); the examples not read again under 0.9.4 (1,291 of last round's, 2,712 older); the pipeline-made test sets still carry the older labelling, reported beside the part a reader of another family agrees with. **Revisit if** a larger reader (the next encoder up, or a second pass for forms) on this same data moves forms and agreements: then keep the data and change the model; if it does not either, the form and agreement programs need a different decoding (a field at a time).

## 2026-10-10 · The trained translator writes a call slot by slot, and says how many lines first

- **What was wrong.** `pod-small-r2-s1` fails by one confident wrong choice far more often than by a wrong copy (the design
  measurements, `runs/translator-decode-design-2026-10-10/` on the run server). It closed a form or a call too early: the
  council's budget form wanting one amount was right 1 time in 4 with `)` chosen at 0.996, yet made to write the field it
  found the value at 0.95 or more in 11 of 11; on the parity test a field or argument left out or added was 55 of 85
  failures (all 14 of the agreements' among them), and answers that did not fit the form shown 19 of 87. And it ended the
  program too early (`eos` at 0.93 or more): 11 of 18 real programs of two lines right, 2 of 7 of three or more.
- **The change** (`translator/model/encode.ts`, "Slot by slot"; `py/slots.py`; a second decoding, `slots`, beside the
  first, `steps`). Code lists what there is to decide and the model decides each thing once: (1) the kind of answer, a
  refusal or a program; (2) how many lines, `lines:N`; then for each line (3) unless it is the last, whether its result is
  named for a later line; (4) its function; (5) each slot of the function, in a stated order: for a form `form`, `to`, then
  every field of that form's line as shown, in the line's order; for any other function every argument the contract allows
  it, in the contract's order (`contracts/calls.schema.json`). A slot is left out (`-`), a closed-set value, or a copied
  span (or a call or a list of its own, as before). Nothing closes a call or ends a program, so neither can end early; an
  argument the contract requires cannot be left out; a field the form's line does not list has no slot and cannot be
  written. The model is told which slot
  each decision is for (a learned mark for each of the contract's arguments; for a form's field, where its name stands in
  the form as shown), and only what a slot allows is in the running, in training as when answering. The closed-set-or-copy
  shape is as it was: the model still writes nothing it was not shown or given, and its sureness is still the product of
  its decisions' probabilities (now among what each slot allows). Lists and data keep their closing mark (`]`, `}`): they
  were not among the failures measured.
- **The number of lines** is one of those the training examples have: 1 to 9 in the closed set (`lines:7` is in no
  example), and 1 to 4, 6 and 8 in what a model trains on (the programs of 5 and 9 lines are longer than the earlier
  decoding takes, and both arms leave the same examples out).
- **The same examples, written the other way.** `export.ts --decoding slots` on round 2's `joined-13`: 57,591 training,
  4,682 validation and 559 real validation rows, the same rows as `data-19`, none added or removed, each coming back to
  its program exactly. The same rule is written
  twice, in the exporter's language and the trainer's; `py/check_slots.py` follows every label with the trainer's and
  found no example the two read differently (and a test holds them together on a few).
- **A form's required field may be left out, in training and in answering alike** (the coordinating agent's decision,
  2026-10-10, before any model was trained). 104 training labels (and 2 of the real validation rows) leave a form's
  required field out because the request does not give it, and they are right as labelled: the answer is then not offered
  as a draft, and the participant is told which fields the form still lacks (`formsMisfit`, as before). Forcing a value
  there would be an invented value offered as a draft. So only the contract's own required arguments (and which form a
  form is) cannot be left out; no label leaves one of those out.
- **A fault found on the way, in the check of a draft against the forms shown.** Where two offices each have a form of
  one name, `formsMisfit` checked a draft against the last such line shown, whichever office the draft went to (a right
  draft for the first office was told it filled in a field that is not the form's). It now reads the line the call fills,
  by name and office, the same line the slots are read off. It applies to every model, and all three scored here are
  scored with it.
- **What was not changed.** No prompt (0.9.4), no data, no label. A model's folder says which decoding it answers in
  (`config.json`, `decoding`; absent means `steps`), and the adapter reads it, so every earlier model answers as it did.
  The check of a draft against the forms shown (`formsMisfit`) stays for both.
- **A decision that follows from it.** Slot by slot, a call that lacks a required argument is no answer (the model asks
  back); in the earlier decoding it was offered and whoever resolved it asked for the argument. No label in the training
