  set leaves a contract's required argument out, so nothing taught is lost.
- **Speed.** Answering slot by slot keeps what the writer made of the earlier steps (`write_next`) instead of writing them
  all again at each step; the earlier decoding answers as before.
- **Measured against a control**, not against the last round alone: the earlier decoding trained again on the same data
  for the same six epochs (the design report saw real validation still rising at epoch 4), one seed each, scored the same
  day with the same code as `pod-small-r2-s1`. The results are in docs/translator-pipeline.md, "Slot-by-slot decoding".
- **What it came to** (one seed an arm; docs/translator-pipeline.md, "Slot-by-slot decoding"). Better on generated forms
  (parity forms 231 of 250, control 214, last round 186; parity 1,425, 1,406, 1,379) and not on what it was built for: the
  budget form with one amount 1 of 5 (control 2), real wrong form drafts 6 (control 7; the mark was 3), agreements 37 of 49
  (the mark was 42), real programs of two lines 11 of 18 (control 12), the 180 real 147 (control 150, last round 153). With
  no way to close a form early the model decides the same field is left out. Most of the parity gain is the six epochs,
  which the control has too. **Decided:** six epochs is the schedule; the slot decoding stays as a second decoding, not the
  default; no pilot is served by `pod-small-slots-s1` on this evidence.
- **Revisit if** the contract gains a function with many more arguments (a decision for each slot, mostly "left out", is
  cheap now: a mean of 8.8 decisions an example against 8.8 before, the longest 145); forms come to be shown some other way
  than a line with its fields (the slots are read off that line, in two languages); a seat needs a program of more lines
  than any example has (the count is a closed choice); the model leaves a form's required field out where the request
  does give it (the early close in another dress: count it on every test before trusting a gain); or lists start being
  closed early (give them a count as lines have).

## 2026-10-11 · Our own trained translator in pilots: it answers first, the prompt-driven one behind it

- **The owner's decision (2026-10-11).** The trained translator is parked at its present quality and used. It translates
  first; when it fails, the prompt-driven translator (`claude-code/claude-sonnet-5-5`, prompt 0.9.4) takes that request.
  An interim arrangement for pilots: one model that works alone remains the goal, no training or prompt change comes with
  it, and it changes nothing in what a translator is (a request in, a program of the call language out, a draft offered).
- **Which model: `pod-small-r2-s1`** (`runs/translator-round-2-2026-10-10/models/`), not the six-epoch control
  `pod-small-steps6-s1`. On the 180 real requests it is right 153 (the control 150), offers 12 wrong drafts (13) and no
  draft on 15 (17); on seats' own requests in the set tests (376) the two are 328 and 331 right, 32 and 33 wrong. That is no
  measured difference (one seed each; three cases in 180 is within what a seed moves), so the choice is the one with most
  right and fewest wrong drafts on real requests, which is also the model every table of round 2 describes. The control is
  better on generated forms (parity forms 214 of 250 against 186), which is not what seats ask. Changing it is one name in a
  queue entry, and `beside` (below) is how the other is measured without touching a world.
- **The arrangement** (`translator/src/arrangement.ts`; `--translator-first decide/NAME`, with the run's translator behind
  it; a queue entry's `translator_first`). Under `then`, the default, the first's draft is offered, and the request goes to
  the one behind when:
  - the first offers no draft: it is under its cut-off of sureness (`unsure`), its draft is not one of the forms shown as
    shown (`form_check`), its answer is no program of the call language (`no_program`), the resolver cannot make acts of its
    call (`not_resolved`), the check of them failed (`check_failed`), it did not answer (`first_failed`), or it refuses with
    a label that does not stand (`refused`);
  - the seat declined a draft of the first's: its next request, whatever it is (`declined_before`); or the seat asks again,
    in much the same words (half or more of the words of the two requests in both), for something answered and not confirmed
    (`asked_again`). Such a matter stays behind until the seat confirms a draft or asks for something else.
- **Which of the first's refusals stand: `not_an_act` only**, and only where it is sure. The evidence, `pod-small-r2-s1`
  on the 180 real requests (right, wrong): `not_an_act` 56, 2; `no_such_act` 13, 2; `look_first` 6, 5; `too_much` 4, 0;
  `unclear` 0, 3; `needs_calculation` 0, 2; `unknown_form` 0, 1. On seats' own requests in the set tests: `not_an_act` 3, 0;
  `look_first` 4, 3; `unclear` 0, 12; `needs_calculation` 5, 0; `no_such_act` 1, 1. So 15 of its 27 failures on real
  requests are refusals, and only `not_an_act` is both frequent (a third of what seats ask) and reliable (59 of 61).
  `too_much` is 4 of 4 on real requests and 44 of 44 on generated ones, and is still sent behind: four cases is too few to
  rest a refusal on. This is the owner's lean, and the scores bear it out.
- **Why the next request after a decline goes behind whatever it says.** The trained model decides without sampling: a
  request said again in other words mostly gets the same draft. Telling whether two requests are one matter by their words
  would miss the reworded ones, and a seat shown the declined draft again is stuck. The cost of being generous is one call
  to the model behind for an unrelated request.
- **What the first is not.** Never a substitute: if the one behind is at a usage limit or cannot be reached, the error is
  the run's as any translator's is (the pilot is parked by the queue), whatever the first had answered. And never asked
  twice: its attempts are one (asked again it says the same), and it no longer hands "its best draft the next time" to a
  seat it was unsure for, since that seat was never told so.
- **`beside`** (`--translator-arrangement beside`): the one behind answers every request and the first's answer is only
  recorded. For measuring a model on a pilot's real requests without it touching the world; a world run so ends as it does
  with the one behind alone (tested).
- **The seat sees one translator.** Drafts are worded from their acts alone and refusals from the call language's fixed
  sentences, whoever answered; the first's own questions back never reach a seat (they go behind). A test reads every
  prompt a seat's model was given and finds no name of either.
- **What a log holds.** Every model call of either, as ever (`usage` and `transcript`, each naming its provider and model;
  our own model's cost is zero and its transcript holds its sureness in parts per million, its time in milliseconds, why it
  offered no draft and what it had written). One note a request, `translation_route`: the arrangement, whose answer was
  used, why it went behind, what each answered, and whether they agree where both did (by meaning, copied free text left
  out, as the real requests' scorer compares). The first is asked for every request, also one that is going behind anyway:
  that costs nothing and is the record of what it would have done. A draft and its act name the model that drew it up. The
  run's `orchestrator` entry says the arrangement, both models and which refusals stand. `pilot-report` has one line of it
  and the counts under `translator_arrangement`; the corpus and the dataset carry `route`, and their example's exchange is
  that of the translator whose answer was used.
- **The contract change:** `dataset.schema.json`, `Translation.route` (optional, opaque). Accepted by the coordinator on
  2026-10-11 under the owner's standing permission of 2026-10-05 for contract changes that ready the platform for
  translator data, and told to the owner: his to look over. Nothing else: the
  route in the log is a `note`, the arrangement is named on the command line and in a queue entry, and no world config,
  participant API or call-language schema changes.
- **A log whose only model is our own may be made again** (`realModelIn`, orchestrator/src/logs.ts): the trained model
  answers from files on disk without sampling, so a dry run of the mock with it in front is regenerable as a mock run is,
  and may be overwritten when asked. A log with any call of a real seat or of a prompt-driven translator is never
  overwritten, as before (tested, case by case).
- **How it is served.** One Python process a run, started and awaited before the run begins (`ready()`): a model that
  cannot load stops the run there, and no request pays the load (about 5 seconds here). It answers lines over a pipe, on
  the CPU, greedily. If the process ends mid-run the request goes behind (`first_failed`) and the next request starts it
  again. Its time in the log is the one thing of a run with it that is not the same twice; no decision reads it.
- **The shake-down** (`runs/tiu-01-shakedown/` on the run server, kept; wave `translator-in-use`, pinned at the commit
  of this entry's code; `runs/translator-in-use-2026-10-11/routes.py <log>` lists each request's route): 30 days, a mayor
  and a finance seat on `claude-code/claude-sonnet-5-5`, profile `ke-nakuru-2026`, seed 351, `then`. It ran to its end
  in four minutes for 0.58 USD of a limit of 6 (seats 0.52, the one behind 0.05 for its one call), with nothing broken,
  and it is small: **five requests**, all the finance seat's (the mayor asked for nothing). The first answered four with
  drafts: three confirmed (single payments of withheld tax), one declined. The declined one is the known failure: a wage
  "less the tax-law withholding" drafted as the gross wage, where `needs_calculation` was right, at a sureness of 0.1009
  against a cut-off of 0.1; the seat saw the preview pay gross and declined. Its next request (the net figure worked out)
  went behind (`declined_before`) and was confirmed; the first would have drafted the same payment without the report
  line the one behind added, so the two did not agree. No request went behind for lack of a draft, and no refusal arose,
  so the pilot says nothing yet on those paths or on `STANDS`. The first took 155 to 317 ms a request (mean 218), not
  the 70 ms of the test sets: a seat's request with its forms is about 450 to 510 of the reader's tokens. No prompt a seat
  was given names either translator. The cost report (`cost.txt`) lists the first's calls under the translator's
  configured model with no price: its table is by purpose, not by model, and was left as it is.
- **Revisit if** a pilot's report shows the two agreeing on a label nearly always over a few dozen cases (it moves into
  `STANDS`), or disagreeing on `not_an_act` (it moves out); seats decline the first's drafts often (then its drafts of that
  kind go behind by rule: forms of several amounts are the known case); the next request after a decline is mostly another
  matter (then tell matters apart); the share the first answers falls under about half (the arrangement then buys little
  over the one behind alone); a trained model passes its mark (the arrangement goes, and that model works alone); or the
  model behind changes (its prompt is not this arrangement's to change).

- **An office's staff say when a routine of theirs has no standing order, and the procedure says who makes one** (2026-10-11; wave 2c's review, fault 1, `runs/pilot-queues/wave-2c.review.md` on the run server; `StandingWork.report` in `participants/src/behaviour/common.ts`, `government.ts` (the clerk's drafters), `worlds/generator/generate.ts` (`proc-<office>-routines`); generator 0.45.3; test `participants/test/staff-report.test.ts`).
  - **What happened.** Four seats in four pilots held an office whose routine work waits for a standing work order, and made none. The council clerk of the 400-day pilot (w2-58) read "The office's own rhythm for it is every 1 day" as an order in force; a passed amendment was never written into law; on day 36 it wrote "I have no form to make or restore a work order", the mayor could not either, and the council passed the same thing again as a law in words while the clerk withdrew the law the amendment was to change. A works seat (w2-47) with a crew of five in post collected nothing in 45 days: "I had no authority to start collection myself." Before them a water seat (w2-36, 29 days) and a works seat for `maintain` (w2-41).
  - **Two causes, both the platform's.** The procedure said the staff work "by the office's standing work orders and only by them" and never who makes an order or how. And the staff reported only on orders that existed: with none, they said nothing, for the whole run.
  - **The staff's report.** From their second working day, the staff's report lists each routine of theirs with no standing order on file: "enact: not being done: no standing work order for enact is on file, and with none the staff do not do it (whoever holds the office makes one); 1 amendment the council has passed and the clerk has declared waits to be written into law." Said the day it is found and weekly after, as every other state of an order is; `state: "no_order"` in the report's data, with no order id. Not on the first day: an office opens with its orders still to make, and a mock seat makes them at its first sitting (so no run of mock seats gains a paper).
  - **The procedure's words.** "Whoever holds the office makes its standing work orders, of the office's own accord: by saying so in their own words (a standing work order for the task, where, and how often or as the procedure has it); it is on no form and needs nobody's direction or leave. None is in force until one is made." It is the town's own procedure saying how its office works; "in their own words" is how every seat is told it acts.
  - **Who real staff are here.** People with work waiting and no instruction tell whoever they work for. That is all this is: nothing is done for the seat, and a seat that reads the report and still makes no order still gets no work.
  - **Not verified.** No model has read either text. A town run by code is unchanged (its offices are whole offices and report nothing).
  - **Revisit if** a seat told both things still makes no order (then the question is whether an office should open with its standing orders made, as it opens with its standing payments); or the weekly "not being done" is noise to a seat that has decided to leave a routine off (it can say so by an order on hold; nothing lets it tell its staff to stop saying).

- **A payroll folder holds the standing payments beside the employment agreements** (2026-10-11; wave 2c's review, fault 2; `worlds/generator/generate.ts` (a model seat's `folders`), `participants/src/llm/render.ts` (`ofKind`), `participant.ts`; test `participants/test/seat-papers.test.ts`).
  - **What happened.** A town opens with a standing wage instruction at its bank for every job (`job-c0009-wages`). A finance seat's Payroll folder showed it the agreements ("As it stands: in force") and not the instructions, which were in the office's files for whoever looked. Two Haiku finance seats paid first wages by hand on day 1 on top of them (w2-17: one worker three times in a week; w2-47: three hand payments and two duplicate standing orders); a Sonnet seat filed the same standing wage twice and paid one worker double for 150 days, remitting tax on the pays that never were (w2-13); two seats could not stop a leaver's wage for two weeks because they had never seen the paper to withdraw (w2-13, w2-58: `look_first`, rightly).
  - **The fix.** The folder's kinds are "employment agreement" and "standing payment": a request to pay again and again (`data.every`, a money outcome) is a payroll paper, shown as it comes, with its id. A payment asked for once is not. Looked into, the folder is still searched for its agreements (a standing payment is no kind a search can be asked: the office's files find it).
  - **Not done.** The folder shows every standing payment of the organisation's, not only wages (a standing rent or a grant paid on would show there too). Nothing joins a standing payment to its agreement in the list beyond the `citing` each line already has.
  - **Revisit if** finance seats still pay by hand over a standing payment they were shown (then the payment's line should say when it next falls due), or a town with many standing payments that are not wages crowds the folder.

- **A payment that names the rates notice pays the rates** (2026-10-11; wave 2c's review, fault 4; `city.rates_officer` 0.4.1 in `participants/src/behaviour/government.ts`; test `participants/test/directions.test.ts`).
  - **What happened** (w2-13, both landlord seats). Each asked "Pay the rates notice rec.8093 (right rec.8094)", the draft read "settling rec.8093, citing rec.8094", and each confirmed. The rates office counted an instalment paid only when a payment named its claim; it charged both interest on day 91 and both paid the instalment a second time.
  - **The fix.** The notice and the claim are one levy, written in one step. A payment into the town's account that names the notice counts for the claim recorded with it (same owner, same sum, same due day). A payment that names the claim counts as before; one that names neither pays neither.
  - **Why here and not in the translator.** Anyone sent a notice pays "the notice"; an office that matches payments to its own second record of the same debt and ignores its own notice's number is the fault. The translator's label for such a request is not changed by this.
  - **Revisit if** other offices keep a paper and a claim for one debt and count only the claim (the tribunal's orders, the utilities' bills: not checked), or part payments are to be counted (nothing counts them today).

- **A day with a time of day is a date** (2026-10-11; wave 2c's review, fault 10; `parseDate` in `participants/src/forms.ts`, `parse_date` in `kernel/crates/resolver/src/forms.rs`; two shared cases added to `contracts/test/forms.json`, which both resolvers are held to).
  - **What happened** (w2-58, the first two births a seat registered). The notification reads "born at: year 1, day 289, 13:00", the registrar wrote "born year 1 day 289 13:00", and was told "not a date ... A date is written like 'year 1, day 12'". It dropped the time and asked again, both times.
  - **The fix.** After the day, a time of day may follow, with or without commas ("year 1, day 289, 13:00", "year 1 day 289 13:00:30"): the moment is that day's start plus the time. A time that is none (25:00) is still not a date.
  - **Contract.** No schema changed; the shared test table gained two cases (it is under `contracts/`, so it is said here: the fix cannot be held in both resolvers without them).
  - **Revisit if** a form's date should refuse a time (none does: a date field holds a moment).

- **The planning office's decision form says what records the permission** (2026-10-11; **replaced the same day** by "A permit granted on the planning office's form is a permit", below: the form now records the permission itself; wave 2c's review, fault 5; `PLANNING` in `participants/src/behaviour/papers.ts`, `city.planning_officer` 0.9.1; test `orchestrator/test/office-papers.test.ts`). **A mitigation, not the fix.**
  - **What happened.** A planning seat granted a park on its `permit_decision` form (w2-59, day 2). The form writes the decision paper. What the building inspector checks is the applicant's liberty to build, which the code office records beside its decision and the form does not. The same day the inspector fined the town 125,200 and ordered the park demolished, as built in breach of the planning law; the seat's letter got the inspector's standing reply. All 18 permits a planning seat granted in w2-13 are the same (its inspector was a seat, and fined nobody).
  - **What changed.** The form's own words: "A decision is the notice of it and no more. The permission is the applicant's liberty to build that kind of building on that lot, which the planning officer records beside a decision to grant, citing the application: the building inspector reads that record, and fines work that has none." (A form's account of itself is at most 400 characters.)
  - **The fix that is owed, for Naz.** A form that grants should grant: `FormWrites` (contracts) gains a claim written with the paper, so that one form makes the decision and the liberty as the code office does; or the planning law and the inspector read a granted decision as the permit. The first is a contract change and was not made.
  - **Revisit when** the next planning seat is seated: if it still grants on the form alone, do not seat one beside a code inspector until the form grants.

- **A draft's preview says each thing it does on a line of its own, and it does not by itself make a seat decline a wrong draft** (2026-10-11; `translator/src/preview.ts`; docs/behaviour/preview.md; tests `translator/test/preview-harms.test.ts` and the preview's other tests; measurement `scripts/preview-replay.ts`, `runs/preview-replay-2026-10-11` on the run server; evidence `runs/translator-wrong-acts-2026-10-10`).
  - **Why.** Seats confirmed 116 of 155 wrong drafts (75%) against 94% of right ones. The clear harms: a payment whose separate report was not drafted (15), the gross paid for a net (2), a budget form without its staff amount (1), employment agreements whose duty was free text or missing (17), "ask the bank to pay" drafted as a payment (5).
  - **Why a careful reader confirmed, from those previews.** Each act was one long sentence that said the payment twice (the sentence, then "Your request will read: ..."), with whatever the request's words carried sitting inside the purpose both times: a reader who looked for "report" found it. Nothing marked one act as one. A form's text and its details repeated each other and said nothing of the fields not filled. An agreement listed what was in it and nothing of the side that was bound to nothing. Everything present was right, and nothing showed what was absent.
  - **What changed.** A first line says how many things the draft does and of what kind ("This does one thing: a payment."; "three things, in this order: two payments and a report"); each is numbered, one alone too; each further fact is a line under its act. A payment says who is asked, how much, from where, to which account and whose, once or how often; its purpose is "For, in words only". A form says "Filled in" and "Left empty". An agreement has a line a side ("would be bound to: ...", "would be bound to nothing: no act of theirs is set down") and says which of its terms are words only. A law with no rule recorded says "Words only". A letter says "A letter only: it pays, files and orders nothing." An offer on a listing or an advertisement reads in words (it was raw data). A worker's place of work reads "come to town-hall/workplace.1" (it read "c0009 will let c0009 live or be in"). Nothing is said twice: a request's own words are left out where they are exactly its figures, and who sees a paper where that is only its maker and those it goes to.
  - **What it must not do, and does not.** It never reads the request, calls no model, and says nothing of the world beyond the draft's own acts and the seat's own papers (whose account a payee's is, only where the seat has seen that account; what a paper is, only where it is the seat's own). The platform is nobody in it.
  - **Length.** Over the replay's 120 drafts: 440 characters on average against 446 before (requests: 260). Payments with a missing report 351 against 554; "ask the bank" payments 238 against 357; the budget form 661 against 964; agreements 487 against 369 (a line a side); right drafts 431 against 401. It is shorter where the old one repeated itself and longer where it now says something that was not said.
  - **The replay** (60 wrong and 60 right drafts from the wrong-acts folder, every one of the five harms' drafts among the wrong; each rendered from its log with the seat's knowledge rebuilt from the observations recorded for it; a seat model shown the seat's own request and reason, then the draft, as at a sitting; one reading each; `claude-code/claude-sonnet-5-5` at its default effort and `claude-code/claude-haiku-5-5` at low; 1,446 calls, 14.02 as Claude Code reckons it):

    | reading | Sonnet: wrong confirmed | right declined | Haiku: wrong confirmed | right declined |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | preview as it was | 54 of 60 | 3 | 53 of 60 | 8 |
    | preview as it is | 53 | 4 | 54 | 6 |
    | as it was, and one sentence more in the seat's instructions | 44 | 7 | 51 | 13 |
    | as it is, and the sentence | 41 | 6 | 48 | 10 |

    (A first pass, before the first line named the kinds: 54 to 53 and 52 to 53.) By kind, preview alone: the budget form is declined by Sonnet (1 of 1; a second budget form, "the filing leaves the services line empty", too) and not by Haiku; the gross for a net was already declined by both (the line of 2026-10-09); nothing else moves. A payment whose report is missing is confirmed 15 times of 15 by both models, before and after, and the seat's note says the report is not in the draft in 2 of 15 (Sonnet) and 0 or 1 (Haiku) either way.
  - **What that says.** The preview was not the whole fault. A seat shown "one thing: a payment" for a request that asked for a payment and a report confirms it, because the payment is right; it is checking what is there, and nothing in its instructions says what confirming a part means. With one sentence in the seat's standing instructions ("What you confirm is all that is done. Anything you asked for that the draft does not list among the things it does is not done: decline, or confirm and ask for the rest.") the note names the missing report in 10 to 12 of 15, with either preview, and wrong drafts confirmed fall to 41 of 60 (Sonnet) and 48 (Haiku) with the new preview, 44 and 51 with the old; the new preview costs fewer right drafts under the sentence than the old (6 against 7; 10 against 13). The differences between the two previews are three drafts in 60 on one reading: within noise. **The sentence is not in the code** (the seat's instructions were not this task's to change): it is proposed, with its cost (right drafts declined roughly double).
  - **Also true of the measure.** "A wrong draft confirmed" counts a seat that confirms the payment knowingly and means to ask for the report next; whether it then does is not measured here (in the pilots it did not). The seat model is shown the request and the draft and none of its papers or forms. 33 of the 116 "wrong" labels look wrong themselves (the folder's README): the five "ask the bank to pay" drafts are payments, as asked, and no reading declines them.
  - **Not verified.** Any pilot with the new preview. Whether seats in a run read a numbered list with lines as readily as the replay's notes suggest.
  - **Revisit if** a pilot's seats decline right drafts for something the new lines say (watch "Left empty" on forms with many optional fields, "would be bound to nothing" on offers made on an advertisement, and "Words only" on laws: each is true and each may read as a fault); previews of forms grow past the form itself; or the sentence goes into the seat's instructions, when the replay should be run again on three readings each.

## 2026-10-11 · A person's own record: held by the kernel, computed by the code mind

Step 1 of the living world (docs/design/ai-citizens.md 10k). Behaviour: docs/behaviour/citizen.md, "The record".

- **Who computes and who holds.** The kernel cannot know what a rent rise or a notice is (no laws in the kernel), so the
  citizen's mind computes each change and the kernel holds the record, bounds it, chains a hash of its changes and is its
  only writer. The kernel reads none of it: sections are opaque whole numbers, as a record's `data` is.
- **A command, not a block.** A mind changing is not an act in the world: it takes no time on a person's timeline, and
  it must not be lost when the act beside it is refused. It is state, so it is in every log (lean ones too) and a replay
  reaches it.
- **Only a code mind sets a record, three ways over.** The participant API has no act for it. The orchestrator takes a
  change only from a non-enumerable symbol on the action of a participant run by code, acting as itself
  (`recordChangeOf`): nothing a model returns, and nothing the code behind a model seat returns, sets anything. The
  kernel will not take the command for a participant whose controller is not code. Tests: `kernel/tests/entity_record.rs`,
  `orchestrator/test/entity-records.test.ts`. **This last lock must change in step 4,** when a model gives an entity's
  odds and platform code beside it keeps the record: the rule then is "the bookkeeping, never the model", and the kernel
  cannot tell them apart by the controller's type. Decide then where the bookkeeping runs.
- **One change a wake at most,** and a section only when it has moved by more than its grain (trust 1%, ties 5%,
  attachments and views 2%, money a twentieth). Without the grain every tie's weekly fading was written for everyone.
  The record in the kernel is therefore a summary within that grain of the mind's own figures.
- **Fixed size.** Every list in `contracts/entity-record.schema.json` is bounded and the kernel refuses a record over
  8,192 bytes (a person's is 1 to 2 KB). A person's record fills as their life does, up to those bounds; the largest
  record in a town stops growing (tested over three years).
- **Contract changes** (the owner's approval of 2026-10-11; listed in contracts/README.md): the log's command
  `entity_record` and event `entity_recorded`; `caps.entity_record_bytes`; the channel kind `own_record` and its data;
  the new `entity-record.schema.json`; the dataset's two files and `records` (format 0.4.0). Profiles gained `outlook`.
- **Revisit if** records are wanted for organisations (the command takes a person's participant only; a firm's would be
  set by whoever acts for it, which needs a rule for who may); the grain hides something a study needs (lower it: the
  log grows); a record is to be read by its entity's model (hand out the `own_record` channel: nobody has it yet);
  or the cap is reached (it would mean a list is unbounded: a fault).

## 2026-10-11 · What moves in a person, how fast, and what reads it

- **Belonging and meaning are needs,** so they count in how satisfied a person is, which decides how they decide.
  **Trust, agency and attachments are recorded and moved and read by no decision yet**: reading them is wants and
  initiative (step 2). The exception is what is said: the gap between a private and an expressed view reads trust and fear.
- **Calibrating the mechanism, found on the 300-person town.** With belonging raised by having gone to a gathering last
  week, those who went were more satisfied, kept their routine and went again: 44% had been in the last month where 30%
  had (180 days, two runs). Before, a goer who was unsatisfied compared going with staying each week and dropped out a
  little over half the time. Belonging to a group now comes from attachment to it, which builds over a year, and the
  two needs' floors (3,200 and 3,700) are set so that the share of gathering decisions made unsatisfied is what it was
  (0.33 before; 0.37 with floors of 3,000 and 3,500, 0.28 with 3,000 and 4,000 and the weekly bonus). After: 40.6 to
  42.9% took part in 180 days, everything else within the noise between runs. The floors are placeholders fitted to
  leave satisfaction where it was; they are not sourced.
- **The year, before and after** (the 1,000-person town, the branch point against the branch, two runs of one town
  with full logs and six lean ones each side; `runs/living-world-1-2026-10-11`; the table is in
  docs/design/ai-citizens.md, "Progress"). One measure of 57 moved beyond the noise between six runs: group participation,
  42.5 to 46.1% (target 50.0%). Recorded, not chased: those who go are a little more often satisfied and keep going.
  Employment to population 59.5 to 59.0%, unemployment 0.7 to 1.2%, hires 202 to 202, median rent share 20.1 to 20.7%,
  union applications 10.8 to 12.2, ballots 1.5 to 1.3, stoppages 0.8 to 0.8, arrivals 47.7 to 52.2, departures 103.7
  to 103.3: all within the noise. **Cost:** 6% more instructions, 7% more wall time side by side (223 to 238 s for six
  runs at once); the log 5% larger in full and 8% larger lean (a lean year of 1,000 people: 1.29 to 1.39 GB raw, 223
  to 246 MB compressed).
- **Seen, not caused here (to look at):** in the after runs a factory's manager published the same paper to the
  outside 40 times in one day (`firm.producer`, seed 1, flagged by the run as a possible retry loop). The baseline's
  same seed did not; nothing in this work touches the producer, and the run is otherwise a different run.
- **A fault found and fixed on the way:** adding two needs made an offer's appraisal an average over seven where it had
  been over five, shrinking every appraised value by two sevenths against what had been learned. An offer's facts say
  nothing of belonging or meaning, so the appraisal is of the five, as it was.
- **Values drift** as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck step each month, about the town's mean, so the town's spread of values is
  stationary and its rates do not drift with it; the size is from measured stability (0.6 over 3.5 years), which
  overstates change. **Shocks** have directions from the literature and one placeholder size.
- **Who lives in a town is the town's.** Every person's values are now drawn by the generator (children's from their
  parents'), not by each participant from the run's seed: `--seeds N` runs the same people N times, as the measurement
  doc already said of everything else about them. Every town's runs moved.
- **Ties are bounded** at contacts plus three (18): the map of everyone ever met at a gathering is gone.
- **Sources:** each profile's `outlook` is the World Values Survey's wave 7, national, read through a summarising tool
  (to confirm). No figure was opened for a sense of agency by place, for how alike parents' and children's values are,
  for the ratio of trust lost to trust won, or for values after a bereavement: each is a named placeholder
  (docs/behaviour/citizen.md; docs/research/references.md, "The richer record").
- **Revisit if** a year's rates move when a placeholder is replaced by a sourced figure (expected: re-fit the two
  floors, nothing else); values should move toward those of the people one is tied to (not built); the shock to values
  should fade as the one study that followed it found; or long runs show the town's values wandering (they should not:
  the drift is mean-reverting and shocks are small).

- **What a seat confirms is all that is done: one sentence in a seat's standing instructions** (2026-10-11; **the coordinator's decision**, on the replay's table; the model seat 0.15.0; `CONFIRMING` and `systemPrompt` in `participants/src/llm/participant.ts`; test `orchestrator/test/confirming.test.ts`).
  - **The sentence**, after "Before anything takes effect, you'll see exactly what will happen, and confirm or decline it.": "What you confirm is all that is done. Anything you asked for that the draft does not list among the things it does is not done: decline, or confirm and ask for the rest."
  - **Why.** The entry above: the preview alone did not make a seat model decline a wrong draft (54 of 60 confirmed before, 53 after). With this sentence and the preview as it now is, Sonnet 5.5 confirmed 41 of 60 and Haiku 5.5 at low effort 48, and of 15 payments whose report was missing the seat's note said so in 12 and 10 (2 and 1 without it). A seat was checking what was there; nothing told it what confirming a part means.
  - **Its cost, known.** Right drafts declined rose from 4 to 6 of 60 (Sonnet) and 6 to 10 (Haiku): a tenth to a sixth.
  - **Where it is and is not.** In the standing instructions only, once. A draft's own words, the `do` and `confirm` tools and the preview are unchanged and say nothing against it (the test holds each to that); it is not repeated with every draft, where it would be skipped. A seat's prompt changes, so a run begun before it cannot be resumed on this code without asking every call again (as with any change to what a seat is shown).
  - **Not measured again.** No new replay: the table is the evidence, one reading a draft. No pilot has run with it.
  - **Revisit if** right drafts declined rise above about one in eight in pilots (the coordinator's mark; `oikos pilot-report` counts declines, and a review reads which were right); or seats start confirming and never asking for the rest (then the sentence taught the wrong half).

- **A permit granted on the planning office's form is a permit: a form may record a claim beside its paper** (2026-10-11; under the owner's blanket approval of that day for contract changes; wave 2c's review, fault 5; `contracts/outcomes.schema.json` `FormWrites.claim`, named in contracts/README.md; `writeClaim`, `claimFields`, `claimFieldsFor` in `participants/src/forms.ts`, `write_claim` in `kernel/crates/resolver/src/forms.rs`, both resolvers 0.7.0; `PLANNING` in `participants/src/behaviour/papers.ts`, `city.planning_officer` 0.10.0; the mock seat 0.6.1; generator 0.45.4; tests `orchestrator/test/permit-granted.test.ts`, `office-papers.test.ts`, `translator/test/preview-harms.test.ts`, three shared cases in `contracts/test/forms.json`).
  - **The fault** (the entry of this morning, "The planning office's decision form says what records the permission", which this replaces): the form wrote the decision paper; the building inspector reads the applicant's liberty to build; a seat's "granted" recorded none, and the town's own park was fined 125,200 and ordered down the day it was permitted.
  - **The contract.** `FormWrites.claim`, optional: `{ when?, position, holder, about, basis? }`. Where `when` holds, filling in the form records the claim in the same act, before the paper. Every field the claim is written from is then needed; where `when` does not hold nothing is recorded and those fields stay empty. No block changed (the claim is an ordinary `record_claim`), and a form that does not declare it is as it was: no world changes unless a form of its declares one.
  - **The planning form** declares the liberty to build where `decision` is granted, held by the applicant, about `{ action: build, object: lot, structure_type }`, citing the application: word for word what the code office records. It gains two optional fields, `lot` and `structure_type`. A grant that leaves them out is asked about: "The permit decision, with decision granted, needs: lot, structure_type. They say what the permission it records is." A permission of nothing is never recorded.
  - **Why fields, and not read from the application.** The decision names its application, which says the lot and the building. A form that looked them up would write a claim from a paper the seat may not have open, and a decision that grants less than was applied for (one lot of two, another kind of building) could not be said. The officer writes what is granted; the preview reads it back as a thing of its own ("This does two things, in this order: a permission recorded and a permit decision.").
  - **Who reads it.** The code inspector reads liberties, as it did: nothing in it changed, and a permit from a seat and one from the code office are now the same two records. The code planning office records both as it always has; a mock seat in that office says both on the one form (its brain's claim line is folded into the form that writes exactly it, and into no other).
  - **Shown.** `orchestrator/test/permit-granted.test.ts`: a small town with a planning seat that grants the town's park on the form: the liberty is recorded with the decision, the building goes up, nothing is fined; the same town where the decision is published with no liberty (what the form wrote before): fined and ordered down. And w2-59's own town on the mock (`bun scripts/pilot-mock.ts permit-2026-10-11 runs/pilot-queues/permit-2026-10-11.json --days 30`, into `runs/pilot-queues/permit-2026-10-11.mock/permit-as-w2-59` on the run server): application rec.1071 for the park, liberty rec.1239 and decision rec.1240 on day 2 in one draft, no fine and no order in 30 days (the pilot: fined on day 2).
  - **Permits granted before the change, in a run that is resumed.** They stay what they were: a decision paper with no liberty, so the inspector still treats that building as unpermitted, and nothing goes back to record a permission (the log is not rewritten, and the platform grants nothing by itself). The planning seat puts it right by its own act: the decision again on the form, now with the lot and the kind of building, or the liberty by itself, citing the application. A fine and an order already made stand until whoever made them withdraws them. (A resumed run also has a seat's prompt changed by this and by the entry above, so its calls are asked again whatever is done.) w2-13's 18 permits and w2-59's one are of this kind; neither run is resumed.
  - **Not done.** Other forms whose paper says something is granted and whose record is a claim were not looked for (a lease is an agreement; a loan decision's loan is an agreement the bank offers; a tribunal's order is its own paper): only planning was found. `counterparty` and visibility are not in the claim's template (smallest addition).
  - **Revisit if** a planning seat grants with the fields empty and reads the question back as a fault of the form (then the form should say "for a grant" on the fields more loudly, or the application's lot be offered); or a second office needs a claim against someone (a `counterparty`).

- **Two smaller faults from wave 2c's review** (2026-10-11; fault 11 and one of fault 12; `police.station` 0.3.1, `outcomeWords` in `participants/src/llm/render.ts`; tests `participants/test/police.test.ts`, `render.test.ts`, `seat-papers.test.ts`).
  - **The police found the registered dead again.** A call at a home reported every death the home had ever seen that the police had not themselves been told was registered: a registrar was sent "found dead" of two people it had registered 82 and 103 days before. Having gone in, the police see who left the home and when. A death that someone else at home outlived by more than a day was that person's to report, and is not a finding of a later call; a death nobody at home outlived is found as before (two who died within a day of each other are both found). Nothing is asked of the register: the police are shown none. Runs in which the police made such a second report change from that report on.
  - **"c0009 will let c0009 live or be in town-hall/workplace.1"** in a seat's own report of an employment agreement (a finance seat held a wage over the "garbled" terms): whoever commits to be in a place themselves "will come to" it, as the preview has said since this morning.
  - **Revisit if** someone dies and the others of the home leave within the day without a word (then nobody reports it and the police no longer find it by the earlier death's trace: only by the home's silence, which the neighbour's request is about).

## 2026-10-11: Welfare in a living world (VISION 15, point 7)

**Decided with Naz, in conversation, sentence by sentence.** Seats are debriefed after every run (his: "debrief every run, not just hard ones") by a fixed interview, not a live interviewer: out of role, shown a summary of what they did, six or so questions one at a time, a few scaled items, an open last word, a single fixed "can you say more?" for a very short answer. No check-in during a run (his lean; a check-in is an intervention). A model that writes a person's words is asked as an author and may decline; exit accounts fall under the same rule. A seat tested against its own interests is told so in the debrief, and the config says why. The point he most wanted talked through was the people of a world: his worry is citizens becoming "more than just stored values". So the point is a line, not an assertion: what continues of a person lives in their record, never in a model's memory; no model is made to be a person over time, in the first person; before any change that would do that, or have a model experience rather than estimate or write, we stop and review. The last bullet (debriefs are acted on) is the coordinator's addition, told to him.

**Revisit if:** the everyday model (design 10e, build step 4) grows beyond a small stateless estimator of odds; a composing model is given a person's memory in its own context; model-welfare research gives a better test than these lines; debriefs show a scenario distressing beyond its question.

## 2026-10-11 · Wants and initiative, in code: an entity acts when a want and an opening meet

- **What was asked** (docs/design/ai-citizens.md 10a, 10b in part, 10j's offices, 10k step 2): entities that set out to get things, on the code mind, with no model anywhere; organisations too; the numbers of step 1 read; a dial; offices that can take the post.
- **A want** (`participants/src/behaviour/wants.ts`; docs/behaviour/citizen.md, "Wants and initiative"; the record's `wants`, up to 6): what it is about, whom it concerns, what would satisfy it as typed outcomes of the blocks' vocabulary seen from the entity (money to me, money from me, occupancy, work, attend, goods), the paper in its way, how much it matters, since when, where it came from, the household it is held with, what has been tried. Born of a need short for long as the person's values weigh it, of an event (let go, unpaid, notice, a rent rise, a death, a slight, a service not done), and of what those one knows say they are after.
- **No list of verbs per want.** An opening is anything the person can see, reduced to what it would bring in the same typed terms; a want meets an opening that brings what it seeks, can undo the paper in its way, or bears on whom it concerns. The acts are those of taking an opening up, one per kind (apply to an offer, attend a practice, write to the other party of a paper, apply to a desk, sign, stand, change one's own spending, turn to those one knows): from the contract's `take_up` and the liberties everyone holds. **What is still a list, said plainly:** which boards and desks a person knows of are the world's telling by parameter (the two boards; the tribunal and what it hears; the town's complaint desk), as before; an offer whose terms are words (the union's) can only be matched by belief, by what was learned and by whom one copies. *Alternatives:* a table of acts per want (ruled out by the brief; the two goals of 2026-09-29 were exactly that and are replaced, for those who take initiative, by wants); a new typed outcome for "a decision on a paper" so desks could publish what they hear as offers (not done: a kernel-validated vocabulary change for one desk; the planned `Offer.about` of the plan sent to the coordinator was dropped for the same reason, and the tribunal's `hears` is a parameter).
- **Which way is the mind's:** a learning area `way` (EWA over kinds of way), with trust in the party or institution against the town's figure, fear of someone depended on, the sense of agency (for acting at all), belief, and those one knows who went that way. Waiting is always an option. Recorded as decisions and outcomes, and as reasons on each record change (so lean logs have them).
- **What wakes an entity:** nothing new. People already wake weekly and when something names them; a want born of an event is gone after in that wake, and again when its way has had its time (45 days, stretched by patience). At most two a week.
- **Readers** (docs/behaviour/citizen.md, "Readers"): trust sways turning to the tribunal and the town; agency sways acting, standing and waiting; attachment sways leaving town and leaving a trade; the said-and-thought gap sways signing a petition; a want long unmet with little trust and agency sways the existing chance of taking from an employer. All by the symmetric `swayed`, read only for those who take initiative.
- **New acts that follow:** a tenant asks a landlord to hold a rise or to stay on, and a worker asks for a rise (`variation_request`, answered by `variation_answer`); a household hunts for another home while it has one and moves before a notice runs out (this was listed as left out of the citizen since the start); joining the union out of a grievance; a debt taken to the tribunal at once; a complaint made as a way chosen.
- **Organisations** (docs/behaviour/firm-wants.md): a firm's or landlord's character is drawn from its principal owner's values (world content at generation; a founder's own when founded), held in the organisation's own record, kept by the one post marked `keeps_record`. It answers requests and sways the landlord's markup and patience with arrears. *Not done:* shops' prices, wages and lay-offs do not yet follow character (moving the wage a firm posts by owner would move the town's wage: wanted a source first).
- **The lock on who writes a record** (kernel `record_target`; orchestrator `recordChangeOf`): step 1 let the kernel take `entity_record` only from a participant whose controller was code, and only for that participant's own person. A model is coming to sit beside platform bookkeeping (step 4), and organisations now have records, so "is it run by code" was the wrong test. The kernel now asks whether the entity has a keeper named in the world's config: a person's is the participant's `record_keeper`, or a code controller's module; an organisation's is the `role_module.code` of its one position marked `keeps_record`, and the command may name that organisation only for a participant holding the post now. Anything else is a protocol error, never logged. The orchestrator takes a change only from the keeper's own output; whatever a model or the code behind a model seat returns sets nothing; the participant API has no act for it (a test reads the schemas and the resolver for one). `entity_recorded` carries `keeper`; chain and digest are unchanged, so old records still verify with `oikos record`. *Not built:* running a keeper beside a model-held participant (step 4's work: today a code module's bookkeeping assumes its own acts were the ones taken). *Revisit if* a record needs two keepers (a handover between modules in one post), or byte-for-byte replay of step-1 logs is needed (the event's new field changes an entry's hash).
- **A town opens with attachments.** Profiles state how long people have lived where they live (`outlook.residence`) and worked where they work (`outlook.job_tenure`) as bands of shares, with sources or marked placeholders: job tenure is the OECD's by tenure interval for six profiles and the BLS's for Ohio (opened), Brazil's as a marked placeholder for Tamil Nadu and Nakuru; residence is the ABS census's for Victoria (built from the one-year and five-year mobility rates) and a marked placeholder borrowing it for the other eight, which is probably too mobile for Lower Saxony and Akita. For a town whose spec has `living` the generator draws each adult's years in the town and each employed adult's years in their trade on a stream of its own, capped by age, and gives every person the town's mean attachment to read their own against. *Found:* those without a home at the start were first given no years in the town and left after half the time; everyone who lives in a town has lived in it. No source for length of group membership: none is given. *Revisit* when each place's own years-at-address figures are found.
- **The dial** (`dials.initiative_bps` in world config; the generator's `living:` section): absent or 0, a town is step 1's to the state hash (`orchestrator/test/living-dial.test.ts`, against the hash origin/main 750bc30 gives for `worlds/town.yaml` after 60 days). Everything else a living town has (starting attachment, firms' owners' values and record posts, the counter) is written by the generator only for a spec with `living`, so every existing town, test and pinned wave is untouched. **Left off by default:** turning it on in `worlds/town*.yaml` is one line and moves most town-simulating tests' expectations; the owner's call at merge.
- **The producer's forty orders** (seen in step 1): the bank pays an order's money in its own batch, hours after the order is made; the works is woken after each act and read the same unspent balance each time, so it ordered the same inputs on every wake (factory-9, day 72, seed 1: 203 inputs forty times in eighty seconds, $20,381 paid at the next batch, $396 left for two staff's wages, both given notice). Smaller repeats (3 to 6 orders a day) appear for two factories in both seeds. Fix, `firm.producer` 0.4.5: the works sets aside the money of its own unpaid orders (`Committed`, `trade.ts`), released when it sees the payment leave its account or after three days. A fault, fixed at the cause; it changes what any town does from the first such day (a year of the 1,000-person town before and after: 0 of 57 measures beyond the noise; factories keep about 6 more people in work). *Seen, not looked at:* shops repeating one delivery note 2 to 4 times; the builder repeating a materials order (it already subtracts what is on order). *Revisit if* the bank's batch pays at once (the hold could go) or three days proves wrong.
- **The counter:** routine is what the office's own procedure says is routine, never a platform guess. A module declares a routine `answer` with `papers` (kinds and how), and a living town (`living`, `counter` not false) is given it: the staff answer those papers only while a standing order for `answer` is in force, as the code office did; the whole office is unchanged; the seat sets the order and does none of it. While the order stands, those kinds do not bring a seat back and are shown as a count and a sample of three, except anything addressed to its own post or resting on a paper it made. Works (complaints) and the registry (death and birth notifications) have one. Orders are now read by post: both offices speak for the town and each has an `answer` order, and reading by organisation let one replace the other. *Measured* (mock seats, 90 days, 1,000 people): a calm town files almost no counter post, and the counter then costs about 2,000 prompt tokens a sitting; where collections lapse and seats sit weekly, the works seat's calls fall 119 to 93 and input tokens 15% with 108 complaints filed. *Not done:* the tribunal's registrar, the union and the electoral office (each needs its module split into seat and staff first); the mayor, who is shown the same complaints and has no view of the works office's procedure; code offices' waking is unchanged (they already take all that has come at each wake, and are held to three wakes an hour). *Seen, not looked at:* a staff report still brings a seat back. *Revisit if* pilots show seats missing something the counter answered; if the 2,000 tokens outweigh what counters save in real towns; when a source for counter practice replaces the "(to confirm)".
- **Calibration and activity** (a year of the 1,000-person town, six runs of one town each: `runs/living-world-2-2026-10-11`): the table is in docs/design/ai-citizens.md, "Progress". Where the sources fix a rate it held: employment to population 59.05 to 59.20% (dial off to living), unemployment 1.42 to 0.97%, median rent share 20.07 to 20.55%, group participation 45.88 to 46.68%, ballots and stoppages unchanged. New activity the sources do not fix: 83 letters a year asking a landlord or an employer to vary something (23 granted), notices to move to another job 75 to 89, union applications 10.7 to 13.7, 4 households a year moving while housed; arrivals 52 to 44 (vacancies go to people already in town), and working-age people at the year's end 520 to 512, the one group of measures beyond the noise. Complaints, tribunal applications and petitions did **not** rise as expected: in a calm town nothing fails that can be complained of, and nothing a tenant holds breaks the law. Against sources (most to confirm): job changes were already about 17% of the employed a year against 9.5% in Australia and are now about 21%; the tribunal and the council's desk are far less used than real ones, with or without initiative. Over two years (three runs each) the aftermath of the first year's rent reviews shows: 248 letters asking, 41 households moving while housed, gatherings a third fuller and group participation 45.6 to 50.7% (target 50.0%), and the congregation's stated affiliation falling 2.9 points a year where it fell 6.8: that fall is what belief's fading was calibrated to, so it is a sourced trend that moved and wants looking at before long runs are read for belief. Recorded, not tuned (calibrate mechanisms, not outcomes): the first is an existing rule with no friction (a better-paid posting is always taken), the others are institutions the town lacks.
- **Performance:** a year of 1,000 people, one run at a time on a quiet machine: 121 s at origin/main, 123 s with the dial off, 127 s as a living town (5% more wall time, 4% more instructions, 1% more wakes). No scheduler change: wants are looked at in the weekly plan and in the wake an event already causes. No performance work was done beyond the producer's repeated orders.
- **Revisit if:** a real-model or long pilot shows the town's sourced rates drifting with the dial on (then the sway sizes, or `event_bps`, are too large); wants pile up as `withdrew` for a kind of want because nothing in a generated town answers it (then the world lacks an institution, which is content: an appeal desk, adult learning, a tenants' group: step 3); sources arrive for how often a landlord holds a rent, how often people ask for a rise, and how often they complain (then `hold_bps`, `rise_bps` per profile and the calibration notes move); the everyday model of step 4 replaces `pursue` (the record's shape and the openings are meant to be its input unchanged: if they are not, that is the thing to fix first); character should reach prices and wages (needs a source for how far owners move them).

## 2026-10-11 · Everyday frictions at real rates, and the venues that hear them

Step 2b of the living world (docs/design/ai-citizens.md 10k). Behaviour: docs/behaviour/frictions.md. No model anywhere.

- **What was asked.** Step 2 gave people wants and the town stayed calm: nothing went wrong in it, and there was nowhere to take a grievance. The owner: "we don't have enough actions occurring"; "we're not trying to simulate utopia, we're trying to simulate reality". Things that really go wrong, as mechanisms at sourced rates; the bodies that hear them, as world content; grievances as wants; three fixes on a real basis; a record for an organisation founded in a run; what a log can show.
- **Depth over breadth** (the coordinator's ruling on the plan). Built: a home in disrepair, pay that comes short, a wrong bill, a claim for support wrongly refused or late, faulty goods; heard by the other side itself, the town's complaints desk, the tribunal's lists, an ombudsman, a consumer desk, the union. **Not built, by that ruling:** a bond withheld, neighbours and mediation, an accident or illness that costs, a road or a clinic's wait or a school place, the paper as a venue, a wrong rates notice, getting even. "A thin friction that fires at a made-up rate is worse than an absent one."
- **One mechanism, not five.** A friction leaves a state or a paper where its cause lives. Whoever suffers it holds a grievance (a want about whoever did it). Asking is one letter (`remedy_request`); the other side answers through one helper (`Respondent`) from its own books and by its character; a venue hears by one procedure (`Hearings`), whether a desk or the tribunal's lists; its decision is words. *Alternatives:* a module a friction (ruled out: five copies of asking, answering and deciding); recording what is owed as a debt and letting the existing machinery collect it (ruled out: a firm pays any debt recorded against it without question, so every claim would carry itself out; a grievance's papers never reach that).
- **Rates from one survey for nine places.** No place had figures for all five, and each national source counts differently. The World Justice Project's 2019 legal-needs survey asks the same questions in all nine countries: the share of adults with a problem of each kind in two years. Each profile states half of it as a yearly share, and the generator turns it into a rate for those exposed with the town's own counts. *Known wrong in known ways:* halving understates; a country stands for a region; "a landlord problem" is all given to disrepair and "disruption or incorrect billing" all to wrong bills; Brazil and Mexico are three cities. Victoria's own figures (a renters' survey, the consumer survey, the tribunal's and the bond authority's reports) are cross-checks in the profile's notes and the references. **Placeholders, named in each profile:** by how much pay is short (5%) and a bill overstated (30%), the share of a trip's goods that is faulty, a repair's hours, the tribunal's fee, a desk's cases a day, the uphold rate without proof, how often an organisation answers a venue and obeys it; and, outside Victoria and England, how often the other side puts a thing right when asked (it stands at each country's share of problems resolved).
- **Disrepair is physics.** A variable of the building the kernel already knows how to keep, a task that takes it down, the builder's crew doing the work in its own hours. Two contract additions for it: a structure's starting variables, and nothing else. Where each building starts is drawn evenly below the level that needs repair: the steady state of wearing and repairing, since no figure for dwellings by age was found. A whole building wears together, so a block of flats has one defect and twelve grievances: true of a roof, less of a tap.
- **Where a venue cannot see the fact** (the coordinator's ruling): the thing happened, nobody lies yet, so every claim is true. The code office's rate stands for failure of proof. An applicant who can show a paper for it (a delivery note, the agreement, the request they made first) is believed; one with only their word, as often as the rate says. A seat in a venue decides for itself. In practice nearly every applicant has something to show, because a venue is gone to after asking: the rate is seldom drawn.
- **A venue only after asking,** and its bother counted. In the first measurement people went to venues more often than they asked the other side (117 applications against 100 requests in a year of the 1,000-person town), where the surveys have about half contacting the other side and a sixth turning to an authority. Two changes, each with a basis: an ombudsman and a consumer desk take a matter only once the other side has been asked, so a person goes to a venue after a no, a silence or a promise not kept; and the bother of a venue (forms, waiting, a hearing) counts against it in the mind's choice (`wants.choice.venue`, **fitted** to the survey's sixth). A person's hours at a venue are not yet taken from their day.
- **The typed way to say what one hears** (`Offer.hears`; contracts/README.md). Step 2 dropped `Offer.about` and left the tribunal's `hears` a parameter; step 3 needs a desk or a group made in a run to be found without belief. It lives inside the offer, so the call language and the translator's schema are untouched. The citizen's openings for a grievance are read from every statement seen that carries one. **Still read by parameter:** the two boards, the town's desk for waste, and the tribunal's two older lists in the citizen's own older code paths (they are also in its notice now).
- **Three fixes asked for from the first living pilot** (lv-01, 60 days, Nakuru). (1) A member's pay was told to the household at every wake where the figure compared was not the figure said ("My pay is now KSh0.00" 478 times): now told when the words change. (2) Landlords' `arrears` wants were born and never pursued: a landlord now writes to ask, and a month on, if it would sooner keep the tenant, applies to a body that hears arrears. Found on the way: the want was held by tenant, so a tenant with two leases (a renewal) had it born and met turn about at every look, which looped once asking was attached to it; it is held by lease. (3) Wants slow to start: **an artefact.** A need had to be short for 60 days from day 0 before it became a want, in every run; a need short in the first week is now taken to have been short for a drawn part of that. (Events, the other source of wants, come when they come: rent reviews fall at a year's end.)
- **Job changes: the mechanism is in, the rate is not reached, and why.** A job is left only for one that pays enough more (10%), more for each year held (2%, to ten), more again in another line of work (20%): **fitted figures with a sourced shape**, in the profile, for a living town. Measured as a labour force survey would (of those in a job at the year's end, the share with another employer during the year: `economy/job-mobility`): 21.4% with no living town, 19.1% in step 2's living town, **16.7% now**, against 7.7 to 9.6%. Voluntary moves fell from 75 to 89 a year to about 45 of 420 employed, and those looked at (the first 25 of one run) are all shop workers going to a factory, the builder or the police for 40 to 80% more: the profile's wages by kind of work differ that much, and no premium with a basis holds someone from that. What holds real people there is that such jobs want a trade: employers here hire anyone. And **firms make 115 to 165 people redundant a year, about 30% of jobs**, by their monthly staffing rule (a real rate is of the order of 2%: to source), which alone moves about one worker in eight to another employer. Neither is fixed here: both are firm-side rules with their own calibration, and tuning the citizen's premium until the total came right would be calibrating the outcome. **For the owner.**
- **Found: a firm's wage rule pays staff less than they agreed.** Of about 31 people a year whose pay comes short in the 1,000-person town, about 13 are the new mechanism (an employer's character or trouble) and about 18 are firms lowering the wage they pay existing staff by their monthly wage rule, to 4 to 48% under what the agreement says. Before this step a worker took any pay but the exact wage for no pay, resigned a fortnight on and recorded the whole wage as a debt; now it is short pay, a grievance, and the firm's books do not own to it (it "set the wage afresh"), so a venue that asks is told nothing is owed. Whether a firm may cut an agreed wage without the worker's agreement is a question for the firms' rules: recorded, not changed.
- **A want given up stops its routine.** Giving up on work stops the looking for as long as a want given up rests; the person notes it (`work_search`, their own), and `economy/summary` counts them out of the labour force. About two a year in the 1,000-person town: most who are let go find work or leave first.
- **Belief's fading, re-fitted for a living town.** The target on file is the census's fall in stated affiliation, 1.6 points a year. Fading at 3% a month gave −6.8 over two years with no living town and −2.9 in step 2's; over one year −4.2 in step 2's living town. In a living town gatherings are fuller. At 2% a month it rose 0.7 a year; at 2.5% it fell 1.2 over two years (three runs: +0.5, −1.6, −2.7) and 1.6 over one (six runs). The profile states 2.5% for a living town (`belief.living_fade_bps_per_month`); the module's 3% is untouched, so a town with no `living` is as it was (and still falls too fast: not this step's).
- **A record for an organisation founded in a run.** The post made with a new business says in its role module that it keeps the business's record; the kernel takes the record from whoever holds that post, as it does for a post the config marks. *Alternative:* a new field on the block that makes a position (ruled out as more contract for the same thing; the role module is already carried, logged and opaque). Nobody founds a business in a year of the 1,000-person town (no premises come up for sale), so this is shown by a test that forces a founding, not by a run.
- **Offices under load** (mock seats, 90 days, the 1,000-person town; `scripts/counter-measure.ts`): see the table in the design doc. A seat sits on its own cadence whatever arrives; frictions add 6 to 12% to the input tokens of the mayor, the works office, the tribunal's member and a landlord, and nothing to finance. The desk has a counter (its staff settle what the record settles; the office-holder decides the rest), which in 90 days saved nothing and cost about 2,300 tokens a sitting, as step 2 found of every counter in a quiet office: venues receive under one application a fortnight each. The tribunal's member has none.
- **Contract changes** (the owner's blanket approval of 2026-10-11; all additions; contracts/README.md): `Offer.hears`; `has: ["hears"]`; `dials.friction_bps`; a structure's `variables`; `role_module.keeps_record` for a post made in a run; dataset 0.6.0. No hard rule and nothing of VISION 15 point 7 is touched: no model, and a record is still written only by platform bookkeeping the config or the founding names.
- **Calibration, twins and cost** (a year of the 1,000-person town, six runs of one town each; `runs/living-world-2b-2026-10-11`; tables in docs/design/ai-citizens.md, "Progress"). The same living town with the dial at 0 and at 10,000: **0 of 57 measures beyond the noise**. Against step 2's living town, what moved beyond the noise follows from the fixes, not from frictions: hires 226 to 197 and jobs filled 250 to 214 (people hold their jobs), people at each gathering 54 to 61 and affiliation (belief's fading). Wall time, one run at a time: 130 s with no living town, 134 s living with nothing going wrong, 133 s with frictions.
- **Revisit if:** a yearly survey by kind of problem is found for a place (replace the halved two-year shares); a venue's own outcomes by kind of case are found (replace the uphold rate, and the grant rates that stand at "resolved"); pilots show seats in venues deciding against the papers shown (the code rule is then not what a seat does: record both); grievances pile up as let go for a kind with no venue (the list for step 3's founding); firms' redundancies are calibrated (then fit `job_move` again: it will bind differently); a town's people need the time a venue takes taken from their day; a block of flats' twelve grievances for one defect distort a study (then disrepair by dwelling: the kernel's variables are per structure).

## 2026-10-11 · What the second living pilot found: a seated office is shown what its code twin acts on, and seven faults beside

`runs/pilot-queues/living-2.review.md` and `living-1.review.md`; the logs `runs/lv-02` and `runs/lv-01` (read, never changed). No model was called for any of this: mock seats and code offices. Behaviour: docs/behaviour/office-books.md, standing-work.md ("The support office"), firms.md, directions.md, credit.md; docs/real-models.md ("A seat's notebook"); docs/measurement.md. Contract additions: contracts/README.md of the day.

- **A seated office is shown what its code twin acts on (fault 2 of the review).** The landlord's code twin wrote to four tenants in arrears on day 37; the seat was shown nothing. The audit, office by office, found the same shape everywhere: the code keeps a running list in its head (who is behind, what waits for an answer, what is unpaid, whose time has run) and a seat is shown each paper once. **Decision:** each office module says what its books hold (`books`), and where a model holds the office a clerk, a post of the office's staff, keeps them and files a paper on the organisation's own file when what stands open has changed: what changed in its words, everything that stands open in its list. *Alternative considered:* working it out from the seat's own observations and printing it in the prompt, as the roster and the ballot count are. Less machinery, but no paper to open, nothing in the log to say what the seat had been shown and when, and the prompt carries the list. The coordinator chose the clerk, on four conditions, all kept: the clerk reads only the office's own papers and accounts; the line says what changed; the paper is the office's own (another office of the same organisation is not shown it); a rule the code acts on that was on no paper is published (the town's rule on petitions, `proc-petitions`). What was missing, by office, is the table in office-books.md. Letters to a landlord were shown at its seat's next sitting but did not bring it back, because they are addressed to the organisation and not to its post: where an office is its organisation's only one, what others address to the organisation is now that office's post, and brings the seat back at the next working day's sitting (a town hall's many offices are unchanged). Held on papers made by hand: a small town's tenants write to no landlord in a hundred days.
- **What is routine is the staff's (fault 7).** The support office's seat paid 52 pensions by hand each month. The office now runs in parts: its staff decide and pay what the support law's conditions settle, under a standing order (`pay_claims`), and refuse nothing; a refusal, a doubt and a review are the office-holder's, on a decision form the office did not have. **A town opens with the standing orders for its routines in force** (`order-<office>-<task>`): the earlier fix (staff with no order say so) stands for an order withdrawn. Finance, the tribunal, the lender and the union are not split: each is one plan in its module; their seats work by hand with the books to say what waits. *Would revisit:* a pilot in which one of those seats spends most of its calls on what its procedure settles.
- **A hire nobody pays (fault 3).** The hiring office's payroll notice named no budget line; a finance seat set an environment hire against the staff line and left the worker unpaid. The notice and its letter now name the line; the payments procedure says a wage is on its office's line and that finance signs no agreement. The code finance office never checked a line (it pays on the notice); the hiring office already refuses to hire beyond its line. *Not done:* payments marked with a line, so that "spent by line" could be read from the books: the office's papers keep a total. *Would revisit:* a finance seat that still refuses a hire its notice puts on a line with room.
- **Things that happened all at once (fault 5).** Two causes, both mechanism. Every lease and loan standing at the start was counted from day 0 though each tenant's and borrower's bank pays on its own day: the agreement now carries its day (`attrs.first_due`) and the landlord and the lender count from it. And every landlord took arrears up at its first look after the threshold, which was the same moment for all (one weekly published paper wakes them all, and the weekly sleep restarts from it): each landlord now has its own day and hour of the week for the rent book. Left as they are, being real: the rates office's instalment and overdue runs (a billing run on the law's dates), and a tribunal list deciding together the cases whose day has come. *Not done:* the scheduler still restarts a module's weekly sleep from any wake, so other offices woken by the same paper still look together; nothing else was found acting on it at once. *Would revisit:* a count by day in a pilot's review that shows another such column.
- **The repeated "My pay is now" message (fault 6): no fault found.** Read by sender and recipient, lv-02's 1,754 messages are 938 pairs with no sentence said twice running to the same person: 137 first tellings on day 0 and real changes after (raises of about 2%, jobs lost and found, an own-business income that moves monthly). Checked twice, independently. The step 2b fix holds; `orchestrator/test/household-saying.test.ts` holds the rule. *Would revisit:* if telling every small change is thought too much, a threshold would need a real-world basis.
- **A seat's notebook (the review's note on growth).** Folded, not left to fill: at 6,000 of 8,000 characters the seat is asked once, in one counted call (purpose `notebook`), to summarise its older untouched entries; nothing is dropped silently (docs/real-models.md). 17 extra calls in 400 sittings of a seat that never prunes.
- **`oikos measure` on larger towns (fault 1).** The reader's limit is sized from the log's own first line; the queue says "done, BUT ITS MEASURES FAILED" (docs/measurement.md). *Chosen over* reading the header outside DuckDB: nine tables unnest the header. *Would revisit:* a header that outgrows memory.
- **The works office and the mayor's direction (lv-01, fault 3 there).** The direction was filed on the form, read, acknowledged and followed; the worker signed an offer made two days before it. The acknowledgement's "takes nobody on" was untrue of an offer already out, and now says what a direction does and names such an offer. **Found on the way, and a fault of the platform:** an office's staff post never read a direction (it looked under its own post's name). It does now. No direction to a seated office's staff took effect before this date: in wave 2 that is the rates office's recovery direction and the works office's collection direction, where one was given to an office a model held; staffing directions were the office-holder's to follow and were not affected. *Not done:* withdrawing an offer not yet signed (needs the kernel).
- **Prompt sizes and sittings** (mock, the pilot's own 3,000-person town, 120 days, twelve seats; `runs/living-pilot-fixes-2026-10-11`): before (origin/main 7d36367) and after, one run each of the same description; the two are different trajectories of the town (rent is counted differently), and a mock seat sits by its code brain's rhythm, so sittings say little of a model's.

  No seat's prompt grew by more than about a thousand characters a sitting; the support office's calls fell by two thirds (its staff pay). The landlord's seat was shown its first tenant in arrears on day 11 and each one after as it fell behind. **Seen, not caused here:** the lending seat's first prompt is 130,000 characters before and after (it is shown the bank's whole ledger and every instruction at each sitting), and the mock in that seat pays out no loan it approves: both for whoever next seats the bank. The same run's arrears letters: 128 on one day of 6 before, 128 over 43 days after (8 the most in a day); applications to the tribunal 23 on one day, then 20 over 16 days. `oikos measure` and `oikos cost` ran on the after run's log (a 36 MB header).
- **After the firm-side fixes landed (the same day).** The landlord's arrears loop is theirs (ask, notice to vacate, application for possession, the tribunal's plan or order, warrant, removal) with this entry's two changes kept on top: rent counted from the lease's own day, and every step of it taken on the landlord's own day for its rent book. The landlord's books show each tenancy being ended at the stage its papers put it at and what the law's procedure has next; the tribunal member's show applications for possession with whether the tenant answered and with what; the registrar's show warrants asked for.
