## 2026-10-13 · Why no tenant in arrears has anything to offer: traced, found to be the town's structure, and nothing changed

**What was asked.** Across six pilots the tribunal seat has had no real choice in possession cases: one answer in fourteen offered a sum, the code member set no plan in twelve runs, and in the latest pilot all three answers said "can pay nothing". The reading to check: households here fall into arrears only when income collapses entirely, and a real town has partial and temporary losses that leave something over after a month or two.

**What was found** (code reading, and code-only runs, no model called: working files in `runs/plat-arrears-2026-10-13/` on the run server; `batch.sh`, `offers.sql`, `apps.sql`, and a temporary trace in the citizen, removed before this commit). A year of the 1,000-person living town; the trace on Nakuru's town, one run.

- **The offer is computed as stated and is not wrong.** `offer = household income (wage or business draw + lasting support + other adults' pay told to the leaseholder) − rent − essentials`, floored at nothing, on the day the tenant answers. It uses what is coming in now, so recovery before the hearing is counted (one tenant in the trace had found work and moved to a cheaper home between two applications: offer 3,563 against 6,000 owed).
- **Households with the means do not get as far as a hearing.** A tenant who misses a rent pays it back as soon as the balance covers it (`citizen.ts`, the `missed` list). Of 102 leaseholders in Nakuru's town who missed a rent in the year, 23 had income above rent plus essentials at the time (a timing miss: money spent on goods and energy before the rent order ran; in work or not); those pay up as the money comes (the run had 76 notices to vacate and 17 applications for possession in the year, against 102 households that missed a rent). Whoever stays behind two rents, then the law's days, then a notice, is whoever is structurally short.
- **Those who stay behind are not all out of income, but all are short.** Of the 13 applications for possession in the traced run: 8 households had nothing, or a support payment, or a little from another member (0 to 4,160 a month); 4 had income (2,361 to 15,563) with rent plus essentials above it; 1 was a tenant back in work in a cheaper home (offer 3,563 against 6,000 owed), who did not answer. Of the 102 first missed rents: 61 in work, 45 of them with income below rent plus essentials; 41 not in work. The wage here is 15,563 a month, the two common rents 6,000 and 13,000 (84% of a wage), essentials 6,000: a worker at the town's wage in a 13,000 home is 3,440 short before anything goes wrong. That is the profile's recorded inconsistency (rents by bedrooms are an urban flat's, the profile's own note and 2026-10-12, "Homes by income"), left on purpose (imperfect profiles are fine). Nothing in the platform makes it.
- **Six runs, Nakuru's profile (means):** 17.3 applications; 7.0 answers, of which 3.0 "we have left", so 4.0 by tenants still at home (about 28% of the 14.3 still in the home; the profile's 40% placeholder read against who they are); **0 answers offering any sum in any run; 0 plans.** Victoria's profile: 2.5 applications, 0.5 answers, 0 offering, 0 plans. The measure said the same before: nothing moved, as nothing was changed.
- **Why so few answer** is a draw (`answer_bps`, 40% a placeholder for Nakuru, read against trust, agency, fear of the landlord and where they could go), plus the tenants who have already gone. It is how it falls, not a fault.

**What is not built, and is real.** Partial and temporary loss of income as a path into arrears: hours cut, short-time, a spell of sickness that stops pay, a benefit paid late. Of these, pay come short, a claim refused or pending and a bill over the usual exist (docs/behaviour/frictions.md) and are small by their sources (1 of the 102 first missed rents had pay short on the day); illness stops no pay here; hours cut is named in docs/behaviour/firms.md as not built (a wage is a sum a fortnight whatever the hours). Building hours means a firm-side model of hours and a rule for when an employer cuts them, with a source for each: not a tenant-side change, and not a thing to add so that plans appear.

**Decision: build nothing.** The mechanism does what its source says; with the town's rents and wages the tribunal's cases are of households that cannot pay, and the code member's rule gives them possession. Changing the offer, the self-cure, or inventing shocks until offers appeared would be calibrating an outcome.

**Contracts, kernel, versions:** none changed.

**Revisit if:** (1) a town with rents sized to its wages (a fixed Nakuru table, or a profile whose rents are 30 to 40% of a wage) shows the same zero: then the cause is elsewhere and this entry is wrong; (2) hours cut or short-time work is built (firms.md) — then measure again, the partial-loss path will exist; (3) a pilot needs cases with an offer in them: use a scenario with a town whose wages carry its rents (say so in the pilot's plan, not a change to the behaviour), or a seat-side framing; (4) the profile's rent table is corrected.

## 2026-10-13 · Hours before heads: a firm over its need cuts hours first, where the place's law lets it

**What was asked.** The finding of "Why no tenant in arrears has anything to offer" named the real path not built: partial and temporary loss of income, hours cut. A firm whose trade fell could only keep everyone on full pay or make people redundant. Build the hours term, the law as profile data, the firm's rule and the worker's reading, and measure honestly without tuning for any outcome.

**What was built** (docs/behaviour/firms.md, "Hours before heads"; `runs/plat-hours-2026-10-13` on the run server).
- **The agreement** may carry its ordinary hours (`agreement(hours=...)`, a second commitment of the worker); absent, the law's ordinary week. Additive: nothing older changes.
- **The law** is `employment.hours` in each of the nine profiles, published as `law-cutting-hours`: by notice, with the employee's agreement, or not at all. Victoria, Minas Gerais, Lower Saxony, England, Nakuru: agreement. Tamil Nadu, Akita, Ohio: notice (Tamil Nadu owes half pay for the hours cut from 50 staff, Akita 60%). Jalisco: no. Three sources were opened (SGB III, Labour Standards Act art 26, ERA Part XI in summary), the rest are marked to confirm. `consent_bps` 9,000 is a placeholder, the same everywhere.
- **The firm** (shops and factories): where it has more staff than the smoothed trade needs and the law lets it, it cuts everyone's hours to need over staff (never under the floor; a change only of 10 points or more) by a paper to each, and restores them when trade is back or the law's spell ends; heads go only for what hours cannot absorb, under the old rule. Shops serve, and factories make, in the hours worked.
- **The worker** reads the paper as the pay agreed from the day it names. Short pay is unchanged: a pay below the wage with no paper behind it, or over a refusal, fires it.

**What was measured** (code only, six seeds, a year of the 1,000-person living town; before = main, after = this branch; means of six runs).

| | Victoria before | after | Nakuru before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| firms cutting hours | 0 | 19.8 | 0 | 5.8 |
| workers put on cut hours (agreed) | 0 | 87 | 0 | 10.3 |
| papers restoring hours | 0 | 79.8 | 0 | 3.8 |
| redundancy notices (all reasons) | 31.2 | 12.0 | 21.2 | 19.5 |
| ...for want of trade | 21.0 | 0 | not split | not split |
| rent payments missed | 19.2 | 20.5 | 570.7 | 579.7 |
| applications for possession | 2.5 | 2.5 | 17.3 | 18.8 |
| answers | 3.2 | 2.5 | 7.3 | 8.3 |
| answers offering a sum | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| plans set | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

The tribunal chain did not move: no answer offered a sum, no plan was set. **That is the honest result, and nothing was tuned toward it.** Why: Victoria's wages carry its rents, so a worker at three quarters of the hours still pays, and few reached a hearing; Nakuru's wages do not (the profile's recorded inconsistency) and its shops had little to cut (6 of 30 cut, 10 workers a run), so most of its arrears come from the households that had no work or a wage below rent already. A town where wages sit between rent and rent plus essentials, and where hours are cut, would show it; neither of these is that.

**What else moved.** Redundancies for want of trade in Victoria fell from 21 to nothing (31 to 12 in all: the 12 are for want of cash, and what the floor leaves). Workers on cut hours leave for better-paid postings more: resignations "moving to another job" rose from 38 to 60 a year, departures from town from 96 to 107 (z 4.5), jobs (hires of all kinds) from 126 to 138; arrivals follow (z 2.9). That is the existing rule meeting a lower wage (a posting is better than a cut wage), not a special case. Unemployment, employed and the other standing measures did not move beyond the noise. A cut lasts 91 days at the median (116 mean) and a worker is cut twice a year on average: some of that is the month boundary of a head count, which is flagged to revisit.

**Contracts, kernel, versions.** Contracts: additive (contracts/README.md "2026-10-13": the call `agreement(hours=...)`, `law-cutting-hours`, the kinds `hours_notice`, `hours_restored`, `hours_reply`). Kernel: none of the world's physics; **the engine's resolver (`kernel/crates/resolver`) gained the same four lines as the translator's, for `hours=`** (without them every agreement a run made lacked the term: the runs use the engine's). **Pinned state hashes moved on purpose** (every town whose profile states the law publishes it): `worlds/test/living.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/living-dial.test.ts` (step 1), `founding.test.ts` (step 2b), `opening-caseload-offices.test.ts` (two world hashes), each with its note; the public-finance test reads an order made after an hours paper as the paper's wage; the founding test's seed is now 7 (seeds 2 and 5 each have one person sharing the want that founds now; a draw, not the rule). Modules: `firm.retailer` 0.15.0, `firm.producer` 0.9.0, `citizen.default` 0.56.0, generator 0.54.0. **The translator's call vocabulary gains one name, `agreement(hours=...)`; no request a seat gets needs it yet, and the forms list it is trained on does not change.** (The gold-coverage test now lists `agreement.hours` among the arguments with no gold, as it does `statement.formal`.)

**Revisit if** a town with wages between rent and rent plus essentials shows the chain moving (then the tribunal's cases will have offers and the measure should be taken again); the quits among workers on cut hours turn out to be too many against a source on short-time workers' job search; the cut-and-restore churn is a boundary effect (add a minimum spell); `consent_bps` gets a source; or a state scheme is built where a profile has one. **Alternatives not taken:** cutting some workers' hours and not others (who is a fairness decision with no source here); a mechanic that lowers a number with no paper; hours for the other employers (the council, the builder, offices: they follow budgets, not trade).

## Open (to decide at the Stage 2 checkpoint or before)

- **Calibration, measured again after the first-year risk fix** (2026-10-05, at 0251d3a, `runs/calibration-2026-10-05` on the run server; the small town, 3 seeds × 2 years, code only, as below). Health: 4 breaches of 15 (8 measured). Recorded, not chased: Naz decides what to do with the numbers.
  - **Still off:** unemployment 2.0% (1.0 to 2.9; target 4.6 ± 1.5), 1.1 points below the band, as before. Group participation 34.5% (32.5 to 36.3; target 50 ± 5), 10.5 points below the band (was 39%). Religious affiliation falling 6.1 points a year (5.3 to 7.0; target 1.6 ± 1), 3.5 points past the band (was 3.1). Demand unmet 16.7% (at most 5; was 7.0%).
  - **Now in range:** employment to population 63.6% (was 68.7; target 63.9 ± 3) and participation 64.8% (was 70.1; target 67.1 ± 3). Saving 4.0% and renters' housing costs 22.4% of income stay in range.
  - **Deaths and illness, two years, about 200 people:** 2, 6 and 3 deaths; 36, 40 and 46 illnesses; 12, 12 and 8 injuries. No health measure has a target for these yet.
  - **Not comparable draw for draw** with the 2026-10-02 measurement: the rename changed every random draw, and the heat and first-year fixes went in between. Which of those moved demand unmet, groups and religion isn't known; nothing was looked into.

- **Calibration after the world expansion (measured 2026-10-02, not chased: for the checkpoint).** The small town, 3 seeds × 2 years, code only, at 2fd20b4. Health: 6 breaches of 15.
  - **Labour market too tight:** unemployment 1.9% (target 4.6 ± 1.5); employment to population 68.7% (63.9 ± 3); participation 70.1% (67.1 ± 3). A likely cause, unconfirmed: the expansion's public jobs (clinic, school, police, environment office) in a small town, all filled from the start.
  - **Social groups and religion:** group participation 39% (50 ± 5); religious affiliation falling 3.1 points a year (1.6 ± 1).
  - **Demand unmet** 7.0% (at most 5).
  - **Saving now in range:** 7% (6.5 ± 5), against 17–21% before. Likely the savings drawn by age, and the energy loop's drain fixed.
  - **Suggestion:** look at each against its mechanism first (who's hired, and why; what keeps people in groups), not by tuning rates. Several moved with today's changes, so a mechanism, not a rate, is likely behind each.

- **Periodic tenancies (a contract change, proposed 2026-09-30).** A lease can say a fixed `term` or none. Real tenancy law (Victoria's included) continues a fixed-term lease as a periodic one when neither side gives notice. Proposal: an optional `then: "periodic"` on an agreement's terms, read by `terms` as "in force after the term until notice". Until signed off, landlords renew instead (above).

- ~~**Construction payments must be fleshed out.**~~ **Resolved by phase B** (noted 2026-10-01): builders buy materials from a supplier (the world market, `world.trade`) as stock that construction consumes (`materials_at`); `materials_cost` and the money paid to nowhere are retired (contracts/README.md, v0.5). A local quarry, if wanted, is world-expansion §6.1. The original note: **Accepted only to unblock us** *(Naz, 2026-09-25: "not happy with this, but will accept it for now")*. In v0.2, `construct` and `demolish` pay materials and demolition costs straight from the builder's own account to the boundary. That skips the builder's bank (contrary to D26: money moves only when a custodian's seat moves it) and doesn't model suppliers at all. To return to it: have builders buy materials from supplier entities (possibly outside-world suppliers via the boundary) through ordinary bank-executed transfers, with materials as a physical stock that construction consumes, or through the work/process model (D24), where building is a task with inputs. Until then it's a documented liberty; see contracts/blocks.schema.json (`construct`, `demolish`). Known quirk: since materials are paid to the outside world, the outside world's own seat builds for free (it pays itself). Only a researcher-configured boundary module can do this; it disappears once construction payments are fleshed out.

- **Fatality by age on a condition's band (a contract addition): signed** (Naz, 2026-10-01: "yes to both, signed off"). A band has one `fatal_bps` for all ages, but real case fatality rises steeply with age, so no single figure can carry a share of the life table's deaths without killing far more children than die. Proposal: an optional `fatal_by_age: [{from, bps}]` on a severity band, read like `other_causes`. The generator would then move each age's "treatable" deaths from `other_causes` into conditions, set so that with care as usual the life table holds, and without care more die. Until signed, care shortens illness but saves no one.

- **Contract additions proposed by M2** (docs/design/m2-llm-participants.md, "Open"): `notices` on the Observation (translation failures and similar orchestrator-to-seat notes), and `framing.debrief_text`.
- ~~Directory refresh interval (D33)~~: superseded by D42 (perception is changes).
- **Calibrating word of mouth** (D45): hires via contacts are far below the 30–60% target. To address with citizen calibration (M3 batch runs give the measurement).
- ~~Citizen behaviour in the Rust kernel vs TypeScript code seats.~~ **Resolved by D30.**
- ~~Which D15 laws become parameters.~~ **Obsolete** under D18/D19: there are no laws in the kernel; laws are records in a world's config.

## 2026-10-13 · What a seat carries between sittings: the office's own file

**What was asked.** Pilots show a seat carrying only its notebook between sittings, and the thinness distorts what we see (a lapse of memory reads as a lapse of judgement). Sort the lapses in the reviews into what a real office-holder would have on the desk and the platform fails to give (ours to fix) and honest lapses a person could make too (not ours); fix the first the way a real office works; no model calls.

**What we found** (the list, with classes, is in `runs/plat-memory-2026-10-13/STATUS`). A seat's conversation is reset at every sitting and each paper reaches it once, as a new paper. So it never sees again what it sent, filed, paid or decided, nor what is still open except as the clerk's paper of changes. Lapses of class (a): the landlord paying a rates notice on day 31 and again on day 73 (and letting a second fall overdue), the tribunal member and others re-looking up due dates and their own earlier decisions, receipts never seen again (unexplained payer), a standing payment re-verified each time. Lapses of class (b), left alone: judgement and initiative (not listing the vacant home sooner, no notice to vacate), reasoning that was never written down, who a payer is (a question for the bank). Not memory, noted: the books can list two records for one rates bill, and paying one leaves the other open.

**What was built** (docs/behaviour/office-books.md, "The office's own file"). An office keeps its own file, and the holder reads it: at every sitting, after the report, a section made by code (`participants/src/behaviour/daybook.ts`) from what the seat itself was shown: its own papers and its staff's, newest first, the last 40 days, each with its date and what followed it; its payments out (a request to the bank is replaced by the payment when it was carried out, and says no payment is seen yet when it was not); money in by payer; and what stands open on its books (the office module's own `books`, the clerk's reader, a few lines to a heading). At most 4,500 characters; older and overflow counted by kind, by code. A code office has none. It extends the books that exist rather than adding a new thing; no new paper is filed by the clerk (a paper is read once, so the file is kept on the seat's side from the papers it was shown, as the roster and the ballot count are).

**Held.** The file is made of the seat's observations only (the knowing rules: it is theirs; test in `orchestrator/test/no-god-view.test.ts`). The seat's standing instructions, the translator's prompt and forms list are unchanged; the platform stays invisible (world terms, no log, no kernel); nothing says what to do with the record. Twin: code runs do not build it; the mock living-6 line-up (90 days, seed 402) gives the same final state hash and command count before and after (48f0b76990a8ed3a, 1,511,048 commands). No kernel change; no contract change (the seat's `dayBook` is a participant-config field internal to the orchestrator); `LLM_PARTICIPANT_VERSION` 0.18.0.

**Prompt size** (mock run of the living-6 line-up, first turn of each sitting, characters; the mock's notebook is near empty and its offices quiet, so these are a floor): finance 2,963 to 5,427 mean (max 9,889 to 11,460); landlord 8,120 to 9,568 (12,358 to 13,075); mayor 5,157 to 6,490 (19,754, unchanged: its first sitting has no file yet); tribunal member 1,182 to 2,783 (11,949 to 12,638). The file itself was at most 3,532 characters in this run. Real seats with busy offices can reach the bound: +4,500 on a first turn that was 12,000 to 24,000.

**Revisit if** a pilot shows a seat treating the file as a to-do list or repeating its own acts; the bound binds (the tribunal's member on a day with dozens of orders: then list decisions by application in a compact form, or a look on request); a seat needs papers older than 40 days (on its file and can be looked up); or the double-record rates bill is settled as a books fix. The finance prompt ceiling in `orchestrator/test/seat-sight.test.ts` went from 52,000 to 56,000 (largest then 52,193). Prompt growth of 20 to 40 percent per sitting is the price; if cost matters, the money-in and older-open sections are the first to shrink.

## 2026-10-13 · Four platform faults from the sixth living pilot (`plat-faults`)

Four small faults found in lv-06 and its review, each traced before it was touched (findings, with the evidence: `runs/plat-faults-2026-10-13/STATUS`). No model was called, no pilot run. One commit each.

### 1. A late signature on a withdrawn offer is refused by the kernel

- **Cause.** Not seen in lv-06 (170 agreements, none withdrawn); a known gap, listed in docs/behaviour/offers.md as "revisit if a kernel-level refusal is wanted": the kernel recorded any signature, and the books (`Book.takenBack`) counted one made after the owner's withdrawal as nothing. A signature that reached the record after a withdrawal could still be read as an agreement by any reader that did not use that rule (the measures, a seat reading the raw record).
- **Change.** `sign_agreement` on an agreement whose owner has withdrawn it, with a party not yet signed, is refused: new refusal code `offer_withdrawn`, in the world's words for a signer ("the offer has been taken back by whoever made it, so there is nothing to sign"). Physics, not law: an offer that no longer stands cannot be accepted. `State::marks` gains the derived `withdrawn_at` (not serialised). Order at one instant is the kernel's one command order: the first stored decides.
- **What moves.** No state hash (the field is derived). Logs that hold such a signature do not replay on the new build (D6); none in the checked pilot logs. The books' reading is kept for old logs.
- **Revisit if** an offer should lapse by itself, or be put back after being taken back.

### 2. Two records for one rates bill: a payment of either settles it

- **Cause** (traced in lv-06's log: records 19350 to 19353, transfers at day 31.33 and 73.33). The rates office writes a notice and a claim for each bill on purpose; it already treated a payment naming either as settling (2026-10-11). The landlord's books did not: "Sums recorded against us" counted the claim paid only when a payment named the claim. The seat paid the notice (day 32), still saw the claim listed, and paid it (day 74). **In money terms it paid twice**: 297,786 cents twice from `acc-landlord-38` to `acc-city`, for one bill of 297,786. No reminder, no opening-caseload paper and no double listing was involved (the first look at "a reminder issued as a fresh notice" found no such thing: the office sends none).
- **Change.** One reading of "settled", `billSettled`/`noticesOf` (common.ts), used by the rates office and by the books; the books line names the notice that came with a rates claim. docs/behaviour/government.md "One bill, two papers"; the note in docs/behaviour/office-books.md ("out of scope") now points to it. Not changed: the claim does not name its notice (matched by owner, due day and sum); the bank and the city still take a second payment of a settled bill.
- **What moves.** What a seat reads (one parenthesis on a rates book line, no form, instruction or prompt); no state hash (code participants never paid twice); nothing in the kernel. Tests: `participants/test/rates-one-bill.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/government.test.ts`.
- **Revisit if** the rates office should refuse or credit an overpayment, or a notice should carry its claim's id.

### 3. "Evicted" for a household that left on an order: its own kind

- **Traced.** lv-06, c0773 (`oikos record`): `ordered_out` (about the tribunal, day 35.3, size 1,000), then a defining `evicted` (about landlord-13, day 67.8, size 5,000). The departure code (`citizen.default`, the leaving branch of `home.vacate`) sets `evicted` for any leaving under a notice or an order (and a removal too), whatever `how`; the outcome record carried `how` (`removed`, `left_on_order`, `left_on_notice`), the memory did not. The exit account is written from the record's memory words as they are, so it said the landlord "evicted us". No warrant was asked for c0773 (the review was right), and there is no bug in whether or when it left. Making someone leave by an order and putting them out by a warrant are different things in a place's law and in ordinary speech; a person who left on an order was made to leave, so a memory of it is fair, but the record could not say which.
- **Change.** Leaving on an order with no warrant carried out is `left_on_order` on the record. `evicted` stays for a notice and for a removal (the warrant's own `put_out` is as before). It weighs exactly as `evicted` does (`LIKE` in `inner.ts`: same dents, shocks and size), so nothing happens more or less often and no person's needs or values move for it. Readers: exit-account strata and the dark rule (`left_on_order` counts with `evicted`), the founding story's dark rule, the everyday event words, the exit-account wording ("left the home on the tribunal's order, with no warrant carried out"), and `town/possession` (new last column `left_on_order`; lv-06, measured on a copy of its log: 3, c0175 day 13.9, c0778 day 20.1 and c0773 day 67.8, beside the 2 removals by warrant). Old records keep `evicted` and are read as before.
- **What moves.** The memory word on records of people who leave on an order, so the entity-record digests of those people and any state hash of a run in which someone does (the mock living-6 line-up: see below); the exit-account brief for them (an author's input, not a seat's: no form, standing instruction or translator prompt). Nothing in the kernel, nothing in how often anything happens. Tests: `participants/test/inner.test.ts`, `participants/test/debrief.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/possession.test.ts` (a tenant who goes on the order: `ordered_out`, `left_on_order`, no `evicted` at the leaving; a tenant put out by a warrant: `put_out` and `evicted`, never `left_on_order`; the measure).
- **Revisit if** a source separates the cost of leaving on an order from being put out (then own dents); a notice gone on is to be told apart as well (`left_on_notice`); or the account author's phrase misleads.

### 4. A mislabelled dial: `opening_caseload_scale_bps` is not a dial on the tribunal's caseload

- **Found.** The sixth living pilot's queue note, copied into its PILOT.txt, called `opening_caseload_scale_bps` "a PILOT'S DIAL" for the opening caseload, and the review (point 2) measured that at 10,000, 100,000 and 300,000 the landlords' and tribunal's papers do not move (14 rent statements, 10 notices, 5 applications, 5 hearing notices, 3 orders). The option's own comment, `docs/behaviour/generator.md` and the 2026-10-12 entry already said the dial scales only the other offices; the wrong words came from the hand-written note of the queue entry (`runs/living-pilot-6-2026-10-13/queues/living-6.json`, outside git) and from `docs/handover.md` ("thickens it", of the whole caseload). `scripts/pilot-queue.ts` and `scripts/pilot-wave.ts` do not generate any text about the dial; they copy a note.
- **Change.** `docs/handover.md` says what it scales; `docs/behaviour/generator.md` and the option's comment say it is no dial on the tribunal's caseload, with the measured evidence; `scripts/pilot-queue.ts` writes a note that names the dial into PILOT.txt followed by one bracketed line saying what the generator does with it (`noteOf`, `orchestrator/src/pilot-state.ts`, tested in `orchestrator/test/pilot-queue.test.ts`), so that a wrongly worded note cannot stand alone. lv-06's own PILOT.txt and queue file are read-only and are left as they are.
- **What moves.** Wording only; no state hash, no run, no seat text, no contract.
- **Revisit if** a pilot needs a dial on the tribunal's caseload (then build it from who cannot pay: a different town or a wider description, not a multiplier on papers made from the households' arrears).

## 2026-10-13 · Shops sized by catchment: measured, and not built (the premise does not hold)

Asked: size each shop's opening staff and stock to the custom its catchment can expect, so that shops are not permanently over- or understaffed by where the town was laid out. Traced first, as the brief said, and stopped there. Findings and the script: `runs/plat-shops-2026-10-13/STATUS`, `shops.py`. A year of six different towns each, the 1,000-person living town, Victoria and Nakuru; no model, no change to the generator.

- **True:** every shop of a kind starts alike (Victoria: 4 staff, 288 in stock, `demand` 577; Nakuru: 1 staff), and trade is uneven and lasts (goods ordered in the first 90 days range 382 to 3,011 in one town; a shop's first quarter against its last, r 0.5 to 0.9). Low-trade shops are where hours are cut (r -0.6 to -0.8 with orders; 170 to 270 notices a year in Victoria) and, in Nakuru, where people are let go for want of money (11 to 17 of a town's 15 to 25 redundancy notices are at shops).
- **Not true:** that the unevenness is where people live. The best catchment the generator can know at founding (dwellings within the shop's reach of 7 cells, each shared among the shops that reach it) correlates with a shop's first-quarter orders at r 0.31 to 0.53 in Victoria (r squared 0.1 to 0.28) and -0.39 to 0.48 in Nakuru, and with its last quarter's less (0.10 to 0.41; -0.22 to 0.41). 39 to 49% of Victoria's orders (39 to 62% of Nakuru's) came from households with neither home nor work in the shop's reach. Custom is made by what a household knows: the adverts board answers a household that knows no shop with the seven newest price lists (`observe.rs`, `search`; `citizen.ts` asks for `shops_known`), and favourites persist. Likely cause, not isolated.
- **So sizing to the catchment makes it worse.** Mean |staff the actual trade needed - staff opened with|, six towns: Victoria 1.42 as it is, 1.54 sized in proportion to the catchment, 1.25 with the best linear weight fitted afterwards; Nakuru 0.60, 0.73, 0.57. Proportional sizing is worse in 3 of 6 Victoria towns and 4 of 6 Nakuru ones. A rule shrunk to a third of the catchment's spread would gain about a tenth, and that third is a fitted number with no source.
- **The redundancy rate has moved since the note.** After hours-before-heads Victoria's redundancies are 1.1 to 4.1% of those in a job (mean 2.3%, sourced 1.8%; shops 0 to 4 notices a town). Nakuru's are 3.9 to 6.3% (mean 5.2%; no sourced Kenyan rate in the profile), mostly shops short of money. A catchment fix would explain at most a tenth to a quarter of the shop-level mismatch behind them.
- **Not changed:** generate.ts, golden files, contracts, hashes. **Revisit if:** the knowing side changes what a household that knows no shop is shown (then re-trace: the unevenness should fall, and a founding rule may then be worth its fit); a source gives staff per unit of turnover by shop size (then a spread of shop sizes can be drawn, but not by place); Nakuru's shop redundancies are looked at on their own (they are for want of money at the low-trade shops, which the shops' stock finance, the trade-credit item, also bears on).

## 2026-10-13 · Reading: plan (what words mean to a person; a plan awaiting the owner's word; nothing built)

**What:** the first model slice under Naz's decision of 2026-10-12 ("Two decisions of Naz's": a model only where code cannot go, as an estimator that shifts the code mind's odds), as a plan: docs/design/ai-citizens.md, section 13. No code, no contract change, no model call, nothing a run does changes.

**Why now.** Seats write orders with reasons, answers to requests and petitions, and notices, and nobody in the town reads them: a careful reason and a curt one land identically, so what a steward's words do cannot be observed.

**Proposed, and why:**
- **Scope: (1) only, three kinds of paper,** in this order: a decision addressed to a person; a public statement or an answer to a petition; a founder's statement read by someone weighing whether to join. A person's letter read by a code office is the fourth kind, after; words that only ask, and promises, are not read (a promise needs the check that it was kept, or a seat gains trust by promising).
- **The model reads the paper, never the person.** It is shown the paper (names, sums and dates as tags), what the paper answers, and the reader's standing (one of four codes). It returns nine small whole numbers (respect, reason, answers, recourse, threat, and appeals to each of Schwartz's four poles) with a quoted phrase for each that code checks is in the paper. The gate of 2026-10-11 found large models tell people apart half as far as the code mind; here the model is not asked to tell people apart at all: the code mind applies the reading to each person by their own values and standing.
- **Every effect is a shift from the plain paper code would have written,** landing on terms the mind has: the weight of `Inner.experience`, `Inner.tried` and `Inner.doneTo`, anger and fear, the tie, a way's `adj` in `pursue`, the draws on complying, `Inner.view`, `Choice.meaning`. Bounded, each size a placeholder and a dial. Words scale what a decision does and never reverse it. No draw is added, moved or renamed.
- **Templates are read by the same reader, once, outside any run, and frozen in a table;** not by a table written by hand. A seat's town and its code twin are then measured on one instrument, and a code town with the dial on is today's town to the state hash (every shift is nothing), which also keeps the calibration.
- **Determinism:** the call is made where the paper is written, through `callModel`; the reading is an annotation in every log; a replay never calls a model. The cache key is the tagged words and the standing: a paper read by 400 people is four calls.
- **The reader:** `claude-code/claude-sonnet-5-5` first, `claude-code/claude-haiku-5-5` beside it, the other family when it answers; never the largest Claude model; never the model that holds a seat in the same run (a model reads its own words as it meant them). About 200 to 700 calls and 2 to 16 USD of plan usage in a 90-day pilot of 3,000 people with four seats, most likely about 5. Later a small reader of our own, trained on the readings (the translator's 1,024-token encoder fits these papers).
- **A gate fixed before any call** (13f): 40 hand-written pairs by kind, controls for length, politeness alone, names, rewording and order, agreement between two readers, an author's-family check, a code town at the dial-off hash, extreme-reader twins within stated bounds, cost under 20 USD.
- **Dial:** `living.reading`, absent by default; absent, byte-identical to today. Contract changes when built are additive (world config, the `reading` annotation, `read` on outcomes, a usage purpose, `readings.jsonl`); none is made here.

**Alternatives rejected:** showing the reader the person's record (the gate's finding; cost of a call a person; nearer to VISION 15 point 7's line for nothing gained); a hand-written table for templates (two instruments in one comparison); letting the plain paper's own reading apply (moves a calibrated code town); reading at the reader's wake (people would wait on a model, and a town's days would move); the seat's own model as reader.

**For Naz:** whether to build it and run the gate; who reads a run that seats Sonnet 5.5 (recommended: Haiku 5.5, held to the author's-family check, until our own reader exists); whether words may only scale a decision's effect or may outweigh it (recommended: only scale, to start).

**Revisit if:** the gate fails on respect, reason or answers, or politeness alone moves the reader; no reader passes the author's-family check for the stewards under study; in two pilots the words' summed effect is under the spread between seeds; the step sizes start being changed after pilots; a later slice would need the reader to see a person's record (the review VISION 15, point 7 requires).

## 2026-10-13 · Culture: plan (what a town holds in common; a plan awaiting the owner's word; nothing built)

**What:** Naz asked whether the world has any mechanism for culture ("we probably need that"). It does not: everything is a person's own. This is a plan for one, in code with no model: docs/design/ai-citizens.md, section 14. No code, no contract change, no model call, nothing a run does changes.

**Proposed, and why:**
- **Three mechanisms.** (1) For a closed list of conducts, each tied to a draw the code already makes (answering a tribunal, staying past a notice, taking a wrong to the tribunal, complaining, taking someone in, joining the union, a strike vote, taking from an employer, and three that are organisations'), a person holds four numbers: what those around them do, what those around them approve of, what they think themself, what they say. (2) A town memory: six slots a person for public events, fading, retold at catch-ups, moving trust in whoever did it once, for people it never touched. (3) An organisation's practice on its own record, shown to whoever holds the office as its history, in counts, with no advice.
- **Nothing is the town's.** No figure anywhere stands for "the norm here": that would be a god's view and the start of a judgement. Each figure is a person's or an organisation's; what is held in common is a measure outside, from logs.
- **Only three ways of learning it:** from those one knows (first-hand, typed phrases on the catch-up that already exists), by being present, and from what is published. No channel is added.
- **One bounded term a conduct,** at the draw the conduct already has, through `swayed`; no draw added, moved or renamed. Dial `living.culture`, absent by default; absent, byte-identical to today; on, the calibrated rates hold at the opening because every person's lean is about the profile's figure.
- **One set of sizes for every conduct.** No conduct has a size of its own, so nothing can be fitted outcome by outcome.
- **Tipping and pluralistic ignorance are not built; they follow** from people who differ, see only those near them, and say less than they think. They are looked for by measures fixed beforehand.
- **Fixed size:** at most 750 bytes of norms and 450 of memory on a person's record, under 500 of practice on an organisation's; the cap of 8,192 stands. Nothing runs daily; the cost to watch is the log's growth, measured at step 1.
- **Profiles:** a new optional key `culture` (not `outlook`, which every town is given), each figure with its source; with none, a conduct runs on its own rate in the profile and a marked placeholder for approval.

**Where the plan departs from the ask as put:** paying rent before other things, paying rates and reporting a neighbour are not choices anyone makes today (standing payments; only shops report), so they are not in the first list and join it when the choice exists. Customs and difference between groups are not new mechanisms: gatherings and local ties carry them; the one addition is a founded body retelling the event it was founded on. Origin as a group is not added.

**Alternatives rejected:** a norm held by the town or by a group as an object (a god's view; and somebody would have to keep it); a tipping parameter (an outcome tuned in); hearsay about what third persons did (one act counted many times); a size a conduct; norms about conducts with no choice behind them; a model anywhere.

**For Naz:** whether to build it; origin as a group (recommended: not now, and only by his separate ruling); whether a seat is shown its office's past practice and the debrief gains two lines and one question (recommended: yes).

**Revisit if:** a year with the dial on moves a calibrated rate out of its band with nothing having happened (halve the one sway once; if that fails, record norms and read them in no decision); in two living pilots the norm figures move less than the spread between seeds (keep memory and practice, drop the rest); a conduct is found to need a size of its own; the log or run time grows by more than a tenth at 3,000 people; the patterns written down before the proof run fail.

## 2026-10-13 · Reading: building it (steps 1 to 4 of design 13h; no model called)

Naz approved building the plan of section 13 and running its gate later, with three rulings, recorded here and corrected in 13:

1. **The reader is an interim external model, and its readings are training data for a small reader of our own.** Haiku 5.5 through `claude -p` on the plan (no paid keys; never the largest Claude model; never the model that holds a seat in the same run: 13e's own-family check stands). The platform's models are to be internal, so this is a stated interim: every reading is logged with the paper's tagged text, the typed reading and the reader's model and prompt version, and the reader sits behind one interface (`Reader`) so ours replaces it without touching anything else. 13e named Sonnet 5.5 as the teacher and Haiku 5.5 as the second reader; the ruling makes Haiku 5.5 the reader, so the gate's "two readers" check runs Haiku 5.5 and (when its window answers) the other family, with Sonnet 5.5 only as a second reader of the gate itself if the owner allows it. 13j's question 2 is answered: Haiku 5.5 reads a run that seats Sonnet 5.5, held to the author's-family check.
2. **Kind words soften, never outweigh** (13j, question 3 answered): the effect of how a paper is put is bounded by the effect of what it decides. It is a property the tests check over every reading and every plain paper, at the defaults and at the extremes the dial allows, and `readingParams` refuses a setting that breaks it (a multiplier floor under 0.1 or a ceiling over 2; a public paper's weight over one half; a swing of the odds of complying over half the rate). A refusal never leaves trust higher than it was; a grant never lower; the words' part is never more than the decision's own.
3. **Build and run the gate: yes; but no model call in this build.** Every step of 13h that needs no model was built in order (steps 1 to 4), one commit each, on a mock reader (deterministic; a "kindest" and a "curtest" mock beside it). The build stops before step 5, the first that calls a model.

**Departures from 13, and why.** (a) The reading is filed as a `note` annotation (`data.reading`), as the composer's and the translator's route are, not as a new annotation kind: no change to the annotation enum, and the dataset and replay machinery that read notes need no special case. The usage purpose `reading` is added to the enum for step 5. (b) The reader names the interim in the dial (`dials.reading.reader`), and `mock` plays it. (c) Step 6 (public papers, founders) and step 7 (extreme-reader twins) come after the first model-calling step and are not built; the public-paper and joining sizes are in `ReadingParams` and tested as arithmetic only.

**Alternatives rejected:** a new annotation kind (more contract for no gain); a reader that sees the person (the gate's finding in 11g); the multiplier floor as a dial only (a dial can be set wrong; the bound is checked by the parameters' validation and by the tests).

**Revisit if:** the reader proves unneeded (13i's drop conditions), or our own reader is ready (drop the external one), or a source gives a size.

**Step 2 (addressed decisions) as built, and where it differs from 13.** The paper's kinds and outcome key (`kind:outcome`, from the typed `granted`, `approved` or `finding`) are in `reading.ts`; a seat's paper counts as having words of its own when one of the text fields of its data (`reason`, `statement`, `answer`, `why`) is filled, which is how the office forms in `papers.ts` carry them; a free-text paper outside those fields is not read yet. The odds of appealing use the score of the ways directly (`recourse_score_bps`, 500 a step) in place of a new `choice.recourse` weight, one dial fewer. The citizen's outcome gains an optional `read` (`OutcomeRecord`, the dataset's `CitizenOutcome`) rather than putting objects in `facts`, which are scalars. The kernel was rebuilt (the engine's source hash covers `contracts/`), with no change to its code. A test seam (`readingSeam`) reads a code office's paper as a seat's, so a whole run exercises the desk, the citizen and the log without a model.

**Step 3 (tags, hashing, cache, standing, table keys) as built.** The reading event holds the paper's words as the reader was shown them (tagged) as well as their hash, because Naz's ruling is that the readings are the training data of a reader of our own and a hash alone is not a training example; the tagged words carry no name, id, sum or day. Found by a run, fixed with a test: an id ending in digits ("c0103") had eaten the sign of the sum after it, so the sum was not tagged; a number now joins another only across one separator. Standing is `addressee` for a decision (a petition's raisers and the rest are step 6). `readings.jsonl` is in the dataset (additive; `Reading` in `dataset.schema.json`). Revisit if the tagged text proves too thin for the reader to read a reason (the step 5 gate will say).

**Step 4 (the gate's harness) as built.** The forty pairs are written as data and the thresholds are in code, frozen, before any reader has been asked; the runner takes mocks only. Two departures from 13f's table, both in the harness: (1) the politeness check's "still under the humane wording's" applies to the pairs that were written to part on respect (a pair that parts on reason alone has no humane respect to be under); (2) a declined asking counts against the cells of the checks it would have fed (conservative), and declines are reported besides. Calls: the reader is asked 480 times (two askings of each of 80 papers, again for the repeat, for the padded and for the polite ones), a second reader 160, so about 640 for two readers against the plan's "about 440 a reader"; the cost check is on the bound, not on the estimate. Not built, on purpose: step 5 (the prompt, the real reader, and the gate for real), steps 6 and 7. **For the owner:** the first step that calls a model is step 5.


## 2026-10-13 · Culture: building it, steps 1 to 3 (the owner's rulings; no model called, no pilot)

Naz ruled on the plan of section 14 (2026-10-13). His rulings, recorded here and corrected in 14:

1. **Build it.** Steps 1 to 3 are built (this entry; commits `culture-1`); no pilot uses culture until step 9's proof run has passed. The dial stays off by default.
2. **Origin is a group.** Where people come from divides a town, beside building, workplace, membership and renting or owning. Its shares are profile data (`values.culture.origin`, `worlds/profiles/`), each with its source; a profile with no figure has no such groups. No place's figure or group name is in platform code (`orchestrator/test/generality.test.ts` now also checks that no profile's group name appears in code). Origin passes to children as the sources say; where they do not say, the rule below. Prejudice between groups may emerge from the mechanisms; the platform records and judges nothing, and nothing in code makes any group better or worse at anything: **origin affects only who one's ties are likely to be (homophily) and, where a source gives group figures, which norms one starts from.**
3. **A seat is not handed its office's past practice as ready counts** (he found it too close to a god's view). That is step 6, not built here; nothing built here leads toward showing it. 14g and 14m item 3 are corrected.

**What was built (step 1).** `participants/src/behaviour/culture.ts`: the conducts (closed list, 12 at most, eleven named), the sizes (`CultureParams`, every one a placeholder, refused if out of range), the norm numbers a person holds (`does`, `approves`, `own`, `says`, `n`), the lean at a decision and the one bounded term, the route a learning may come by, and the record section. The dial is `living.culture` in a spec and `dials.culture` in the world config, absent by default; the profile's figures for the conducts and for those of each origin group travel with it. The citizen holds a `Culture` only where the dial is on; with it off no line of the new code is entered.

**Choices and where this departs from 14.**
- **The record's shape is compact:** `norms: [{ conduct, numbers: [does, approves, own, says, n] }]`, not a row of named fields. 14 estimated 62 bytes a conduct; named fields come to about 80, and the section is rewritten on every change, so the log pays for each byte. The compact form is about half. Measured: see the log-size note below. Whole percent, written again only when a figure has moved by 2 (the `grain_percent` size).
- **`own` settles by half in `internalise_days` (1,095), worked out when it is read from the days gone, not by a daily pass;** `says` is computed when read (never stored) by the arithmetic of `Inner.view` (belonging's weight times what integrity leaves, `Inner.integrity()` factored out of `view`, same figures).
- **A person holds a conduct only where their world gives it a rate or the profile gives a figure.** `take_in` has no rate of its own: it starts at a marked placeholder (5,000). The three organisation conducts are held only where the profile gives a figure; no decision uses them.
- **Origin is generated on a stream of its own (`generator/origin`), and only where the dial is on and the profile has `culture.origin`.** The generator's version (0.54.0) and goldens are unchanged: the dial-off config is byte-identical (tested against the hash of the config as origin/main generated it, three profiles). In each household, whoever has no parent in the town: the first is drawn from the groups' shares, each other is of the same group with the profile's `same_household_bps`, else drawn again; whoever has parents (a child, or a grown child in another household) takes one parent's group (equal chance where the parents differ, since none of the sources found gives a split: recorded in the profile's source note). A child born in the run and a newcomer have no group until step 4 (children take their parents' at coming of age, as values are asked), and until then hold the profile's picture.
- **Homophily** (step 2): a profile's `homophily_bps`, a source or a marked placeholder, makes a tie to someone of one's own group likelier.

**Proof the dial off changes nothing.** `orchestrator/test/culture-dial.test.ts`: the generated config of `town.yaml` on `au-vic-2026`, `gb-eng-2026` and `ke-nakuru-2026` hashes as origin/main's did, and the state hash after 60 / 30 / 30 days is origin/main's (the pinned `46e3ae5e...` for the first). The living and reading dial tests and `twin-draws.test.ts` are unchanged and pass.

**Contracts (additive; contracts/README.md).** `entity-record.schema.json`: `norms` on a person; `world-config.schema.json`: `dials.culture`; the profile's `values.culture` (a TypeScript type; profiles are not schema-checked). No kernel change, no new act, no channel. The translator, the seats' instructions and the forms list do not change.

**Log size and time with the dial on (step 1 only: the first write of each person's `norms`).** Living town, 90 days, lean log: 3,000 people 1,102,512,085 bytes off, 1,104,857,472 on (+0.21%); time 115.2 s off, 116.4 s on (+1.0%). 200 people, 60 days: +0.33%. Well under the tenth that would coarsen the grain; steps 2 and 3 move figures and are measured again below. Origin: eight of the nine profiles have groups (au-vic, gb-eng, br-mg, de-ni, in-tn, jp-akita, mx-jal, us-oh), each with its source note and how sure; `ke-nakuru-2026` has none (no county table by community was reachable), so that town has no groups. Homophily is a placeholder (5,000) everywhere.

**Step 2 as built: learning what others do.** Documented in docs/behaviour/culture.md ("Learning what others do"). Routes: a tie's own words (the phrases `Occasion: I did it.` / `I say <thing> is <right|wrong ...>.`, and `I come from the <group> group.`), a published count (a declared strike ballot's yes share, once), and presence (the rule and weight exist, `here`, and a test refuses every other route; **no occasion in today's code lets a person see another's act without a tie or a paper, so no presence sighting is wired yet**: a walk-out at one's workplace and an officer at a door need what step 5's memory builds). **A year of the 1,000-person living town** (`runs/culture-2026-10-13/year/`, outside git: `oikos run worlds/town-1000.yaml --seeds 3 --until 31536000 --set profile=P --set living.initiative_bps=10000 [--set living.culture=true]`, P = au-vic-2026, gb-eng-2026, ke-nakuru-2026; three run seeds of one town each, so the noise is that town's alone; no model; nothing tuned).

The standard errors here are of three runs of one town and so overstate what a difference means; nothing says a norm moved a measure.
