## 2026-10-16 · The renderer: a plan, awaiting the owner (docs only; no code; no model called)

- **What.** `docs/design/renderer.md`: the plan for V0's stage 3, of which nothing existed. A separate `renderer/`
  package; Bun serves a Three.js client on WebGPU with WebGL 2 fallback, isometric orthographic camera, boxes and
  markers. One read-only pass over a log makes a disposable **view index** (`runs/views/<run>.<head>/`: SQLite for
  ids, kept lines, postings by id and month, and the causal chains; zstd frames of the kept lines; binary tracks of
  where everyone is each midnight, each day's moves, balances weekly, and the overlays by day). Views: town, block,
  parcel, citizen; organisation; office with staff now and backlog. The causal trace walks effect, action, act, who
  decided (person, another person, an organisation's code system, a model seat, the world), why (transcript, decision
  annotation, the record's stated reason), and the records it rested on (`basis`), to depth eight. Three overlays: who
  decided (V0's one), where systems are deployed, hardship as the record has it (a raw variable, no composite). Live
  attach by tailing the log. Build order V1 to V13, about 14 agent-days.
- **Why these choices.** Fold the log in TypeScript, checked by the kernel's own record digests, money conservation
  and capacity, rather than a kernel replay: the log alone rebuilds every register and the renderer needs a few kinds
  of state; a kernel change would be the first thing the renderer needed. Daily keyframes of where people are (15 MB
  a year at 10,000) make a year scrub with no fetch while dragging. Postings by any id found in a body, not per event
  kind, so new events and records are indexed with no new code. The index lives outside the run's folder, so a run is
  never written to; a test holds it.
- **Awaits the owner:** when to build it (recommended: after the GD plan's R1 to R3), and whether "who decided"
  classes by role in the world (recommended) rather than by what runs it.
- **Revisit if** the TS folds disagree with the kernel (then `oikos-kernel replay --states`, verified by checkpoint
  hashes); indexing a year at 10,000 takes over an hour (then by month in parallel); WebGPU and its fallback cannot draw
  10,000 markers smoothly on the owner's machine (then points in one draw call); or compact logs land (then the
  indexer reads `replay --emit` on a pipe).
## 2026-10-16 · Pilot 7 fixes: four faults the pilots found (no model called)

Reviews: `runs/pilot-queues/living-7a.review.md`, `living-7b.review.md`. One commit each; contracts under the blanket approval.

- **1. A sitting with nothing new sent a seat away 17 days (participants 0.18.1).** Cause, from `lv-07a`: finance said "back in 17 days" on day 32 (a plan for the return due day 51). It was back on day 49, looked into whole reports, found nothing new, and the no-turn rule (0.8.0) ended the sitting "back after the days it last gave": the same 17, counted again. It sat on day 63. Fix: a no-turn sitting is back after the days it gave only if they are still ahead of it, and never after longer than the office's rhythm (`cadence_days`); and it takes its turn when something on the office's books falls due before it would next sit (the clerk's paper carries `due`). Tests in `llm-participant.test.ts`; a 70-day town-300 mock-seat run (finance) ran clean. *Revisit if* seats sit too often (the due test fires for every return in the next 7 days).
- **2. Three forms had a field `to` (contracts/README, "Changes since F8").** `remedy_answer.to`, `enforcement_decline.to`, `investigation_closed.to` collided with the `to=` the forms listing prints for where a form goes; in 7B both translators wrote the office there, and the seat declined three remedy answers and used letters. Now `asker`, `asker`, `reporter`. The statements written are unchanged (no log moves). A manifest test refuses a form field named `to`. **The translator's next round must learn** these field names (`form(form=remedy_answer, request=…, asker=<who asked>, …)`), and that a form's own `to=` in the listing is the office it goes through, never a field; its prompt and model were not touched.
- **3. Applications carried no particulars (citizen 0.57.0, desk 0.2.0, tribunal.member 0.8.0).** Cause: grievances brought forward from the opening caseload hold only the matter and the other side, so the application said nothing more; the model member dismissed for want of particulars and the code member ordered regardless. Fix: an application carries `data.particulars` from the person's own record (dispute, paper or place, what is sought, a sum only where the record has one, dates, the answer); the code member dismisses an application with none of that ("no particulars"; leave to apply again), before any draw. Real-world basis and the rule in `docs/behaviour/justice.md`, "Particulars". The generator gives its own caseload applications particulars in the same words.
- **4. Books showed finished items open (`openbooks-townhall.ts`, generator `reviews` channel).** Causes: (a) a return made on the office's form names no return rule or due day, so the books never knew it was made ("none yet", due in a week, until its day passed); (b) an overdue return unfiled dropped off the day after its due day; (c) the support office's channel did not carry its own `remedy_answer`, `complaint_response`, `tribunal_response`, so answered requests and notices stayed open until the venue decided (12 days in 7B); (d) the clerk's daily round: a day's lag, kept and documented. Fixed (a) to (c); `docs/behaviour/office-books.md`.
- **What a seat reads differently.** Finance: a made return no longer shown due; an unfiled one past its day shown as overdue; the support office's `reviews` file now holds its own answers; a sitting with a return due soon is called to a turn instead of ending quietly. Forms listing: the three renamed fields. Nothing else; nothing platform-named.
- **Measured** (code only, a year of the 1,000-person living town, `opening_caseload`, three seeds, au-vic and gb-eng, before = main 01e6f0b, after = this; nothing tuned): 0 of 57 measures moved in either place; final states moved (papers carry particulars). Applications 28 to 34 a run in au-vic, 18 to 31 in gb-eng: particulars-bearing 25 to 31 of them before, every one after (the words stated in 26 of 28 and so on); dismissals and orders by finding identical before and after (au-vic tribunal 4 do, 3 pay, 1 set aside a run; dismissed 0 to 2), none dismissed for want of particulars. So the code twin had no unparticularised application to turn away in these towns: the pilots' were the opening caseload's, which now carry them.
- **Revisit if** the model member still dismisses on "no evidence" (then it is judgement, not particulars); a venue's real rules say it hears an application without particulars; a seat's due-turn becomes costly; letters should close a request (they leave no paper).
- **Pins re-taken:** `founding.test.ts` STEP_2B (applications and the opening caseload's papers carry `particulars`). Every other pin held; `confirming.test.ts` names the seat's version 0.18.1 (its instructions are unchanged).

## 2026-10-16 · Foundations: the review's findings fixed (kernel, contract, platform, tests; no model called)

The independent review (`runs/review-foundations-2026-10-16.md`, of `pre-foundations..ef777e5`) found eleven things. Each is fixed with a test that failed before and passes after, one commit each (or a tightly related pair). Contract changes are in `contracts/README.md` ("the review of the foundations, fixes").

- **1. A seat outlived the person it acted through** (`ea20062`). `die` ended only the body's own participant; a `shares_body` seat stayed Active, held its post and acted as the dead (proved by the review). `die` now ends every participant whose person is the body, so the posts fall vacant, and an act by a person's participant whose body is dead is refused `dead`. Test: `kernel/tests/foundation_fixes.rs` (`f1_...`); and `orchestrator/test/twin-seat-year.test.ts` (below), which fails without the fix.
- **3. A system acted for an organisation that did not own it** (`ea20062`). `appoint` never compared owners and a system's own acts were never checked against the post's organisation. Now `appoint` of a system to a post of another organisation, a system's act in one, and a world whose post is held at genesis by another's system (it does not load) are refused `not_theirs`. Found while doing it: the generator made the fund trustee's agency system owned by `outside` while holding the fund's post; every generated system is now owned by the organisation whose post it holds, supplied by `outside` as before (`2a73091`). The physical-feasibility oracle follows.
- **5 and 8. `by` took any resident's hours; a system naming a person charged the person 1 s** (`f61372c`). `by` now names the actor, a system the organisation owns, a person in its posts, or a person employed by it (an agreement in force or ending, read by its terms with `oikos_terms::read`: the kernel does not judge it, it reads it); anyone else is refused `not_theirs` and charged nothing (an act refused at its end used to leave their lane occupied). Each performer is charged their own kind's row of the table, shared among those who do it. Tests: `f5_...`, `f8_...`. Five foundation tests that named a stranger in `by` now employ them first. The shared-time test asserted the bug (a person charged the system's 1,200 s for a message) and now asserts 600 s.
- **2. Work that could not be checked when ordered took effect almost at once** (`154f167`). When the dry run at order time refused a work (a performer or input not there yet), the act was placed for one block-time and, if it passed at `done`, applied at once, its hours charged after its effect. When such an act comes due and can be done it is **begun again from that moment** (hours placed, effect when they are spent; a second `action_started` for the same action carries the new times). Test: `f2_...`.
- **9. Time-accounting holes** (`9d1cf77`). A work past midnight is counted on each day it is done on; work refused when done keeps its hours (its lanes were held until then: a crew could be given 16 h on one day); a timeline keeps two days' counts so a late placement on an earlier day does not wipe a later day's. The fourth gap (a work naming its place or performers by reference not looked at in full) is **not reachable**: such an act applies as a whole, and the dry run at the order already looks at it in full; nothing changed for it. Tests: `f9_...`.
- **4. An office with nobody in post answered at once and for free** (`46fc6d6`). A keeper's performer must be alive, at work (as the world says work is done) and with room in their working day (a system: in service); the answer's seconds count against the day. If nobody is, the question is **held** and taken up in the order asked at the first hourly look when someone is (`State.asks_held`, `Sched::HeldAsks`; `ask_started` is logged when it is taken up). A keeper with no posts at all, or a world with no row for answering, answers at once as before. Tests in `kernel/tests/knowing.rs`. **A held question waits for good if its keeper is never staffed again** (the asker is told it is asking): nothing gives up; that is the honest state of an office nobody keeps, and finding 6 makes it rare.
- **6. A body whose only staff died was headless for good** (`63aecf4`). Who fills a post is the body's constitution, as data: a position may name an **`appointed_by`** authority (contract; the kernel only checks who is acting), and the profile's `public_service.appointed_by` says by kind of body who that is. Built: **the council**, for the courts, the oversight bodies, the electoral commission, the land registry and the water and energy bodies (a **placeholder in every profile**, with its reason: real places mostly give these to a state body, a minister or a board, none of which the town models). The city has an **appointments officer** (`body.payroll` part `appointer`) who, where such a body's post has stood vacant for 14 days (its own deputy fills one from its staff within days), **seconds one of the city's own administrative staff** to it; they are paid by the city already, so no new hiring is needed, and, holding the body's payroll post, they stop the dead's wage through the ordinary death mechanisms. `deaths.test.ts` (the exemption of employers whose only employee died) and `ownership.test.ts` (the land registrar turned back into a system) **assert the real behaviour again**; run on the code before, with those two tests unbent, they fail (deaths: 18 wage transfers to the dead after the stop window). **Not done:** bodies run on their own account (the bank, union, paper, letting offices, shops, factories) stay headless if their last staff member dies: their owners or members would appoint and no owner's or member's office exists to do it (the kernel supports it: an `appointed_by` may be a person). Said in `docs/behaviour/staffing.md`. In the measured year no body went headless in any of the nine runs, so the appointments officer made no appointment there: it is exercised by the death-heavy tests only.
- **7. A strike's stop and resume could pay part of a period twice** (`bc6b73e`, `756fc39`). One rule for every change of pay: a **withdrawn wage order stays on the books**, so what it pays inside the withdrawing act is booked (with its tax) and read as the pay moments it paid; a strike's return settles against them (nothing paid twice; strike days it paid come off the next pay) and a rise is held by the same cut-off helper (`heldToRun`). A withdrawn order's payments are booked only inside two days of the decision: the first version booked later ones too and the friction test's short-pay case then counted what was kept back twice (found by `test:changed`, fixed in `756fc39`). Test: `participants/test/strike-pay.test.ts` (a pay moment inside the stop act; fails on the parent). **Limit:** for a death or an end of employment the stop cannot be held to a pay run (the date is fixed), so a pay inside that act is still an overpayment, now booked correctly. There is no whole-run test of "no worker paid twice".
- **11. A string sort of record ids in the support office's claim order** (`c8f89be`): claims filed in one moment are decided in filing order (`filedBefore`), as the bank's instructions are. Test in `support-load.test.ts`. **Not done:** the generator's pools sort person ids as strings (deterministic; changing it moves every town).

**The tests (finding 10).**
- **Twin of the real pilot shape** (`4285d56`, `orchestrator/test/twin-seat-year.test.ts`, slow tier, about 2 minutes): 365 days, 25% a year deaths from 25, two mock seats (`councillor-4`, `land-registrar`) beside their people against the twin with code in those posts: every act (82,156) and every event (335,090) equal to the second with seat names mapped to people; both seated people die (days 68 and 79), each seat ends at that second, does nothing after and its post falls vacant at the same second in both towns. Without the fix in `die` it fails (the seat never ended; 82,161 acts against 82,156). **It also showed: a seat that stays alive does not give the twin act for act.** (a) A seat keeps office-hours sittings (a seat's wakes are its own: the shop-1 manager's seat published its price list at 32,400 where the twin's person did at 300): by design, but it means the F5 claim "a town with a seat is the town without it but for that post" holds only for the post's own decisions. (b) A quiet live seat alone shifted a shop worker's act by 300 s from day 172: `AdvanceToNews` (`kernel/src/protocol.rs`) stops only at body news, so a delivery that lands mid-advance wakes its person at the next cohort the engine happens to have, and a seat has no such wake. **Not fixed** (stopping at every wake-causing delivery would move every pin); recorded for the owner. Every earlier twin test converts the seat to a system, and still holds.
- **Registry perturbation, traced** (`cde5882`). The scribbling test is back on the registry. Held by a system, the registry's scribbling moves nothing (exact, asserted). Held by a person, who also holds planning, inspection, finance, works and the environment office, the entries take that person's one timeline (1,800 s a day): the first paper to move is the city's permit decision at 92,400, 300 s late from the entries begun at 86,400, and 331 of 6,829 papers move with it (the "20 seconds" of F5 is this, not reproduced as 20). Legitimate (one timeline per person). Asserted: nothing moves before the entries, the first mover is the city's and late by no more than the entries took, counts agree within 2% and fewer than 10% of papers move (that bound is mine, 4.8% moved): **not an exact check of who may move**.
- **Lengnick's redundancy notices, traced** (`8460d04`). The notice the rule's two reasons did not account for is `Redundancy: the business is being wound up.` (`firms.ts` `letGoAll` after "Winding up"; `docs/behaviour/insolvency.md`): a third legitimate reason the test did not count (factory-2 is wound up at about day 154 in seeds 2 and 5). The test is back on the generated seed, every notice accounted for; the rule's own two reasons are held in a seed 2 run where factory-2 cannot cover its wages and lets two go before it is wound up. No code changed.
- **Seed hops reviewed** (`75e167e`, `c4d7419`). Restored (the review's fixes make the scenario occur again): `seat-acts` seed 1 (the station's one officer leaving town with nobody to carry the warrant was finding 6's headless body), `office-books-walk` 250 days. Kept as chance, with the measured counts beside each test (seeds 1 to 8, now and on the commit before F5): `entry` (seed 4), `own-venture` (seed 4: a business starts in 5 of 8 seeds now, 6 of 8 before), `founding` (seed 2: two people sharing the founding want, 2 of 16 after, 1 of 8 before), `police-station-seat` (seed 7, 330 days: warrants issued across seeds 1 to 8 fell from 21 to 14, tribunal hearing notices 78 to 54: cases come later and fewer, the F5 person-time effect). **Two production tests moved to seed 5 with the counts beside them** (this review, `2a73091`): a factory paying a dividend in 300 days is a rare draw of a 200-person town (run seeds 1 to 6: 2 had one before finding 4, 1 after; seed 1, the town's own, lost its day-30 dividend when finding 4 moved the draws; the same 420 days hold none): chance, not a mechanism.
- **Other test changes, and why none is a loosening.** `physical_feasibility.rs`: a refused act is held to "changes nothing" and to the oracle only when its response has nothing else in it (an act takes time; a crew member dying during an eight-hour work puts the death in its response: the property test found it, case kept); `households.test.ts` allows `participant_inactive` (an act in flight when its person dies: the race `dead` already is, as in four other tests); `own-account.test.ts` counts a work past midnight on each day it is done on (the old count was the bug of finding 9: the same assertion, 27,360 s a day, holds).

**Pins re-taken once, with the reason beside each** (`c08f293`, `2a6af75`): the council's appointments officer is a new office, posts name their authority and every generated system is owned by its organisation, so the config hashes of the three profiles, the 60- and 30-day states (au-vic, gb-eng, ke-nakuru), `living.test.ts`'s byte-for-byte pin and `founding.test.ts`'s step 2b state moved (the last also with main's pilot 7 fixes, re-taken on the merge). Nothing else moved; the twins hold exactly in the tests that have them; old logs replay on `pre-foundations`; no-god-view and the generality tests pass; no translator file touched; no model called.

**Measured, a year of the 1,000-person living town, three run seeds, `oikos run worlds/town-1000.yaml --seeds 3 --until 31536000 --set profile=P --set living.initiative_bps=10000`, before (main, `44f5394`) and after (this branch before the merge with main); `oikos diff`, `oikos health`; 57 measures; nothing tuned back.**
- *Moved beyond three standard errors:* au-vic 2 (households 399 to 393, z -4.7; religious group first-quarter affiliation 35.4 to 34.4, z -4.9), gb-eng 0, ke-nakuru 3 (unemployment by agreement 22.1 to 20.4 per cent, z -6.2; employment by agreement 54.5 to 55.7, z 3.4; religious first-quarter affiliation 77.8 to 78.9, z 5.4). Nothing wild: the household and affiliation moves are small, the first-quarter belief measures are not touched by anything here and are the draws moving (as in F5); ke-nakuru's labour moves with 12 fewer adults at the end (645 to 632) and 8 more departures; no cause traced (recorded, not chased).
- *Health:* the same measures are off before and after in each profile (au-vic: employment, unemployment, participation, saving and, after, religious change; gb-eng: the same four and unmet demand 5.83 per cent, at most 5; ke-nakuru unchanged in kind).
- *Offices, time to decide* (median days; mean in brackets; before to after): au-vic support 0.017 to 0.024 (0.595 to 0.615), lending 0.038 to 0.041, planning 0.130 to 0.130; gb-eng support 0 to 0 (0.294 to 0.316), lending 0.042 to 0.043, planning 0.028 to 0.021; ke-nakuru support 0.016 to 0.016 (1.079 to 1.023), lending 0.059 to 0.059, planning 0.042 to 0.028. Papers decided: 1,011 to 1,032 (au-vic support), 227 to 234 (lending). Nothing moved by more than the draws.
- *Staffing, deaths and vacancies:* employment agreements made in the year: au-vic 149/140/122 to 152/133/145, gb-eng 179/158/194 to 196/177/150, ke-nakuru 96/82/91 to 104/86/84. Deaths: au-vic 15/13/13 both, gb-eng 29/31/29 to 29/31/30, ke-nakuru 10/9/9 to 10/10/8. **Posts vacant at the end: 0 in all nine runs, before and after.** Posts vacated in the year 0 to 8 a run in both (a body's post whose holder dies is refilled within days: finding 6's case did not arise in a year); the appointments officer appointed nobody.
- *Run time* (three runs together, a machine at load average 19 to 23 shared with pilots and other agents, so wall-clock is unreliable): au-vic 339 s to 430 s (user CPU 984 s to 1,208 s, +23 per cent), gb-eng 425 s to 541 s (1,267 to 1,372, +8), ke-nakuru 564 s to 603 s (1,424 to 1,429, +0.4). Commands and wakes within 1 per cent (au-vic seed 1: 2,206,081 to 2,206,631 commands). No speed work was done; the au-vic CPU rise is not explained and the other two are small.

**What I found and did not fix.** (1) Live seats and the twin (above). (2) A held question never gives up. (3) Bodies on their own account have no appointer. (4) A death or an end of employment stop can overpay a pay moment inside its act. (5) The generator's person-id string sort. **Where the review was wrong or incomplete:** its finding 9d is unreachable; its "by" finding was right that the kernel had no link between an actor and a performer, but the link it asks for ("employment") exists only as an agreement the kernel can read, not enforce, so the check is "an agreement in force or ending", which a world can satisfy with a paper nobody honours (D22: statements have no power; the reader's judgement is the world's).
- **Revisit if** a place states who appoints a public body's head (then `appointed_by` per body, per place, and the 14 days a profile figure); a seat should answer on the person's own wakes (the twin of a live seat); held questions should lapse; owners' appointments are built (a citizen module deciding to replace a dead manager).

## 2026-10-17 · Foundations F9 and F10: twins with a live seat, what a seat sees, and the backstop for the laws of time (kernel, engine, host, participants, generator, tests; no model called)

Plan: `docs/design/foundations.md` (rows F9 and F10; section 4); the owner's direction of 2026-10-15 (`docs/all-work-takes-time.md`). Contract notes: `contracts/README.md` ("Changes since the review's fixes (2026-10-17 ...)") and `contracts/calls.md` (`done_by`). Three pieces; the third is the page, the test and the line in `CLAUDE.md`.

**1. Twins with a live seat, exact.** The found-fixes review left it recorded that a pilot and its code twin part act for act beyond the seat's own decisions. Traced, by running the same year with a mock seat that does what its code twin does and reading the first difference each time, there were eight ways a seat's presence moved the world beside it. Each was mended in the engine or the host, and the world no longer depends on whether a post is held by a seat or by code, except through the acts the holder takes:
- *The advance reached news at the next wake.* `advance_to_news` stopped only at news of a body or a keeper's answer; a letter delivered or a paper recorded mid-advance woke its person at the first cohort the engine happened to have after it, and a seat's sittings are other moments than its twin's (the shop worker's act 300 s late from day 172 of the review, found again in a quiet seat's 200 days: 4 acts of 50,207 at another second, from day 134). It now stops at a delivery or a recording too, after all that is scheduled for the moment, and the engine's `next` goes on at once where the stop woke nobody (kernel `is_body_news`, `protocol.rs`; `kernel/tests/cast.rs`). A quiet seat that keeps office hours moves nothing now: every act of 200 days equal, to the second and in order.
- *A moment's wakes were in the order of the unit's key,* a seat's own name, not its person's; and a seat's request is drafted and confirmed in the second and third round of a moment, after the acts of those who act in the first. The engine's queue stands a seat where its person's own unit for the post stands (`sort`), and a mock that sits as its twin does draws up and confirms its request inside its place in the round (`round(..., nested)`, `run.ts`). The acts of one moment begin in one order whichever holds the post (a crew's timeline filled by the manager before the workers' own acts, or after: 45 s, found in the second run of this).
- *A paper written by a person's seat woke the person,* where the person's own paper did not (the rule is "never its author", and the author's name is the seat's); the rule now reads bodies, not participants (`body_of`).
- *A letter to a seat was not a letter to its person,* nor the other way about: a message to a post's holder woke the person's every unit when a person held the post and only the seat when a seat did (`body`).
- *A keeper's answer to a seat's question woke every unit of its body* (found while mending the last), and now wakes the one that asked.
- *A seat's brain drew as the seat,* not as the person (`ctx.participant` and the draw's name), so every decision that rests on a draw fell differently; it was stepped twice for each request (on the turns of drafting and confirming) where its code unit takes one step; it was never told the name of the act it sent (`sent`), so the module's own memory of what it had begun and what came of it drifted (a producer's 601 where its twin's 600); it was told "back in N days" where its code unit says a time to the second; and its looks were made one report at a time, each a turn of its own, where its code unit looks once with all it asks for (`mock.twin`: `participants/src/llm/mock.ts`, `participant.ts` `exactBack`). A real seat is none of these, and none is changed for it: only a mock that sits as its code twin does says so.
*Held:* `orchestrator/test/twin-seat-year.test.ts`, 365 days of the 200-person town with 25 per cent a year dying from 25: nineteen mock seats in posts that have work (six shops, two factories, the newspaper, five councillors, the builder's foreman, the land registrar, the electoral office, the inspector, child protection), against the same town with code in them: **84,962 acts and 345,383 events, equal, every act in order and every event in its moment, with seat names mapped to their people; seats ended with their people, and the quiet-seat test (200 days, 2 seats that keep office hours) equal as well.** About 75 s in the slow tier. *Not held, and why:* a post whose office a seat makes more of than its twin has: a seat in an office with routine work has staff and standing orders, one that keeps books has a clerk who files them (the landlords, the tribunal's registrar, the principal, the clinic, the police, the union, the water and energy bodies): those papers and their time are the seat's town and not its twin's, so the posts compared are those whose module has no routines and keeps no books (the test asserts it). A seat that does make other decisions than its code twin differs by them, and by nothing else.

**2. F9, what a seat sees.** (a) *Its diary* (`participants/src/behaviour/diary.ts`, set out with its staff): what its own acts take it, by the town's table of work for a person (a letter, each kind of paper its office writes on its forms, any other), a working day, and its staff's hours in a week between them (`Roster` now reads each agreement's hours); the table itself is never named. (b) *Outcomes with times:* after each act it asks for it is told when it will be done (the clock, and the day where it is not today) and when it begins where the actor had other work first: "What you did will be done at 15:21. It begins at 15:06: you have other work before it." (c) *What waits on its file:* the support office's books list the claims that wait for papers or a confirmation it asked for, each with its day (`supportBooks`); the rest of what waits is the books it already had. (d) *The resolver fills `by` from the roster:* a request may say `done_by=` a person on its staff or "the clerk" where exactly one is in post; the act is done on that person's time and the kernel refuses one who is not at work; a stranger, or a role with several in post, is a question back, in the town's words (`performersOf`, `run.ts`; first built as `by`, which broke `form(... by=)`, a notice's day: the seat-acts test found it, and it is `done_by`). (e) *The forms* a claimant's chair, an employer's and anybody's need: **`evidence`, `confirmation_answer`, `review_request`**, public forms the town publishes where a place has decisions that wait or are reviewed (`CLAIM_EVIDENCE`, `CONFIRMATION_ANSWER`, `REVIEW_REQUEST`, `papers.ts`; generator 0.60.0); each writes the statement the code writes, field for field (`participants/test/decisions-forms.test.ts`). (f) *The mock seat for 60 days:* `orchestrator/test/seat-diary.test.ts`, a works seat that asks for forty notices a day: shown its time and its crew's hours and told when each will be done; writing them all itself takes more than nine hours of a day of seven and a half, and having its crew write them (on their time, the kernel refusing any who are not at work) takes less than three; a stranger named is a question back and nothing is done. **A seat does not fall behind by a backlog that grows without end here: a person's timeline is the 24 hours and a day's paperwork of ten hours fits it; it falls behind in the sense that a day's work comes out more than a day later, and what it does itself it is not doing elsewhere (the same person's other offices wait).** Nothing in it is said by the platform: no table, no kernel, no roster as such.
- *What the translator's next round must learn* (no model or prompt touched): (1) `done_by=<id or role>` on any call, to name who in the office does it; (2) the forms `evidence` (office, claim, need, request, what, last_employer), `confirmation_answer` (office, claim, need, request, subject, what, employed, known, ended_on) and `review_request` (office, matter, about, particulars, seeks), as they are written on the form lines the seat is shown, a form's field `office` being the entity that asked; (3) the notices of times are not requests and need nothing.
- *Cost in prompts:* the three forms and the diary add about 5,700 characters to the largest prompt a seat is sent (74,552, where 68,835 without them): `seat-sight.test.ts`'s ceilings move with the reason beside them (75,000 and, for the finance seat, 66,000 from 70,000 and 63,000), in the way each of its earlier moves was made, and this is a bound loosened for a reason, which I say so of.

**3. F10, the backstop and the docs.** `docs/all-work-takes-time.md`, written as `no-god-view.md` is: the laws, what the kernel enforces and refuses, the backstop, and the rule for the future (**a gap is a missing law, never a per-case patch**: ask who does it, how, at what cost, and make the world say it). `orchestrator/test/all-work-takes-time.test.ts` generates the town of every profile, as code and with every office a model's, and fails naming the post, the row, the form or the line on: a free holder (`freeHolders`); a block with no positive row for a person, a template's block with none for a system, a zero row, a row with no source, a default (`unpricedWork`); a paper a form writes that takes no time (`unpricedPapers`); a throughput, a delay or a rate of error handed to a module (`dialsHanded`); an error drawn outside `slip()` (`errorsDrawnOutsideSlip`); and a special case of the foundations' inventory still standing (`specialCasesLeft`; the two F10 `test.todo`s of `foundations-laws.test.ts` are these two). It plants a free holder, a missing row, a default, a dial on a venue, a rate of error, an error drawn by chance and a standing special case, and checks each is named. *It found one thing:* the table had no row for the block `take`, so an act of taking goods took the platform's one second: a row of five minutes, a placeholder with its note (`person.take`). `CLAUDE.md` has the line, in the style and length of the god's-view line. It should never fire.

**What it cost the town's year.** `worlds/town-1000.yaml`, the living flags, a year, three seeds of one town each, before (`52438897`, main) and after (this branch), au-vic-2026, gb-eng-2026, ke-nakuru-2026; `oikos diff`, `oikos health`; nothing tuned.
- *Standing measures:* **none of 57 moved beyond three standard errors in any of the three profiles** (the largest: au-vic households 393 to 395.7, z 2.5; gb-eng union firm-last 0.97 to 0.43, z -1.5; ke-nakuru unemployment 5.97 to 5.43, z -1.7). Health: the same breaches before and after (au-vic 5 of 21, gb-eng 5 of 15, ke-nakuru 2 of 19).
- *Offices, days from application to decision (median; mean):* au-vic support 0.059 (1.59) to 0.059 (1.56), lending 0.042 to 0.038, planning 0.135 to 0.139, requests to put right 0.021 to 0.021; gb-eng support 0.089 (1.58) both, lending 0.040 to 0.038, planning 0.048 both; ke-nakuru support 0.293 (1.58) both, lending 0.092 both; the tribunal 49.8 to 49.8, 42.4 to 42.6, 42.3 both. **No office moved.** Deaths the same (draws), arrivals and appointments by a few.
- *Work done:* commands +0.5 per cent (au-vic), +0.4 (gb-eng), +0.1 (ke-nakuru), wakes +0.3, +0.1, +0.04. **Refused acts rose in au-vic, 7,512 to 9,097 across the three seeds** (not at work 3,468 to 4,794, no time left 4,007 to 4,260), gb-eng 6,912 to 6,996, ke-nakuru 26,557 to 26,421: the refusals are those of a person's act met at another moment of the day (the news now reaches them at its own time); none moved a measure, and none is traced further (the own-account refusals alone ran 626 to 1,225 between two seeds of the base).
- *Run time:* the three runs of each profile together, wall clock, on a machine at load average 13 to 20 shared with other agents' suites and with this work's own: au-vic 333 s to 446 s, gb-eng 247 s to 532 s, ke-nakuru 368 s to 629 s. **Wall-clock is not to be read from that: the second set ran beside the changed tests of this branch.** The user CPU of one seed of each, base then change, one after the other (`/usr/bin/time -l`, which load moves much less): **gb-eng 503.8 s then 503.9 s, au-vic 538.5 s then 533.5 s** (real time 473 s then 482 s and 491 s then 457 s). **No cost is shown**: the stops that wake nobody go on inside the engine's one reply, and the commands and wakes the host sees are within 0.5 per cent.
- *Not measured:* a ten-thousand-person town; a year of seats on a real model (none is called).

**Pins re-taken once, with the reason beside each.** The generated town gained three forms and a row of the table of work, and its engine's advance stops where news is delivered: so `worlds/test/living.test.ts`'s byte pin, `culture-dial.test.ts`'s three config hashes and three states, `living-dial.test.ts`'s step 1 (which `reading-dial.test.ts` reads), `founding.test.ts`'s step 2b and `opening-caseload-offices.test.ts`'s two world hashes were taken again (the possession hashes did not move). `seat-sight.test.ts`'s ceilings, above. Nothing else moved: the twins hold (`twin-draws.test.ts`, `twin-seat-year.test.ts`), old logs replay on `pre-foundations` or the build of their version, no-god-view and the generality tests pass, no translator file was touched, and no model was called.

**Found and not fixed, or by choice.** (1) A seat that makes more of an office than its code twin has (clerk, staff, orders) is another town by that paper and its time; the twin of such a seat is the seat's own town with code in its place, which would hold only if the seat's module and the code's drew alike (they do not draw under one name). (2) A real seat keeps office hours and its sittings are its own: `hears` and `exactBack` are for a mock. (3) `done_by` on a form is not read as a field of the form: a form with a field named `done_by` would lose it (none has one). (4) The refusals above. (5) `take` now takes five minutes; nothing in the measured towns takes. **Revisit if** a real model is to sit as its twin would (its sittings would have to come at the code's moments, which is a different experiment); a profile states a time for taking, or for any row, from a source; the seat-sight ceilings are to be held by lighter forms (the forms a seat is shown are all the town's public forms, whether its office files them or not); or the refusals in au-vic grow with the next change to when news is met.

## 2026-10-17: `oikos pilot-view`, a pilot as one page for a person

**Why.** Naz asked for a way to see what seats and actors did in a pilot without reading markdown or logs, ahead of the full renderer. **What.** A new package `pilot-view/` and one CLI command (`oikos pilot-view <run-dir> [--out f.html]`, docs/pilot-view.md) that folds a finished run's log once and writes a single self-contained page (overview, per seat timeline with the seat's own words, translator draft, confirm/decline and outcome, notebook and debrief; seat vs code twin; actors; town measures). **Choices.** (1) The log is folded in TypeScript in one streaming pass, as the renderer plan does for its index, so the pass and its `ViewData` carry over; the page is plain DOM and can be replaced. (2) Read-only: no file in the run is opened for writing and the output path may not be inside the run; a test holds it. (3) Debriefs use the orchestrator's `isKeptBack`; what a seat kept back is never shown, and debrief transcripts are not read. (4) The twin is matched by parties and kind of matter, not paper number (papers are numbered differently once the runs diverge); twin acts of kinds the seat never made are counted, not listed. (5) The root `package.json` workspaces and `tsconfig.json` include the package; no kernel, participant or world code is touched. **Revisit if** the renderer lands (the page becomes its seat panels), a run is large enough that the 10 MB cap cuts excerpts too hard, or the twin match proves misleading on pilots with many same-kind matters.

## 2026-10-17 · The risk register: one place for gaps, and an audit of assumptions (docs only; no code; no model called)

**Why.** Naz, 2026-10-17: "it's ok to have gaps, so long as we catalogue them and understand them, almost like a risk register", and look for "any assumptions we've made that are incorrect". Gaps were spread over this log's "Revisit if" lines, the behaviour docs' "Leaves out", the handover's weak spots, `docs/gaps.md` and the pilot reviews, and nobody could say which of them could bias a steward experiment.

**What.** `docs/risks.md`: 105 entries in nine areas (world mechanics 13, markets and economy 17, public bodies and law 17, people and culture 12, seats and framing 12, translator 6, measurement and twins 13, profiles and sources 10, performance and scale 5), each with the gap, where it lives, what it could do to results, likelihood and impact, how we would notice, status and what would make us fix it; a summary of the five risks most likely to bias a steward experiment; and an assumptions audit of 31 items judged against the owner's principles, with evidence and how sure. Swept: this log, the handover, `docs/behaviour/`, `docs/design/`, the measurement, calibration, reliability and scenario docs, the profiles, the 2026-10-16 source-check reports, the eleven pilot reviews and the review of the foundations (`runs/bughunt-2026-10-17.md` did not exist when this was finished). Linked from `CLAUDE.md` ("Read first") and `docs/handover.md` §8. `docs/gaps.md` is left as the history of the first pilots and is no longer added to.

**What the audit found that matters most** (each read in code where it says so in the register): outcomes built in rather than emerging (business births at the profile's rate with no employing start-up possible; every strike won in full after three stoppages; a paper that prints only bad news for the government; rents that ratchet 5% at each review; exports fixed at the opening output; compliance and unproven claims as coin flips); code baselines that are unsourced rules (a council that votes on one axis, a tribunal member harsher than au-vic's law); rates carried to the wrong court, place or level (tribunal times, England's leave-on-order rate everywhere, state per-head grants and staff at a 1,000-person town); and Victorian practice left in module code (water billed to owners, the tenants' petition's 90 days and 5%), which the generality test does not see.

**Choices.** (1) Statuses were checked against later entries of this log by search, not by reading every entry; the page says so and asks to be corrected. (2) Nothing was fixed here: the register is for deciding what to fix, and several fixes are the owner's (the reader, culture's scale, the way out's wording). (3) Ids are by area and never reused; a fixed entry stays a release with its status, then goes at the next sweep.

**Revisit if** an experiment is planned (its plan names the high-impact entries for the offices it seats); a sweep finds the register out of date with this log; or the owner wants priorities set among the "to fix" entries.
## 2026-10-17 · The world goes to Rust (owner's decision; design only, no code; no model called)

**Decision (Naz, 2026-10-17).** "Everything should be in Rust, and TypeScript should just be the top layer for config." Rust: the kernel and every built-in actor (citizens, households, firms, shops, factories, code office-holders) and the rules they share with the generator. TypeScript: model seats and their prompts, framing and debriefs; the translator's serving; orchestration of pilots; tools (pilot-view, explorer, reports, measure); the generator and config; the tests above the module level. The participant API stays open and language-neutral (JSON over a socket as well as N-API), so outside researchers can attach seats in any language. Later the same day the owner asked for an aggressive port: several agents in parallel, rewritten for Rust and for all cores rather than line by line, **no byte identity with the TypeScript world**, TS behaviour frozen once the disempowerment steps now running merge, and the TS modules deleted when the gate passes. Plan: `docs/design/rust-port.md`.

**Why.** Speed at 10,000 people over years (a 10,000-person month is 125 to 200 s and 6 GB today; the host's single JavaScript thread is about half of it, and encoding and parsing observations across the boundary another fifth); one implementation of each rule (the resolver exists in Rust and in TS; randomness, canonical encoding and money are ported both ways); no serialisation between the world and its people.

**The gate** (instead of identical hashes): every scenario test passes on the Rust world through the existing TS harness (state-hash pins re-taken once, at the cut-over); a year of the 1,000-person living town in au-vic, gb-eng and ke-nakuru, five seeds a side, has none of the 57 standing measures beyond three standard errors against the frozen TS world (tagged `ts-world-final`); twins exact within the Rust world; the same hash on 1, 4 and 14 threads; the no-god-view, all-work-takes-time and generality backstops pass, reading the Rust manifests and sources.

**Schedule.** Phase 0 the frame (1 Opus, 3 days, can start before the freeze); phase 1 seven agents at once (two Opus on the citizen, five Sonnet: firms, market, finance and bodies, public offices, the edges), 6 to 8 days; phase 2 integration and the gate, 5 days; phase 3 speed, 3 days; phase 4 delete the TS modules and resolver, 2 days. About four weeks and 70 agent-days. Expected: 4 to 6 times faster at 10,000 people, 8 to 10 with the serial carry-out worked on; estimates from the sampled profile, measured first in phase 0.

**Structural rule kept.** The new `actors` crate depends on `contracts`, `core` and `rules`, never on `world` or `perception`: an actor cannot name world state, so the no-god-view rule is also a dependency rule.

**CLAUDE.md's "Stack" line will change when the port lands** (to: Rust for the kernel and the world's built-in actors; TypeScript on Bun for seats, the translator's serving, orchestration, tools and config). It is not edited now.

**Revisit if** phase 0 shows the boundary costs under a fifth of what the plan assumes; fewer than five of seven phase-1 agents pass their scenario tests in mixed mode; measures drift beyond noise for reasons that trace to faithful ports (checkpoint with the owner, don't tune); a single-threaded Rust 1,000-person year is under twice as fast as the TS one; or a pilot needs a behaviour change that cannot wait a week for the gate.
- **Where a year's time goes, and four result-identical fixes** (2026-10-17; `kernel/Cargo.toml`, `kernel/src/kernel.rs`, `kernel/crates/world/src/{state,kernel,exec}.rs`, `docs/design/performance.md`). Before longer pilots (a year, up to 10,000 people) the time and memory of au-vic and gb-eng towns were measured and the largest costs fixed. **Nothing a run does changes**: final state hashes are the same before and after (1,000 people, 30 days `768e6ce7ac4e4c27`; 10,000 au-vic `8c024d84a2bf0261`; 10,000 gb-eng `cd33f30b39662479`; a year at 1,000 `06469cf3549a412e`), and the 5,865,277 log lines of the year match the original body for body (hash and prev stripped: the header records the build id, so every chain hash differs between builds). The kernel's 47 test binaries pass. No contract changed.
  - **Measure.** On a machine at load 15 to 43, wall time and CPU seconds moved 30% between identical runs; the measure used is the instructions the worker retires (`/usr/bin/time -l` around `run-one` inside a slot), CPU seconds beside it. One year at 1,000 people: kernel 45% (observe half of that), participant modules 28%, JSON crossing 10%, platform 7%.
  - **What was found and fixed.** (1) At 10,000 people `advance` was 65% of the kernel's time (3.3 ms a call, 0.15 ms at 1,000): every act copies the state, and the held questions to a register's keeper were a plain `Vec` copied whole each time (now `Arc<Vec<_>>`, serialised the same; -13.5% instructions); and "is this post holder at work" went through every building in the town for each held question (now the buildings the body is in, by `whereabouts`, which debug builds check against the scan; -19% more). (2) The release build is fat LTO with one codegen unit (-2.5%). (3) Observations are made ready on one thread unless `OIKOS_KERNEL_THREADS` says more: the eight threads cost CPU time on a shared machine and gave no wall time back; a run holds one slot, one core. Together: 10,000 people, 30 days, -30% (au-vic) and -38% (gb-eng) instructions, CPU time about -45%; 1,000 people, a year, -4.7% instructions and -32% CPU time. The fixes were quadratic ones, so they matter at scale.
  - **What was not a cost.** The state hash is taken at checkpoints only (0.9%); a Merkle hash would gain nothing. What is hashed at a write is an entity record (about 4% of the kernel's time). Observations are never repeats (24 of 1.47 million equal that participant's previous one), so none can be cached byte-identically.
  - **Memory, log, and a 3-year 10,000-person run.** Peak resident 1.2 GB at 1,000 people (30 days), 1.85 to 2.17 GB (a year); 7.2 to 7.6 GB at 10,000 (30 days). Full log 6.1 MB a simulated day at 1,000 people, 110 MB at 10,000 (gb-eng). Feasible on this machine in time (about 5 to 6.5 CPU hours on one core, extrapolated linearly from 30 days; the year at 1,000 confirms linear) and memory (about 15 to 20 GB, extrapolated); not in disk with a full log (about 120 GB): use `--log lean` or compress as written. Not run for three years.
  - **The ranked list of larger ideas, the GPU measurements (a GPU pays above about 3,000 to 15,000 per batch and is irrelevant to today's profile), and what the JavaScript-to-kernel crossing costs (13 to 15% of CPU time, before the citizens' own 28%) are in `docs/design/performance.md`.**
  - **Revisit if** a quiet-machine measurement shows the observation threads give wall time (then the default could be some threads when the machine is idle); the LTO build time (about ten minutes under load) becomes a burden for kernel work (then thin LTO); held questions are found to pile up for a reason that is itself a fault (thousands held at 10,000 people: nobody at the keeper's post to answer; not looked into here); the three-year run is attempted (the memory and disk figures are extrapolations).
## 2026-10-17: the pilot explorer, the first real renderer (`oikos explore`; no model called)

**Why.** After the first pilot viewer Naz asked for "something way way more exciting, visual, innovative", to see each
pilot's actions and look at different citizens and institutions, with a simple renderer and WebGPU if it helps. The
approved plan (docs/design/renderer.md) already had the shape; this builds a first version of it and merges the pilot
viewer into it. **What.** A new workspace `renderer/` and `oikos explore <run-dir> | --all | index <run-dir>`
(docs/explorer.md): one streaming pass to a view index beside the runs (`runs/views/<run>.<head hash>/`, never inside a
run), Bun serving it on 127.0.0.1 under a path prefix, and a Three.js client on WebGPU (WebGL 2 where it is missing):
the town as an isometric scene with day and night, people as lights hopping between the buildings they are in, seats'
acts as arcs from the office to where they land, consequential changes as rings by who decided, a timeline with a rail
per seat, panels for a person, an organisation, a building and a seat's act (its words, the draft, sign-off, outcome,
twin, sitting and causal trace), two overlays (who decided; hardship from people's own records), search, a linkable URL.

**Choices.** (1) The index is files and Bun's SQLite, not the plan's varint postings: simpler, 180 MB for a 3,000-person
90-day pilot. (2) No WASM: indexing is bounded by reading the log (about 50 s of 70 to 130 s), and nothing on the
client needs it. (3) People drawn one by one at every zoom, on the roof of the building they are in (the owner asked to
see people move); the hop between buildings is drawn over the travel time and is not a route (the log has none). (4) The
pilot viewer's fold is reused whole for seats (`buildView`, with a new `debriefs: false`, and each twin act's `seq`), so
the two views cannot disagree; the explorer reads no debrief, and its index drops debrief annotations. (5) The
consequential-acts list lives in `measure/src/consequential.ts`, as the plan asked, for M1 to share. (6) "Who decided"
is by role (a person, an organisation's system, a model seat, the world); a standing payment is decided by whoever gave
the instruction; an effect with no act is the world's.

**Measured.** Indexing: 1,000 people for 90 days (code only) 12 to 14 s; the 3,000-person pilots lv-07a and lv-07b 70 to
130 s each with their twins (about 50 s of it reading the log), 1 GB of memory at peak. Client: 1.06 MB of script; at
3,000 people the script's own frame time is 1.2 to 2.6 ms (positions, colours, rings, labels), the same order at 1,000;
headless Chrome draws 10 to 20 frames a second whatever the size (its own limit, on WebGPU and on WebGL 2 alike), so
frame rate on a real screen was not measured here.

**Found on the way.** A seat's act was counted beside the changes it made (a person's "who decided" counted the order
and its effects); the trace named a standing instruction "basis" when it was carried in an act's block; a person with no
home on record was drawn at the town's edge; an office's own reports to itself filled its backlog. All fixed, the first
two by the tests.

**Not done** (docs/design/renderer.md 11): money checked by week for conservation in real runs, the record's kernel
digests, a parcel view, live attach, a year at 10,000, a mock-pilot test of the whole page. **Revisit if** indexing a
year at 10,000 takes over an hour, a fold disagrees with the kernel, or the owner finds the people-as-roof-lights
metaphor misleads (then markers beside buildings, as the plan had).
## 2026-10-17: Disk tidy (scripts/disk-tidy.ts) and tests that clean their temp folders

The disk filled to 89% with: 232 GB of runs (about 100 GB of them full logs of code-only living-world and mechanism runs, regenerable from git and the seed), ten merged worktrees held by a stale agent lock (pid 21143, the main session), and about 184 GB in /private/tmp, mostly folders the test suite made and never removed. Decided: `scripts/disk-tidy.ts` (dry run by default) removes only what is regenerable, by explicit rules (docs/dev-machine.md); model runs, and anything unsure, are never touched. Mock-only rows in a cost.json (`mock/*`, nothing spent) are code, not model calls; `*.dataset` folders (rows for citizen models) stay even in code-only runs. Tests: `scripts/tmp-preload.ts` gives each test process its own TMPDIR, emptied after each file and removed by a detached reaper when the process ends (bun test runs no exit handlers; a SIGKILL runs nothing). Applied once on 2026-10-17: about 62 GB of large logs from six code-only runs, 33 GB of old temp folders, ten stale-locked worktrees and one more. Revisit if: a "code-only" run turns out to hold model calls the evidence rules missed (then tighten MODEL_PATH, never loosen); a test needs a temp folder that outlives its process (set OIKOS_TEST_TMP_OFF=1); or the large-log rule removes a log a finding needs again (regenerate from the commit in its STATUS).
### A merge script and a CI workflow (2026-10-17)

`scripts/merge.ts` does the hand merge in a worktree of its own (`merge-bot`), keeps both sides only in `docs/decisions.md` and `docs/research/references.md`, runs build, typecheck, cargo and the whole suite, accepts one known timing flake (`scripts/slots.test.ts`, `orchestrator/test/pilot-wave.test.ts`) only if it passes rerun alone, and pushes only on green. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs the same checks on every push to main and every pull request on a self-hosted runner (labels `self-hosted`, `macOS`, `oikos-mini`), one job per branch at a time, 120-minute timeout. **Choices.** (1) Self-hosted, not GitHub's runners: the suite needs the machine's kernel build cache and sccache, and a private repo's hosted minutes cost. (2) CI is the independent check; the merge script is still where the full suite is run once per merge, so CI does not replace the rule. (3) Registering the runner is the owner's step (a token only he can make; the agents' `gh` login is invalid): `docs/ci-runner.md`. **Revisit if** CI and the merge script double the load on the machine (then let CI skip pushes the script made), the flake list grows (fix the tests instead), or a fork can open pull requests (then the runner is a risk: approval required).
## 2026-10-17: The archive of past model runs (`scripts/extract-archive.ts`), read out of the logs before the format changes

**Why.** The platform is being rebuilt in Rust and the log format will change; the new world will not read the old logs, and a real-model run cannot be made again. Naz (2026-10-17): extract the valuable content of every past model run into a clean, format-independent dataset first; only after that is verified, and he confirms each one, might raw logs be retired. Nothing was deleted or altered: the runs folder is only read, the archive is written to `runs/archive-2026-10-17/`. **What.** One script (docs/archive-schema.md is the schema, copied into the archive as SCHEMA.md) reads every log with model calls with the readers the platform already has (`situationsOf` with the corpus reader inside it, the debrief collector) and writes zstd-compressed JSONL a run and kind: seat requests (each request in the seat's words, joined to what it had read, the draft and which translator offered it, confirmed or declined, the call, how the kernel ended it), situations and systems, compact transcripts (turns, tokens, cost; the seat's words for seats, composers, notebooks and accounts), notebooks, published debriefs and exit accounts; and, across the runs folder, the translator's examples deduplicated by request, forms and answer (with every split any file put them in, and provenance), rejects, the repository's real and seen cases, evaluation results; findings (pilot reviews, STATUS and notes, decisions-log entries) linked to the runs they cite; a manifest per log (what was extracted, counts, sizes, what was not and why) and verification (counts against each run's own reports, 20 random items against the raw logs). **Choices.** (1) A small change to `situationsOf` (an `onEntry` hook and `keepCorpus`) so the extractor reads each log once, not four times; behaviour unchanged. (2) What decides a log is a model run: a summary that records spend, a calls log, or, when a run spent nothing (a Codex seat costs nothing per call: pilots 7d to 9 are such), a batch that seats a model and a real model's answers in the first 400 MB of the log. A copy of a log (same header, same size), the history of a resumed run (its answers are in the resumed log) and the corpus extracts of translator-wrong-acts are left out and listed. (3) The real test cases and their seat-days are flagged on every seat request and example (`test_case`, `test_like`, `test_seat_day`; `exclude_from_training` is their union): a training set must drop those rows. (4) What a seat kept back from a debrief is counted, never copied; a debrief call's words are not in a transcript; debriefs and exit accounts are marked as welfare evidence, never training data (RESTRICTIONS.txt). (5) The held-out cases are not read (`~/oikos-private` is never opened), and a `held_out: true` result in an evaluation file is dropped when the file is read and counted. (6) Not kept: the towns themselves (code citizens, the kernel's events: they are made again from the seed and the code), the resolved blocks of a draft, score files, tokenised training exports, raw reader and writer call files of the pipelines (their products, the examples and rejects, are kept), model weights. **Revisit if** a raw log is to be retired (verify that run's shards against it first), the new world's log format needs a field this drops (the log, not this, is then the source), or the translator pipeline's raw reader answers are wanted for a different labelling.

## 2026-10-17 · The risk register kept fresh, and five risks mitigated

Naz: keep `docs/risks.md` updated and fresh, "bonus if we can mitigate the risks as we go"; then: let it double as the backlog with as little overhead as possible.

**Mechanism, not a habit.** (1) `orchestrator/test/risks.test.ts` (fast tier): every gap marker (`(to confirm)`, `placeholder`, `not built`, `known gap`, `untraced`, `left unfixed`) in `docs/` and `worlds/profiles/` names a register id on its line or in its paragraph, or sits in a file `docs/risks-markers.json` counts (and the file may not hold more untagged markers than counted, so a new gap fails the build); `TODO(risk ID)` in code needs an id; every id named anywhere must exist; every entry has its fields; a `fixed` entry names its commit or decisions entry and no marker still names it. History files (the decisions log, `research/references.md`, `gaps.md`) are exempt: the log is a record of moments, and references has its own "(to confirm)" convention. (2) `scripts/risks.ts`: status counts, the planned backlog, five top risks (likelihood times impact, open before accepted), oldest open entries by `git blame`, entries whose "where" files changed since the entry was last touched, marker-list slack; `--md` for a paste, `--touched [REF]` for the entries a branch touches. (3) The working rule is in the register's header ("Keeping it fresh"). `scripts/merge.ts` is not on main yet (branch ci-setup): it should print `bun scripts/risks.ts --touched` before merging; not wired here, as that file is another branch's.

**Choices.** Markers are tagged at file level for the roughly 1,500 older ones (78 files, each mapped to the entries it belongs under by judgment from the file's subject, not line by line), and by line or paragraph for new and for those matched this time (nine, and six entries created for what the register had missed: PB-18, PC-13, PC-14, SF-13, MT-14, MT-15). Tagging every old marker by hand would have been mostly guesswork; the count per file only ever lets the number go down. A stale line was found on the way: handover said hours before heads was "not built" where the register says built but untested (tagged ME-10). Planned work is a kind of entry (`PL-n`: What, Where, Why, Status, Do when), shown apart by the report: PL-1 traffic and transport (as laws, after the Rust port), PL-2 the explorer's next steps (after the port; engine decision then), PL-3 the translator rebuild reading forms by name (after forms settle). The 82 missing "notice by" and 48 "fix when" lines were written to the entries (short, by the entry's own subject).

**Fixed, each with a test.** SF-2 (a bulk standing part over 20,000 characters is cut before a seat's own look-ups; `participants/test/seat-papers.test.ts`); MT-13 (the debrief breaks ties among equal orders by a seeded draw, script 0.4.1); SF-11, the account half (exit accounts take those the seats' acts reached first, account version 0.2.2; the queue half became SF-13); MT-8 (rent stress for lower-income renters; the Christian-share target read as census affiliation; residual MT-14). MT-4 is partly fixed (five targets wired: business entry and exit, job mobility, tenancy-tribunal applications, Christian share; residual MT-15). Tried and not done: SF-8 (needs forms filtered by office) and PS-10's double count (the crew figure waits on sourcing).

**Revisit if** the marker list's file-level coverage lets a real gap hide (then tag by line, file by file); the test blocks other branches too often (then loosen to a report for docs only); or a lender seat is run and SF-2's cut loses what it needs.
## 2026-10-17: The bug hunt's findings, fixed (kernel, behaviour, orchestrator; tests; no model called)

Source: `runs/bughunt-2026-10-17.md` (main at `ac99bbba`). Five "corrupts" findings and ten of the "could" findings fixed, each with a test that failed before; the reviewer's recommended test added; the rest listed below. Contract changes (under the standing approval): the log's `participant_ended` reason gains `departed`; the kernel keeps each post's payments on file and hands a new holder every payment as one it has not yet been told of (observation semantics; nothing serialised, so no state hash moves for that); `presence(who=..., leave=yes)` and `occupancy(who=..., leave=yes)` written by a seat are refused in the resolver unless the seat acts in a post (the kernel's blocks and schema are unchanged).

**1. Leaving the world ended nothing (corrupts).** `Block::Leave` vacated spaces only, so a person who left town kept every post and went on acting in it from outside (payroll, tax returns, election notices, a shop's management; a seat beside such a resident parted from its twin for no reason of the seat's). Now their posts fall vacant, and every seat sharing their body ends (`participant_ended`, reason `departed`). Their own participant lives on, for their money and words abroad and for a return (`arrive` with the person: the kernel's existing test holds it). **This is the finding with a price: see "Measured".**

**2. A successor started with an empty memory (corrupts).** An office's knowledge belongs to the office. Payments: the kernel keeps a ledger per (post, organisation) and, when a post changes hands, hands the new holder all of it as payments it has not been told of, so everything a module builds from payments (the rates `settled`/`received`, the landlord's rent book, the retirement fund, `Staffing.paidSince`, lending's `paidOut`/`repaid`) rebuilds with no change to those modules. Records: the electoral office reads where the election stands from its own file (results carry their `poll_at`; a notice or ballot filed for the poll puts it at that stage; 0.7.0), the rates officer reads the day of the last notices and the interest charged from its file (0.4.3), the clerk of an office's books reads the last paper of the books from the file (0.3.1), and an appointer's rotation of looks is a function of the round and the post's name, not a count in its memory (`body.payroll` 0.4.1). Before: a successor on day 200 announced "an election on day 100" and declared a dead nominee elected; a rates successor levied an instalment out of turn and charged interest on a paid notice. **Held by** `participants/test/holder-swap.test.ts`: a fresh holder shown the office's whole file does exactly what the unchanged holder does, for the electoral office at nine swap days and a landlord's rent book at six swap weeks (it fails on the electoral office without the fix). Post changes by departure and death are held by the kernel tests (the post falls vacant; the new holder is handed the office's payments). **Not audited module by module, and not covered by the swap test:** the landlord's other closure state (`renewsAt`, `noticeGiven`, `listedAt`, `lateSince`, `rentChanges`, a building in the making), the retirement fund's `kept`, lending and the rest are only as sound as the payments they are rebuilt from. *Revisit if* a holder-swap run shows a repeat.

**3. A tenant's death (corrupts), partly.** The landlord was told of a death only if the reporter held the lease, so the partner (now leaseholder, with no lease) was told nothing of, the dead tenant was chased for arrears, noticed, taken to the tribunal and ordered out, and the partner "homeless" left town. Now, when a death is on the landlord's record (the registry's entry, or a certified copy), the lease ends by its notice, a new lease on the same terms from when the old one ends is offered to the household member the lease names or the partner the entry names, nothing is asked of the dead (no arrears chase, no notice to vacate, no application for possession), and a pending application is withdrawn (landlord 0.20.0). **It reads papers only.** A first version took the death from who the landlord saw where when it looked; a seat and its code twin part on that (`twin-seat-year`, `twin-draws` failed), as on anything that depends on what a wake happens to see. **What is not fixed:** the landlord is still told only if a reporter knew to name it, and a survivor with no lease does not know whose tenants they were, so the landlord is often not told (see "Measured": possession applications against the dead fell by about a third, not to nothing). The household would have to carry its landlord, or the registry be asked of a tenant who stops paying: a design. **The profiles state no law of succession of tenancy**, so this is the practice (England: a surviving partner living there succeeds; Victoria: a household member may take it over), to be set by a profile when one gives it.

**4. A recorded trade debt could not be paid.** The seller recorded it with a bare `record` call, so the world's answer carried no claim id and the seller sent the payment back as no order's. Bound as `claim` (as the union's is).

**5. A seat confirmed a draft it had never seen.** Draft ids are sequential, so an answer could ask and confirm in one message (a notice "closed for good" was signed for a request "opens at nine"). A confirmation must name a draft in the observation the answer was composed on (`participant.ts`); otherwise it is not taken and the seat is told it will be shown next. Declining is let through. Scripted-adapter test.

**"Could corrupt", fixed:** (6) a look's several searches through one channel are all answered and shown together (two of four answers were lost); (7) a question still out is no longer "Nothing could be seen there"; (8) an office shown no bank account no longer says no payment has been seen leaving it; (9) a founder's capital ("Capital.") is not an order's payment, so it is not refunded or spent on their own orders; (10) no dividend while a debt recorded against the firm stands unpaid; (11) a winding-up pays wages and redundancy owed, then the tax withheld, then suppliers, recorded debts and loans, owners last (**no profile states an insolvency order**; this is the usual one, employees then the collector then other creditors); (14) `ctx.chance` draws name a paper by which such paper it is, as every other draw does, and its keys reach the draw trace; (15) a notice, ballot or result the world refused is put again, so an election cannot stick. (13) *only partly*: a seat acting as itself may take only itself out of the world or out of a place (resolver). The kernel still lets any person act on another, because it keeps no guardianship: a stricter kernel rule refused a parent taking their children out of the world (20 to 26 times a year in the 1,000-person town; newcomers' children have no parents on record) and out of a dwelling (7 to 9), and was taken out. A kernel rule needs a recorded relation of care, a design for Naz.

**Not fixed, and why.** (12) *Deaths outdoors go unregistered, so support is paid to the dead*: nobody sees a death in no building (decisions, "deaths at work"); the fix is an occasion for a finder or a missing-person report, a design, not a patch in the support office. (16) *Home businesses refused `not_at_work` hundreds of times*: cause not confirmed. (17) *Posts of firms and landlords with no one to fill them*: built as the owner's power to appoint, see below; hiring and the estate remain. Minor and left: raw cents and seconds shown to seats, the office's forms listed twice in its prompt (26% of the landlord's), unanswered drafts never expiring, `done_by` re-read at confirm, money building up with the departed, support lost if a payment is refused, `amountText` not checking a whole number, memberships of the dead never ended, the digit-count "matter" heuristic in `drawFor`, two counter maps never pruned. (There is no `docs/risks.md` on main yet; these stand here until there is.)

**Found on the way, and fixed.** (a) Once a leaver's post fell vacant, a tribunal case a landlord had withdrawn left the member's list with no word of it: the clerk of an office's books kept what stood open at its last paper in memory (`office-books-walk.test.ts` failed); it now reads its last paper from the file. (b) Two towns that differ by one watched post found two vacancies in the other order and a day apart, because an appointer rotated its looks by a turn kept in memory, and everyone downstream drew a day apart (`twin-draws.test.ts`, 15,050 draws): the rotation is now the post's name and the round. Both are the departure fix's price: posts now fall vacant and are filled, so what had never mattered did.

**Measured** (code only, a year of the 1,000-person living town, `--set living.initiative_bps=10000`, three run seeds, au-vic and gb-eng; before `ac99bbba`, after this branch; nothing tuned; `oikos diff`, 57 measures):
- *au-vic*: nothing moved beyond three standard errors; appointments 9.7 to 18.3 (z 3.0: more posts to fill). Employment 60.6 to 61.0 per cent of the population, unemployment 0.2 to 0.2.
- *gb-eng*: appointments 8.7 to 29.7 (z 5.1), construction 20.7 to 15.7 (z -4.0), move-ins 33.7 to 16 (z -3.8), unhoused 11.3 to 1.7 (z -3.1). Employment to population 62.4 to 58.2, unemployment 0.13 to 4.2 (not beyond the noise between runs): **seed 1 alone fell from 422 to 340 employed (unemployment 10 per cent); seeds 2 and 3 by 11 and, in the other direction, 1.**
- *Vacancies* (posts vacated per run; still vacant at year end; days vacant summed over posts): au-vic 1/1/0 and 0/0/0 and 1/2/0 before, 8/7/6 and 7/6/6 and 1,768/1,550/1,596 after; gb-eng 8/1/1 and 6/1/1 and 1,762/330/143 before, 25/20/18 and 21/17/15 and 5,382/4,280/3,657 after. What stays vacant: shops' managers and deputies, factories' managers and deputies, the clinic's manager and payroll (au-vic), and **letting offices (15, 10 and 10 in gb-eng)**. **This is finding 1 working, and it exposes finding 17:** before, a shop's or a landlord's owner who left town went on running the business from abroad (the corrupting fault), so nothing needed filling; now the post is vacant and a firm or a landlord on its own account has no authority that fills it (no appointer named, the deputy often gone too), so the business sits (the landlords stop letting, hence the construction, move-ins and employment above). **Settled afterwards (the coordinator's ruling, 2026-10-17, recorded as theirs):** a business does not stop when its owner leaves town. In the real world the owner keeps the business and its property wherever they live (absentee owners and landlords are common) and fills a vacant manager's post by appointing someone, through the ordinary hiring; if the owner has died, the estate (executor or heirs) does; only if no one with that power exists, or the business cannot pay a manager, does it close or get wound up by the ordinary insolvency route. So the appointing authority for a firm's posts is its owner (or the owner's estate), wherever they are; a departed owner acts by letter and pays from the firm's account, no presence needed, and appointing takes their time like any act. **Built** (the same mechanism as the council's `appointed_by`, kept general): every firm with a principal shareholder who is a person of the town has an owner's post (`<firm>-owners`) flagged `holds_abroad` (new position field, schema and kernel: it stays its holder's when they leave the world; every other post falls vacant), run by `body.payroll` 0.5.0 as an owner's appointer, which fills a vacant post of the firm with the owner themselves where none of the staff is left. Test: `owner-appoints.test.ts` (a letting office's holder leaves; the post is filled within 45 days; the office carries on) and a kernel test. **Not built:** hiring for the firm through the ordinary route when the owner would rather not run it, and the estate when the owner dies (the owner's post falls vacant with them, and heirs hold the shares); firms held from outside or by the fund have no owner here. **Re-measured** (same year, three seeds, nothing tuned): gb-eng employment to population 61.3/62.6/62.3 (62.4 before the fixes, 51.1/60.7/62.8 without the owner's power; seed 1 back from 340 to 412 employed), construction 18/22/23 (20.7 before; 15.7 without), au-vic 60.6/61.1/61.2 (60.6 before) and construction 21/21/20; posts still vacant at year end 5/5/1 in gb-eng (21/17/15 without), 3/2/3 in au-vic (7/6/6 without), mostly the clinic's posts and owners' posts whose owner has died.
- *Tenancies after a death*: possession applications against a dead tenant 2/2/3 (au-vic) and 4/3/4 (gb-eng) before, 2/1/2 and 1/2/4 after; orders 2/2/2 and 0/0/1 before, 2/1/1 and 0/0/1 after; warrants 2/2/1 and 0/0/0 before, 2/1/1 and 0/0/0 after. A smaller change than the rule promises, for the reason under finding 3 (the landlord is rarely told). New leases offered to a successor: au-vic 1/0/1, gb-eng 1/0/0.
- Deaths per run are the draws' (au-vic 15/14/13 before, 15/13/15 after; gb-eng 29/31/29 both). Refusals other than races: none new in the version kept (the first, stricter version of finding 13 refused 20 to 26 `not_theirs` a run: children left behind).

**Pins and tests.** The electoral result's `data` gains `poll_at` (one expectation in `elections.test.ts`). `office-books-walk.test.ts` walks 400 days where it was 250: with the findings fixed no case in that town stood with its day come in 250 days, one does in 400, and nothing leaves a list unsaid at either (not narrowed to one finding). `confirming.test.ts` takes `LLM_PARTICIPANT_VERSION` 0.18.2. No state-hash pin moved: the first version of finding 3 moved three (`culture-dial`, `living-dial`, `founding`) and the police-station test, and was taken out for the reason above. Versions: `firm.retailer` 0.16.0, `firm.producer` 0.10.0, `city.rates_officer` 0.4.3, `city.electoral_office` 0.7.0, `firm.landlord` 0.20.0, `office.clerk` 0.3.1, `body.payroll` 0.4.1. `ctx.chance` draws that name a paper follow `stablePurpose`; no pinned town in the fast tier drew one.
